abstract: Patterns of activity over real neural structures are known to exhibit timedependent behavior. It would seem that the brain may be capable of utilizing temporal behavior of activity in neural networks as a way of performing functions which cannot otherwise be easily implemented. These might include the origination of sequential behavior and the recognition of time-dependent stimuli. A model is presented here which uses neuronal populations with recurrent feedback connections in an attempt to observe and describe the resulting time-dependent behavior. Shortcomings and problems inherent to this model are discussed. Current models by other researchers are reviewed and their similarities and differences discussed.

paragraphs: This paper investigates time-dependent activity in neural networks as a possible basis for computation. Its motivation is that real neural structures exhibit changing activity patterns, and the timing of those patterns may help support functions such as producing sequences of behavior or recognizing stimuli that change over time.

The proposed model uses populations of neurons connected through recurrent feedback. Feedback makes earlier activity relevant to later activity, giving the model a way to generate temporal behavior through its own interactions. The authors use this organization to observe and describe the patterns that result, making the evolution of network activity the object of study.

The paper also discusses shortcomings of the model and compares it with models developed by other researchers. Its contribution is an exploration of how recurrent populations behave over time and how that behavior relates to other modeling approaches. The suggested roles in sequential behavior and stimulus recognition supply the motivation; the stated investigation centers on describing the dynamics and examining the model's problems.
summary.tldr: The paper explores time-dependent activity in recurrent neuronal populations as a possible basis for sequence generation and recognition of changing stimuli.

title: Temporal Patterns of Activity in Neural Networks

paragraphs: The paper addresses reinforcement learning and adaptive control when the learner's interface to its environment may be non-Markovian. In such an interface, the current information alone need not provide everything relevant to subsequent behavior. The work also considers online learning through system realization and critics whose outputs are vectors rather than single values.

The proposed algorithm uses two interacting, fully recurrent networks that run continually and may learn in parallel. The formulation connects system realization with the interaction between a model and a controller. Recurrent operation provides an architecture whose ongoing internal state is part of the computation, making temporal behavior central to the design.

The authors introduce adaptive randomness to address difficulties associated with parallel learning. They also describe combining interacting model/controller systems with vector-valued adaptive critics, extending the scalar form used by previous critics. The contribution is an algorithmic treatment of these connected problems: learning during operation, handling an interface that may require history, and supplying a richer form of evaluative feedback.
summary.tldr: Interacting recurrent networks, adaptive randomness, and vector-valued critics form an approach to online control with potentially non-Markovian interfaces.

title: Reinforcement Learning in Markovian and Non-Markovian Environments

paragraphs: This paper modifies backpropagation so that its computations require only shifts and additions. The motivation is practical: multiplication can be costly in hardware, and high numerical precision increases implementation demands. The authors investigate whether training can preserve its effectiveness while using a much simpler arithmetic representation.

The method assigns different representations to different quantities. Network states use floating-point numbers with a one-bit mantissa and three exponent bits, while gradients use a one-bit mantissa and five exponent bits. Weights retain a 16-bit fixed-point representation. This arrangement allows the computations to be performed without multiplication while preserving more precision for the learned weights.

Networks containing more than 100,000 weights were trained with performance matching full-precision networks in the reported demonstrations. Separately, a circuit estimate suggests that a large network could fit on one chip and exceed one billion weight updates per second. That speed is an implementation estimate. The authors also expect a speedup on machines where shifting is faster than multiplication.
summary.tldr: Low-precision representations let backpropagation use shifts and additions while matching full-precision performance in the reported large-network tests.

title: Backpropagation without Multiplication

abstract: We have developed an artificial neural network based gaze tracking system which can be customized to individual users. Unlike other gaze trackers, which normally require the user to wear cumbersome headgear, or to use a chin rest to ensure head immobility, our system is entirely non-intrusive. Currently, the best intrusive gaze tracking systems are accurate to approxi(cid:173) mately 0.75 degrees. In our experiments, we have been able to achieve an accuracy of 1.5 degrees, while allowing head mobility. In this paper we present an empirical analysis of the performance of a large number of artifi(cid:173) cial neural network architectures for this task.

paragraphs: The authors develop a neural-network gaze tracker that can be customized to individual users. Its practical goal is to estimate gaze without requiring cumbersome headgear or a chin rest to keep the head still. Allowing head movement is part of the system's reported operating conditions and an important part of its usability.

The paper includes an empirical comparison of many neural network architectures for this task. This makes network design a central part of the investigation: the authors examine how different architectures perform within the gaze-tracking application. User customization and freedom from physical restraints define the kind of tracking system they are trying to achieve.

The reported experiments reach an angular accuracy of 1.5 degrees while permitting head mobility. The abstract contrasts this with approximately 0.75 degrees for the best intrusive systems it discusses. The result therefore demonstrates a tradeoff between angular accuracy and an unrestricted setup. Its significance is that useful gaze estimation is achieved under conditions that let users move their heads and avoid worn equipment.
summary.tldr: A customizable neural gaze tracker achieves reported accuracy of 1.5 degrees while allowing head movement without intrusive equipment.

title: Non-Intrusive Gaze Tracking Using Artificial Neural Networks

abstract: In integrated service communication networks, an important problem is to exercise call admission control and routing so as to optimally use the network resources. This problem is naturally formulated as a dynamic programming problem, which, however, is too complex to be solved exactly. We use methods of reinforcement learning (RL), together with a decomposition approach, to find call admission control and routing policies. The performance of our policy for a network with approximately 10⁴⁵ different feature configurations is compared with a commonly used heuristic policy.
originalAbstract: In integrated service communication networks, an important problem is to exercise call admission control and routing so as to optimally use the network resources. This problem is naturally formulated as a dynamic programming problem, which, however, is too complex to be solved exactly. We use methods of reinforcement learning (RL), together with a decomposition approach, to find call admission control and routing policies. The performance of our policy for a network with approximately 10⁴⁵ different feature configurations is compared with a commonly used heuristic policy.

paragraphs: A communication network must decide which calls to admit and which routes they should use. These decisions share a common objective: making effective use of limited network resources. The paper treats admission and routing as a sequential decision problem, where a choice about one call affects the resources available for subsequent traffic.

Dynamic programming provides a natural formulation, but solving that formulation exactly is too complex for the network considered. The authors instead combine reinforcement learning with a decomposition approach to obtain decision policies. Decomposition breaks the overall problem into more manageable parts, while reinforcement learning supplies a method for learning how to make decisions within that approach.

The policy is evaluated on a network with approximately 10^45 different feature configurations and compared with a commonly used heuristic. The stated scale explains why exact enumeration is impractical and why approximate policy methods are relevant. The abstract establishes the comparison without specifying its outcome. The contribution is the application of learning and decomposition to the coupled resource-allocation decisions.
summary.tldr: Reinforcement learning and decomposition provide call-admission and routing policies for a network too complex for exact dynamic programming.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Call Admission Control and Routing in Integrated Service Networks

abstract: We propose and analyze a class of actor-critic algorithms for simulation-based optimization of a Markov decision process over a parameterized family of randomized stationary policies. These are two-time-scale algorithms in which the critic uses TD learning with a linear approximation architecture and the actor is updated in an approximate gradient direction based on information pro(cid:173) vided by the critic. We show that the features for the critic should span a subspace prescribed by the choice of parameterization of the actor. We conclude by discussing convergence properties and some open problems.
originalAbstract: We propose and analyze a class of actor-critic algorithms for simulation-based optimization of a Markov decision process over a parameterized family of randomized stationary policies. These are two-time-scale algorithms in which the critic uses TD learning with a linear approximation architecture and the actor is updated in an approximate gradient direction based on information pro(cid:173) vided by the critic. We show that the features for the critic should span a subspace prescribed by the choice of parameterization of the actor. We conclude by discussing convergence properties and some open problems.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to improve a decision-making policy using simulated experience from a Markov decision process. It considers a parameterized family of randomized, stationary policies: the controller can choose actions probabilistically, while its decision rule does not explicitly change with time. The goal is to optimize within that family.

The proposed algorithms divide the work between an actor and a critic. The critic uses temporal-difference learning and a linear approximation to supply information about policy quality. The actor uses that information to move approximately in a direction of improvement. These components learn on two different timescales, making their interaction part of the algorithmic design.

A central finding concerns how to choose the critic's features. They should span a particular subspace determined by the actor's parameterization. This connects the critic's representation directly to the actor's optimization needs. The paper also discusses convergence properties and unresolved questions, rather than claiming an unrestricted convergence guarantee.
summary.tldr: Actor-critic optimization benefits from choosing critic features that match the actor's policy parameterization.

title: Actor-Critic Algorithms

abstract: Prior knowledge in the form of multiple polyhedral sets, each be(cid:173) longing to one of two categories, is introduced into a reformulation of a linear support vector machine classifier. The resulting formu(cid:173) lation leads to a linear program that can be solved efficiently. Real world examples, from DNA sequencing and breast cancer prognosis, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Numerical results show improvement in test set accuracy after the incorpo(cid:173) ration of prior knowledge into ordinary, data-based linear support vector machine classifiers. One experiment also shows that a lin(cid:173) ear classifier, based solely on prior knowledge, far outperforms the direct application of prior knowledge rules to classify data. Keywords: use and refinement of prior knowledge, sup(cid:173) port vector machines, linear programming

paragraphs: A classifier can receive information from labeled examples and from prior knowledge about which inputs belong to each category. This paper incorporates such knowledge into a linear support vector machine. The knowledge is expressed as multiple polyhedral regions, each associated with one of the two classes, giving it a geometric form the classifier can use.

The authors reformulate the learning problem so that incorporating these regions leads to a linear program that can be solved efficiently. This provides a direct route from structured prior knowledge to a learned decision boundary. It also makes it possible to refine how the supplied knowledge is applied through the classifier formulation.

Examples involving DNA sequencing and breast cancer prognosis demonstrate the method, with reported improvements in test accuracy after prior knowledge is added. In one experiment, a linear classifier built solely from prior knowledge substantially outperforms direct application of the corresponding rules. That finding shows that the form in which knowledge is used can matter, alongside whether training examples are available.
summary.tldr: Encoding prior knowledge as class-associated geometric regions improves linear SVM test accuracy in the reported applications.

title: Knowledge-Based Support Vector Machine Classifiers

abstract: Given a directed graph in which some of the nodes are labeled, we inves- tigate the question of how to exploit the link structure of the graph to infer the labels of the remaining unlabeled nodes. To that extent we propose a regularization framework for functions de(cid:2)ned over nodes of a directed graph that forces the classi(cid:2)cation function to change slowly on densely linked subgraphs. A powerful, yet computationally simple classi(cid:2)cation algorithm is derived within the proposed framework. The experimental evaluation on real-world Web classi(cid:2)cation problems demonstrates en- couraging results that validate our approach.

paragraphs: The paper considers a directed graph in which labels are known for only some nodes. The goal is to infer the remaining labels by using the links between nodes. This is a semi-supervised problem because labeled examples and the structure connecting unlabeled examples both contribute information to the classifier.

The authors propose a regularization framework for prediction functions defined on the graph's nodes. It encourages those functions to vary slowly within densely linked subgraphs. The guiding idea is that strong local connectivity should influence how predictions fit together, allowing the graph to constrain possible classifications beyond what the labeled nodes alone would determine.

From this framework, the authors derive a classification algorithm described as computationally simple. They evaluate it on real-world web classification problems and report encouraging results supporting the approach. The contribution is both a formulation of smooth prediction over directed graphs and an associated practical algorithm, connecting the structure of directed links to the task of learning from incomplete labeling.
summary.tldr: A graph regularization method infers missing labels by encouraging similar predictions within densely linked regions of a directed graph.

title: Semi-supervised Learning on Directed Graphs

abstract: Can we leverage learning techniques to build a fast nearest-neighbor (NN) retrieval data structure? We present a general learning framework for the NN problem in which sample queries are used to learn the parameters of a data structure that minimize the retrieval time and/or the miss rate. We explore the potential of this novel framework through two popular NN data structures: KD-trees and the rectilinear structures employed by locality sensitive hashing. We derive a generalization theory for these data structure classes and present simple learning algorithms for both. Experimental results reveal that learning often improves on the already strong performance of these data structures.
originalAbstract: Can we leverage learning techniques to build a fast nearest-neighbor (NN) retrieval data structure? We present a general learning framework for the NN problem in which sample queries are used to learn the parameters of a data structure that minimize the retrieval time and/or the miss rate. We explore the potential of this novel framework through two popular NN data structures: KD-trees and the rectilinear structures employed by locality sensitive hashing. We derive a generalization theory for these data structure classes and present simple learning algorithms for both. Experimental results reveal that learning often improves on the already strong performance of these data structures.

paragraphs: The paper treats the construction of a nearest-neighbor search structure as a learning problem. Instead of choosing its parameters without observing how it will be queried, the proposed framework uses sample queries as training evidence. The goal is to configure the structure so that retrieval is faster, misses are less frequent, or both objectives improve.

The authors develop this idea for two established families: KD-trees and the rectilinear structures used in locality-sensitive hashing. They provide simple learning algorithms for both families. This makes the proposal more concrete than a general suggestion to tune search systems: it identifies existing structures whose parameters can be learned from examples of their intended use.

The paper also derives generalization theory for these classes of data structures, addressing the connection between performance on sample queries and performance beyond those samples. Experiments show that learning often improves the already strong performance of the underlying structures. The qualification matters: the reported benefit is frequent improvement, not a claim that learned configurations always outperform their alternatives.
summary.tldr: Learning search-structure parameters from sample queries often improves nearest-neighbor retrieval time or miss rate.

title: A learning framework for nearest neighbor search

abstract: We present a simple new Monte Carlo algorithm for evaluating probabilities of observations in complex latent variable models, such as Deep Belief Networks. While the method is based on Markov chains, estimates based on short runs are formally unbiased. In expectation, the log probability of a test set will be underestimated, and this could form the basis of a probabilistic bound. The method is much cheaper than gold-standard annealing-based methods and only slightly more expensive than the cheapest Monte Carlo methods. We give examples of the new method substantially improving simple variational bounds at modest extra cost.
originalAbstract: We present a simple new Monte Carlo algorithm for evaluating probabilities of observations in complex latent variable models, such as Deep Belief Networks. While the method is based on Markov chains, estimates based on short runs are formally unbiased. In expectation, the log probability of a test set will be underestimated, and this could form the basis of a probabilistic bound. The method is much cheaper than gold-standard annealing-based methods and only slightly more expensive than the cheapest Monte Carlo methods. We give examples of the new method substantially improving simple variational bounds at modest extra cost.

paragraphs: Assessing a latent-variable model requires determining how much probability it assigns to observed data, even though some of its variables are hidden. This calculation can be difficult for complex models such as deep belief networks. The paper introduces a Monte Carlo algorithm designed to make that evaluation less expensive.

The method uses Markov chains, yet probability estimates from short runs are formally unbiased. That property is distinct from the behavior of their logarithms: the estimated log probability of a test set is too low in expectation. The authors suggest that this expected underestimation could support a probabilistic bound; they do not describe every individual estimate as a guaranteed lower bound.

The proposed method costs much less than gold-standard approaches based on annealing and only slightly more than the cheapest Monte Carlo alternatives. Examples show substantial improvements over simple variational bounds for modest extra computation. The contribution is therefore a way to obtain stronger probability evaluations without paying the full computational cost of the more expensive reference methods.
summary.tldr: A low-cost Monte Carlo method gives unbiased probability estimates from short Markov-chain runs and improves example variational bounds.

title: Evaluating probabilities under high-dimensional latent variable models

abstract: Many interesting problems, including Bayesian network structure-search, can be cast in terms of finding the optimum value of a function over the space of graphs. However, this function is often expensive to compute exactly. We here present a method derived from the study of reproducing-kernel Hilbert spaces which takes advantage of the regular structure of the space of all graphs on a fixed number of nodes to obtain approximations to the desired function quickly and with reasonable accuracy. We then test this method on both a small testing set and a real-world Bayesian network; the results suggest that not only is this method reasonably accurate, but that the BDe score itself varies quadratically over the space of all graphs.
originalAbstract: Many interesting problems, including Bayesian network structure-search, can be cast in terms of finding the optimum value of a function over the space of graphs. However, this function is often expensive to compute exactly. We here present a method derived from the study of reproducing-kernel Hilbert spaces which takes advantage of the regular structure of the space of all graphs on a fixed number of nodes to obtain approximations to the desired function quickly and with reasonable accuracy. We then test this method on both a small testing set and a real-world Bayesian network; the results suggest that not only is this method reasonably accurate, but that the BDe score itself varies quadratically over the space of all graphs.

paragraphs: Searching for a Bayesian network structure can be viewed as optimizing a score over candidate graphs. The difficulty addressed here is that evaluating this score exactly can be expensive. The paper studies how to approximate a function defined on graphs, making score evaluation a more practical part of searching through possible structures.

The method draws on reproducing-kernel Hilbert spaces and exploits regularity in the collection of all graphs with a fixed number of nodes. Rather than treating each candidate graph as an unrelated object, it uses the structure of that collection to obtain function approximations quickly and with reasonable accuracy. The fixed node count defines the graph space considered by the approach.

Tests on a small testing set and a real-world Bayesian network suggest that the approximations are reasonably accurate. The results also suggest that the BDe score varies quadratically across graph space. This second observation is an empirical suggestion, rather than an established universal property, and points to potentially useful structure in the scoring function itself.
summary.tldr: A kernel method exploits the structure of graph space to approximate expensive Bayesian network scores quickly and reasonably accurately.

title: Bayesian Network Score Approximation using a Metagraph Kernel

abstract: We investigate a topic at the interface of machine learning and cognitive science. Human active learning, where learners can actively query the world for information, is contrasted with passive learning from random examples. Furthermore, we compare human active learning performance with predictions from statistical learning theory. We conduct a series of human category learning experiments inspired by a machine learning task for which active and passive learning error bounds are well understood, and dramatically distinct. Our results indicate that humans are capable of actively selecting informative queries, and in doing so learn better and faster than if they are given random training data, as predicted by learning theory. However, the improvement over passive learning is not as dramatic as that achieved by machine active learning algorithms. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first quantitative study comparing human category learning in active versus passive settings.

Furthermore, we compare human active learning performance with predictions from statistical learning theory. We conduct a series of human category learning experiments inspired by a machine learning task for which active and passive learning error bounds are well understood, and dramatically distinct. paragraphs: The paper asks whether people learn categories more effectively when they choose which examples to investigate. This active setting is compared with passive learning, where examples arrive randomly. The question connects cognitive science with machine learning: choosing useful questions could improve learning beyond what is possible from simply receiving more arbitrary examples.

The authors conduct human category-learning experiments inspired by a machine-learning task with well-understood, sharply different error bounds for active and passive learning. This choice supplies a theoretical reference for interpreting human performance. The experiments assess both whether people select informative queries and whether that selection translates into better learning.

The results indicate that people can choose informative queries and learn better and faster than participants given random training data. The direction of the advantage agrees with learning theory, but its size is less dramatic than for machine active-learning algorithms. The study therefore offers quantitative evidence for a human benefit from active information gathering while preserving a distinction between human performance and algorithmic gains.
summary.tldr: People learn categories better by choosing informative examples, although their gains are smaller than those of machine active-learning algorithms.

title: Human Active Learning

abstract: Kernel density estimation is the most widely-used practical method for accurate nonparametric density estimation. However, long-standing worst-case theoretical results showing that its performance worsens exponentially with the dimension of the data have quashed its application to modern high-dimensional datasets for decades. In practice, it has been recognized that often such data have a much lower-dimensional intrinsic structure. We propose a small modification to kernel density estimation for estimating probability density functions on Riemannian submanifolds of Euclidean space. Using ideas from Riemannian geometry, we prove the consistency of this modified estimator and show that the convergence rate is determined by the intrinsic dimension of the submanifold. We conclude with empirical results demonstrating the behavior predicted by our theory.
originalAbstract: Kernel density estimation is the most widely-used practical method for accurate nonparametric density estimation. However, long-standing worst-case theoretical results showing that its performance worsens exponentially with the dimension of the data have quashed its application to modern high-dimensional datasets for decades. In practice, it has been recognized that often such data have a much lower-dimensional intrinsic structure. We propose a small modification to kernel density estimation for estimating probability density functions on Riemannian submanifolds of Euclidean space. Using ideas from Riemannian geometry, we prove the consistency of this modified estimator and show that the convergence rate is determined by the intrinsic dimension of the submanifold. We conclude with empirical results demonstrating the behavior predicted by our theory.

paragraphs: Kernel density estimation describes where observations are concentrated without choosing a fixed parametric distribution. Its worst-case performance deteriorates severely as dimension increases. This paper considers a more structured setting: observations occupy a lower-dimensional Riemannian submanifold inside a higher-dimensional Euclidean space, so the number of recorded coordinates can exceed the data's intrinsic dimension.

The authors propose a small modification of kernel density estimation for this setting. Using Riemannian geometry, they prove that the modified estimator is consistent and that its convergence rate depends on the submanifold's intrinsic dimension. The geometric structure is therefore central to the result, determining the dimension that governs statistical convergence.

Empirical results demonstrate behavior predicted by the theory. The significance is that high ambient dimension does not by itself determine the estimator's rate in the studied setting. When the data satisfy the submanifold formulation, the analysis captures their lower-dimensional structure and provides a theoretical basis for density estimation that reflects that structure.
summary.tldr: A modified kernel density estimator has consistency and convergence rates governed by a submanifold's intrinsic dimension.

title: Submanifold density estimation

abstract: Dependencies among neighbouring labels in a sequence is an important source of information for sequence labeling problems. However, only dependencies between adjacent labels are commonly exploited in practice because of the high computational complexity of typical inference algorithms when longer distance dependencies are taken into account. In this paper, we show that it is possible to design efficient inference algorithms for a conditional random field using features that depend on long consecutive label sequences (high-order features), as long as the number of distinct label sequences in the features used is small. This leads to efficient learning algorithms for these conditional random fields. We show experimentally that exploiting dependencies using high-order features can lead to substantial performance improvements for some problems and discuss conditions under which high-order features can be effective.
originalAbstract: Dependencies among neighbouring labels in a sequence is an important source of information for sequence labeling problems. However, only dependencies between adjacent labels are commonly exploited in practice because of the high computational complexity of typical inference algorithms when longer distance dependencies are taken into account. In this paper, we show that it is possible to design efficient inference algorithms for a conditional random field using features that depend on long consecutive label sequences (high-order features), as long as the number of distinct label sequences in the features used is small. This leads to efficient learning algorithms for these conditional random fields. We show experimentally that exploiting dependencies using high-order features can lead to substantial performance improvements for some problems and discuss conditions under which high-order features can be effective.

paragraphs: Sequence labeling assigns labels to positions in an ordered input, and relationships among nearby labels can help determine the right assignments. In practice, models often use only adjacent-label dependencies because incorporating longer sequences makes standard inference expensive. This computational obstacle limits the patterns that a model can conveniently exploit.

The paper shows how a conditional random field can support features that depend on long consecutive sequences of labels while retaining efficient inference. The key condition is that the features involve only a small number of distinct label sequences. Thus, long patterns need not automatically make computation impractical; the variety of patterns represented also matters.

Efficient inference in turn enables efficient learning for these models. Experiments show that high-order features can produce substantial improvements on some problems, and the paper discusses when such features are effective. The contribution provides a conditional route to using richer label dependencies, with benefits tied to the structure of the features and the problem being solved.
summary.tldr: CRFs can efficiently use long label-sequence features when those features contain only a small number of distinct patterns.

title: Conditional Random Fields with High-Order Features for Sequence Labeling

abstract: The nested Chinese restaurant process (nCRP) is a powerful nonparametric Bayesian model for learning tree-based hierarchies from data. Since its posterior distribution is intractable, current inference methods have all relied on MCMC sampling. In this paper, we develop an alternative inference technique based on variational methods. To employ variational methods, we derive a tree-based stick-breaking construction of the nCRP mixture model, and a novel variational algorithm that efficiently explores a posterior over a large set of combinatorial structures. We demonstrate the use of this approach for text and hand written digits modeling, where we show we can adapt the nCRP to continuous data as well.

Since its posterior distribution is intractable, current inference methods have all relied on MCMC sampling. In this paper, we develop an alternative inference technique based on variational methods. To employ variational methods, we derive a tree-based stick-breaking construction of the nCRP mixture model, and a novel variational algorithm that efficiently explores a posterior over a large set of combinatorial structures. We demonstrate the use of this approach for text and hand written digits modeling, where we show we can adapt the nCRP to continuous data as well.

paragraphs: The nested Chinese restaurant process is a nonparametric Bayesian model for learning tree-shaped hierarchies from data. Its posterior distribution is intractable, so learning requires an inference method that can handle uncertainty over possible structures. The authors note that existing methods had relied on Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling.

This paper develops a variational alternative. To make that possible, the authors derive a tree-based stick-breaking construction of the mixture model. This provides a representation suited to the new inference procedure. Their variational algorithm efficiently explores a posterior over a large collection of combinatorial structures, addressing the challenge of reasoning over many possible hierarchies.

The method is demonstrated on text and handwritten-digit modeling, and the authors show that the nested Chinese restaurant process can also be adapted to continuous data. The contribution is thus a new computational route for hierarchical Bayesian modeling, supported by a representation that enables variational inference. The applications illustrate its use across different data types while retaining the tree-based structure at the center of the model.
summary.tldr: A tree-based stick-breaking construction enables variational inference for the nested Chinese restaurant process, with text and handwritten-digit applications.

title: Variational Inference for the Nested Chinese Restaurant Process

abstract: A new Le ́vy process prior is proposed for an uncountable collection of covariate- dependent feature-learning measures; the model is called the kernel beta process (KBP). Available covariates are handled efficiently via the kernel construction, with covariates assumed observed with each data sample (“customer”), and latent covariates learned for each feature (“dish”). Each customer selects dishes from an infinite buffet, in a manner analogous to the beta process, with the added constraint that a customer first decides probabilistically whether to “consider” a dish, based on the distance in covariate space between the customer and dish. If a customer does consider a particular dish, that dish is then selected probabilistically as in the beta process. The beta process is recovered as a limiting case of the KBP. An efficient Gibbs sampler is developed for computations, and state-of-the-art results are presented for image processing and music analysis tasks.

paragraphs: The kernel beta process extends feature learning so that feature availability depends on covariates associated with each observation. The model assumes those observation-level covariates are known and learns latent covariates for the features. A kernel connects these quantities, giving a covariate-dependent family of feature-learning measures.

The paper explains selection through an infinite-buffet analogy. An observation first decides probabilistically whether to consider a feature, based on their distance in covariate space. If it considers that feature, a second probabilistic step determines whether to select it. The ordinary beta process is recovered as a limiting case of this construction.

This two-stage mechanism allows contextual information to influence which features are considered while retaining probabilistic feature selection. The authors develop an efficient Gibbs sampler for computation and report state-of-the-art results on image-processing and music-analysis tasks. These findings provide empirical support for the model in the evaluated applications, alongside its formal connection to the beta process.
summary.tldr: The kernel beta process uses covariate-dependent consideration and selection steps to learn features, with strong reported image and music results.

title: The Kernel Beta Process

abstract: Expectation Propagation (EP) is a popular approximate posterior inference algorithm that often provides a fast and accurate alternative to sampling-based methods. However, while the EP framework in theory allows for complex non-Gaussian factors, there is still a significant practical barrier to using them within EP, because doing so requires the implementation of message update operators, which can be difficult and require hand-crafted approximations. In this work, we study the question of whether it is possible to automatically derive fast and accurate EP updates by learning a discriminative model e.g., a neural network or random forest) to map EP message inputs to EP message outputs. We address the practical concerns that arise in the process, and we provide empirical analysis on several challenging and diverse factors, indicating that there is a space of factors where this approach appears promising.

paragraphs: Expectation propagation approximates posterior distributions by passing and updating messages. Although its framework permits complex non-Gaussian factors, using those factors in practice requires implementing suitable message-update operators. These operators can be difficult to derive and may depend on handcrafted approximations, creating a barrier between the framework's flexibility and its practical use.

The paper investigates whether a learned discriminative model can supply the update instead. Its input is an incoming collection of expectation-propagation messages, and its output is the corresponding outgoing message. Neural networks and random forests are examples of models considered for this mapping. The aim is to obtain updates that are both fast and accurate while automating part of the factor-specific implementation work.

The authors address practical issues arising from this strategy and evaluate it on several diverse, challenging factors. Their empirical conclusion is deliberately qualified: there appears to be a range of factors for which learned updates are promising. The work establishes a direction for automating approximate inference rather than a universal replacement for manually designed message operators.
summary.tldr: Learning expectation-propagation message updates with discriminative models appears promising for some challenging factors that otherwise require handcrafted operators.

title: Learning to Pass Expectation Propagation Messages

abstract: Detecting the emergence of an abrupt change-point is a classic problem in statistics and machine learning. Kernel-based nonparametric statistics have been proposed for this task which make fewer assumptions on the distributions than traditional parametric approach. However, none of the existing kernel statistics has provided a computationally efficient way to characterize the extremal behavior of the statistic. Such characterization is crucial for setting the detection threshold, to control the significance level in the offline case as well as the average run length in the online case. In this paper we propose two related computationally efficient M-statistics for kernel-based change-point detection when the amount of background data is large. A novel theoretical result of the paper is the characterization of the tail probability of these statistics using a new technique based on change-of-measure. Such characterization provides us accurate detection thresholds for both offline and online cases in computationally efficient manner, without the need to resort to the more expensive simulations such as bootstrapping. We show that our methods perform well in both synthetic and real world data.

paragraphs: Change-point detection seeks to identify abrupt shifts in data. Kernel-based methods can do this with fewer distributional assumptions than traditional parametric approaches, but choosing a detection threshold requires understanding how extreme the statistic can become. The paper targets the computational difficulty of obtaining that information, particularly when a large amount of background data is available.

The authors introduce two related M-statistics and characterize their tail probabilities using a new change-of-measure technique. Tail probabilities describe how likely unusually large statistic values are. This characterization provides an efficient way to calculate accurate thresholds without relying on more expensive simulation procedures such as bootstrapping.

The thresholds serve related but distinct purposes in the two detection settings. Offline, they help control the significance level when examining a collected dataset. Online, they support control of average run length while monitoring incoming observations. The authors report good performance on synthetic and real-world data. The contribution joins kernel-based detection with a computationally practical method for calibrating its decisions.
summary.tldr: Two kernel M-statistics use theoretical tail-probability calculations to set efficient offline and online change-detection thresholds.

title: M-Statistic for Kernel Change-Point Detection

abstract: We present discriminative Gaifman models, a novel family of relational machine learning models. Gaifman models learn feature representations bottom up from representations of locally connected and bounded-size regions of knowledge bases (KBs). Considering local and bounded-size neighborhoods of knowledge bases renders logical inference and learning tractable, mitigates the problem of overfitting, and facilitates weight sharing. Gaifman models sample neighborhoods of knowledge bases so as to make the learned relational models more robust to missing objects and relations which is a common situation in open-world KBs. We present the core ideas of Gaifman models and apply them to large-scale relational learning problems. We also discuss the ways in which Gaifman models relate to some existing relational machine learning approaches.

paragraphs: Knowledge bases describe objects and the relations among them, making prediction depend on connected information rather than isolated records. The paper introduces discriminative Gaifman models, a family of relational learning models that builds representations from local regions of a knowledge base. Those regions are connected and limited in size.

The model learns feature representations from these bounded neighborhoods and builds upward from them. Restricting the amount of relational structure considered at once makes logical inference and learning tractable. The authors also identify reduced overfitting and easier weight sharing as benefits. Locality is therefore both a computational choice and a way to organize what the model learns.

Gaifman models sample neighborhoods to improve robustness when objects or relations are missing, a common feature of open-world knowledge bases. Sampling makes incomplete local views part of the modeling approach. The paper presents the core construction, applies it to large-scale relational learning problems, and discusses connections with existing relational methods, emphasizing learning from manageable pieces of a larger knowledge structure.
summary.tldr: Gaifman models learn from sampled, bounded knowledge-base neighborhoods to make relational learning tractable and more robust to missing information.

title: Discriminative Gaifman Models

abstract: We consider the problem of learning causal structures with latent variables using interventions. Our objective is not only to learn the causal graph between the observed variables, but to locate unobserved variables that could confound the relationship between observables. Our approach is stage-wise: We first learn the observable graph, i.e., the induced graph between observable variables. Next we learn the existence and location of the latent variables given the observable graph. We propose an efficient randomized algorithm that can learn the observable graph using O(d\log^2 n) interventions where d is the degree of the graph. We further propose an efficient deterministic variant which uses O(log n + l) interventions, where l is the longest directed path in the graph. Next, we propose an algorithm that uses only O(d^2 log n) interventions that can learn the latents between both non-adjacent and adjacent variables. While a naive baseline approach would require O(n^2) interventions, our combined algorithm can learn the causal graph with latents using O(d log^2 n + d^2 log (n)) interventions.

paragraphs: Learning causal relationships becomes harder when unobserved variables can influence multiple observed variables. This paper studies how to choose interventions to recover both the relationships among observables and the existence and location of latent variables that could confound them. Its main concern is how many interventions that recovery requires.

The approach separates discovery into stages. It first learns the graph induced among observed variables, then uses that graph to find latent variables. For the first stage, a randomized algorithm uses O(d log² n) interventions, where d is graph degree. A deterministic alternative uses O(log n + l), where l is the longest directed path.

The latent-discovery algorithm uses O(d² log n) interventions and handles latent variables between both adjacent and nonadjacent observed variables. Combining it with the randomized first stage gives O(d log² n + d² log n) interventions, compared with O(n²) for the stated naive baseline. The bounds show how graph structure, especially degree, shapes the intervention requirement rather than making it depend only on the number of variables.
summary.tldr: A staged intervention strategy learns observable causal structure and locates latent confounders with intervention bounds depending on graph structure.

title: Experimental Design for Learning Causal Graphs with Latent Variables

abstract: In order for machine learning to garner widespread public adoption, models must be able to provide interpretable and robust explanations for their decisions, as well as learn from human-provided explanations at train time. In this work, we extend the Stanford Natural Language Inference dataset with an additional layer of human-annotated natural language explanations of the entailment relations. We further implement models that incorporate these explanations into their training process and output them at test time. We show how our corpus of explanations, which we call e-SNLI, can be used for various goals, such as obtaining full sentence justifications of a model’s decisions, improving universal sentence representations and transferring to out-of-domain NLI datasets. Our dataset thus opens up a range of research directions for using natural language explanations, both for improving models and for asserting their trust

paragraphs: Natural language inference involves judging how the meaning of one sentence relates to another. A prediction alone leaves the reasoning behind that judgment unstated. This paper extends the Stanford Natural Language Inference dataset with human-written explanations of the entailment relations, creating an additional source of information for both training and examining models.

The resulting dataset, e-SNLI, supports models that incorporate explanations during training and produce explanations when making predictions. Human explanations therefore serve two purposes: they provide learning material beyond the original labels, and they make it possible to study systems that express justifications in complete sentences.

The authors demonstrate uses spanning sentence-level justifications, improved general-purpose sentence representations, and transfer to inference datasets outside the original domain. These findings position explanations as potentially useful training signals as well as outputs for people to inspect. The contribution creates opportunities to investigate model quality and trust through language, rather than establishing that generating an explanation alone makes a model trustworthy.
summary.tldr: e-SNLI adds human-written explanations to natural language inference data and demonstrates their use in training and explaining models.

title: e-SNLI: Natural Language Inference with Natural Language Explanations

abstract: In this work, we address the problem of modifying textual attributes of sentences. Given an input sentence and a set of attribute labels, we attempt to generate sentences that are compatible with the conditioning information. To ensure that the model generates content compatible sentences, we introduce a reconstruction loss which interpolates between auto-encoding and back-translation loss components. We propose an adversarial loss to enforce generated samples to be attribute compatible and realistic. Through quantitative, qualitative and human evaluations we demonstrate that our model is capable of generating fluent sentences that better reflect the conditioning information compared to prior methods. We further demonstrate that the model is capable of simultaneously controlling multiple attributes.

We propose an adversarial loss to enforce generated samples to be attribute compatible and realistic. paragraphs: This paper studies sentence rewriting with explicit control over textual attributes. The model receives an original sentence together with attribute labels and attempts to produce a sentence that fits both. The challenge is to satisfy the requested attributes while retaining compatible content, rather than allowing the controls to overwhelm what the original sentence says.

The authors address these requirements through two training objectives. A reconstruction loss interpolates between auto-encoding and back-translation components, supplying pressure to preserve content. An adversarial loss encourages generated sentences to match the requested attributes and resemble realistic text. Together, these objectives connect preservation of the input with the desired properties of the output.

Quantitative measurements, qualitative examples, and human evaluations show that the model generates fluent sentences that reflect the conditioning information better than prior methods. The authors also demonstrate simultaneous control of multiple attributes. This extends the task beyond adjusting one property at a time and provides evidence that several requested changes can be coordinated within a single generation process.
summary.tldr: Combining reconstruction and adversarial losses enables fluent sentence rewriting that preserves compatible content while controlling multiple attributes.

title: Content preserving text generation with attribute controls

abstract: Training deep neural networks requires an exorbitant amount of computation resources, including a heterogeneous mix of GPU and CPU devices. It is critical to place operations in a neural network on these devices in an optimal way, so that the training process can complete within the shortest amount of time. The state-of-the-art uses reinforcement learning to learn placement skills by repeatedly performing Monte-Carlo experiments. However, due to its equal treatment of placement samples, we argue that there remains ample room for significant improvements. In this paper, we propose a new joint learning algorithm, called Post, that integrates cross-entropy minimization and proximal policy optimization to achieve theoretically guaranteed optimal efficiency. In order to incorporate the cross-entropy method as a sampling technique, we propose to represent placements using discrete probability distributions, which allows us to estimate an optimal probability mass by maximal likelihood estimation, a powerful tool with the best possible efficiency. We have implemented Post in the Google Cloud platform, and our extensive experiments with several popular neural network training benchmarks have demonstrated clear evidence of superior performance: with the same amount of learning time, it leads to placements that have training times up to 63.7% shorter over the state-of-the-art.

summary.tldr: Post combines probabilistic sampling and policy optimization to find device placements with up to 63.7% shorter training times in reported benchmarks.

title: Post: Device Placement with Cross-Entropy Minimization and Proximal Policy Optimization

abstract: Huge scale machine learning problems are nowadays tackled by distributed optimization algorithms, i.e. algorithms that leverage the compute power of many devices for training. The communication overhead is a key bottleneck that hinders perfect scalability. Various recent works proposed to use quantization or sparsification techniques to reduce the amount of data that needs to be communicated, for instance by only sending the most significant entries of the stochastic gradient (top-k sparsification). Whilst such schemes showed very promising performance in practice, they have eluded theoretical analysis so far. In this work we analyze Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with k-sparsification or compression (for instance top-k or random-k) and show that this scheme converges at the same rate as vanilla SGD when equipped with error compensation (keeping track of accumulated errors in memory). That is, communication can be reduced by a factor of the dimension of the problem (sometimes even more) whilst still converging at the same rate. We present numerical experiments to illustrate the theoretical findings and the good scalability for distributed applications.

paragraphs: Distributed training can be limited by communication between devices rather than by computation alone. Sending only a few gradient entries reduces that traffic, but it also leaves information out of each update. This paper analyzes sparse or compressed stochastic gradient descent, including strategies that keep the largest entries or select entries randomly.

The central addition is memory that records accumulated compression errors. With this error compensation, the authors show that the analyzed scheme converges at the same rate as ordinary SGD. Remembering omitted information is therefore essential to the stated result: the guarantee applies to compression equipped with compensation, rather than compression considered on its own.

The analysis shows that communication can be reduced by a factor equal to the problem's dimension, and sometimes more, while retaining the convergence rate. Numerical experiments illustrate the theoretical findings and good scalability in distributed applications. The contribution gives theoretical support to a practical communication-saving strategy, explaining how retaining compression errors can preserve optimization progress even when each transmitted update is much smaller.
summary.tldr: Remembering accumulated compression errors lets sparsified SGD retain ordinary SGD's convergence rate while sharply reducing communication.

title: Sparsified SGD with Memory

abstract: Navigating through unstructured environments is a basic capability of intelligent creatures, and thus is of fundamental interest in the study and development of artificial intelligence. Long-range navigation is a complex cognitive task that relies on developing an internal representation of space, grounded by recognisable landmarks and robust visual processing, that can simultaneously support continuous self-localisation ("I am here") and a representation of the goal ("I am going there"). Building upon recent research that applies deep reinforcement learning to maze navigation problems, we present an end-to-end deep reinforcement learning approach that can be applied on a city scale. Recognising that successful navigation relies on integration of general policies with locale-specific knowledge, we propose a dual pathway architecture that allows locale-specific features to be encapsulated, while still enabling transfer to multiple cities. A key contribution of this paper is an interactive navigation environment that uses Google Street View for its photographic content and worldwide coverage. Our baselines demonstrate that deep reinforcement learning agents can learn to navigate in multiple cities and to traverse to target destinations that may be kilometres away. A video summarizing our research and showing the trained agent in diverse city environments as well as on the transfer task is available at: https://sites.google.com/view/learn-navigate-cities-nips18

paragraphs: Long-range visual navigation requires an agent to connect what it sees with both its current location and its destination. This paper develops an end-to-end deep reinforcement learning approach for navigation at city scale. It builds on earlier maze-navigation work while addressing the need to combine general navigation behavior with knowledge of a particular place.

The proposed architecture has two pathways that allow locale-specific features to be encapsulated while supporting transfer across cities. This organization reflects the fact that some navigation knowledge concerns a particular environment and some can be useful elsewhere. The paper also introduces an interactive environment using Google Street View photographs and its worldwide coverage.

The reported baselines demonstrate that reinforcement learning agents can learn to navigate in multiple cities and reach destinations potentially kilometres away. These results establish city-scale navigation capability within the photographic environment used for the study. The combined contribution is an architecture for separating local knowledge from transferable behavior and an environment in which long-distance urban navigation can be learned and evaluated.
summary.tldr: A dual-pathway reinforcement learning architecture learns city-scale visual navigation in a Street View environment and supports transfer across cities.

title: Learning to Navigate in Cities Without a Map

abstract: Bayesian inference in state-space models is challenging due to high-dimensional state trajectories. A viable approach is particle Markov chain Monte Carlo (PMCMC), combining MCMC and sequential Monte Carlo to form ``exact approximations'' to otherwise-intractable MCMC methods. The performance of the approximation is limited to that of the exact method. We focus on particle Gibbs (PG) and particle Gibbs with ancestor sampling (PGAS), improving their performance beyond that of the ideal Gibbs sampler (which they approximate) by marginalizing out one or more parameters. This is possible when the parameter(s) has a conjugate prior relationship with the complete data likelihood. Marginalization yields a non-Markov model for inference, but we show that, in contrast to the general case, the methods still scale linearly in time. While marginalization can be cumbersome to implement, recent advances in probabilistic programming have enabled its automation. We demonstrate how the marginalized methods are viable as efficient inference backends in probabilistic programming, and demonstrate with examples in ecology and epidemiology.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference in state-space models involves reasoning about long, high-dimensional hidden trajectories. Particle Gibbs methods combine sequential Monte Carlo with Markov chain Monte Carlo to approximate otherwise difficult Gibbs updates. The paper observes that improving this approximation alone remains limited by the performance of the underlying ideal Gibbs sampler.

The authors instead change the inference problem by marginalizing out one or more parameters. They apply this strategy to particle Gibbs and particle Gibbs with ancestor sampling, improving performance beyond the ideal Gibbs sampler they originally approximate. The approach requires a conjugate relationship between the eliminated parameters' priors and the complete-data likelihood.

Removing parameters this way produces a non-Markov model for inference. Nevertheless, the authors show that their methods retain computation that scales linearly with the time dimension. They also explain how advances in probabilistic programming can automate otherwise cumbersome marginalization. Examples in ecology and epidemiology demonstrate the resulting methods as efficient inference backends, connecting a statistical improvement with a practical route to implementation.
summary.tldr: Marginalizing conjugate parameters improves particle Gibbs methods beyond their original ideal sampler while preserving linear scaling in time.

title: Parameter elimination in particle Gibbs sampling

abstract: Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), the mathematical framework underlying most algorithms in Reinforcement Learning (RL), are often used in a way that wrongfully assumes that the state of an agent's environment does not change during action selection. As RL systems based on MDPs begin to find application in real-world safety critical situations, this mismatch between the assumptions underlying classical MDPs and the reality of real-time computation may lead to undesirable outcomes. In this paper, we introduce a new framework, in which states and actions evolve simultaneously and show how it is related to the classical MDP formulation. We analyze existing algorithms under the new real-time formulation and show why they are suboptimal when used in real-time. We then use those insights to create a new algorithm Real-Time Actor Critic (RTAC) that outperforms the existing state-of-the-art continuous control algorithm Soft Actor Critic both in real-time and non-real-time settings.

In this paper, we introduce a new framework, in which states and actions evolve simultaneously and show how it is related to the classical MDP formulation. We analyze existing algorithms under the new real-time formulation and show why they are suboptimal when used in real-time. We then use those insights to create a new algorithm Real-Time Actor Critic (RTAC) that outperforms the existing state-of-the-art continuous control algorithm Soft Actor Critic both in real-time and non-real-time settings.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning is often formulated as though the environment waits while an agent selects its next action. Real environments can keep changing during that computation. This paper examines the mismatch, which becomes especially consequential when learned controllers are applied in settings where the timing of actions matters for their outcomes.

The authors introduce a framework in which states and actions evolve simultaneously and establish its relationship to the classical Markov decision process formulation. They then analyze existing algorithms within this real-time framework, showing why those algorithms are suboptimal when used under its timing conditions. The analysis motivates a new method called Real-Time Actor Critic.

Real-Time Actor Critic outperforms Soft Actor Critic in both real-time and non-real-time settings in the reported results. This suggests that taking the interaction between computation and environmental change seriously can guide effective algorithm design. The paper's contribution includes both a formulation that accounts for simultaneous evolution and a learning algorithm developed from the shortcomings exposed by that formulation.
summary.tldr: A framework for environments that evolve during action selection motivates Real-Time Actor Critic, which outperforms Soft Actor Critic in the reported settings.

title: Real-Time Reinforcement Learning

abstract: A deterministic approximation algorithm is presented for the maximization of non-monotone submodular functions over a ground set of size $n$ subject to cardinality constraint $k$; the algorithm is based upon the idea of interlacing two greedy procedures. The algorithm uses interlaced, thresholded greedy procedures to obtain tight ratio $1/4 - \epsilon$ in $O \left( \frac{n}{\epsilon} \log \left( \frac{k}{\epsilon} \right) \right)$ queries of the objective function, which improves upon both the ratio and the quadratic time complexity of the previously fastest deterministic algorithm for this problem. The algorithm is validated in the context of two applications of non-monotone submodular maximization, on which it outperforms the fastest deterministic and randomized algorithms in prior literature.

paragraphs: The paper considers choosing at most k elements from a set of n to maximize a non-monotone submodular objective. Submodularity expresses diminishing returns, while non-monotonicity means that adding an element can reduce the objective. Together, these properties make careful selection important even when there is room to add more elements.

The proposed deterministic algorithm interlaces two greedy procedures and uses thresholds to guide their choices. It achieves a tight approximation ratio of 1/4 minus epsilon with O((n/epsilon) log(k/epsilon)) objective-function queries. For fixed accuracy, this query count grows nearly linearly with the ground-set size, making objective evaluations a central measure of the algorithm's efficiency.

The result improves both the approximation ratio and the quadratic complexity of the previously fastest deterministic algorithm for this problem. The authors also evaluate it on two applications of non-monotone submodular maximization. In those applications, it outperforms the fastest earlier deterministic and randomized methods, adding empirical evidence to the theoretical improvements.
summary.tldr: Interlacing thresholded greedy procedures gives a deterministic near-linear-query algorithm with a tight 1/4-minus-epsilon approximation guarantee.

title: Interlaced Greedy Algorithm for Maximization of Submodular Functions in Nearly Linear Time

abstract: Two commonly arising computational tasks in Bayesian learning are Optimization (Maximum A Posteriori estimation) and Sampling (from the posterior distribution). In the convex case these two problems are efficiently reducible to each other. Recent work (Ma et al. 2019) shows that in the non-convex case, sampling can sometimes be provably faster. We present a simpler and stronger separation. We then compare sampling and optimization in more detail and show that they are provably incomparable: there are families of continuous functions for which optimization is easy but sampling is NP-hard, and vice versa. Further, we show function families that exhibit a sharp phase transition in the computational complexity of sampling, as one varies the natural temperature parameter. Our results draw on a connection to analogous separations in the discrete setting which are well-studied.

paragraphs: Bayesian learning often involves either finding a most probable explanation or drawing samples from a posterior distribution. These correspond to optimization and sampling. In convex settings, the two tasks can be efficiently reduced to each other. This paper examines how their computational relationship changes when the functions involved are non-convex.

The authors first strengthen an existing separation showing that sampling can sometimes be provably faster than optimization. They then establish a broader conclusion: neither task is computationally easier in general. They construct families of continuous functions where optimization is easy but sampling is NP-hard, and other families with the opposite relationship.

Its arguments draw on related separations already studied for discrete problems. Together, these results show why success at one task does not establish that the other will be tractable. The conclusions concern particular constructed families and computational regimes, rather than a universal ranking of practical sampling and optimization algorithms.
summary.tldr: For non-convex problems, sampling and optimization are computationally incomparable: either can be easy while the other is NP-hard.

title: Computational Separations between Sampling and Optimization

abstract: A popular model of preference in the context of recommendation systems is the so-called ideal point model. In this model, a user is represented as a vector u together with a collection of items x_1 ... x_N in a common low-dimensional space. The vector u represents the user's "ideal point," or the ideal combination of features that represents a hypothesized most preferred item. The underlying assumption in this model is that a smaller distance between u and an item x_j indicates a stronger preference for x_j. In the vast majority of the existing work on learning ideal point models, the underlying distance has been assumed to be Euclidean. However, this eliminates any possibility of interactions between features and a user's underlying preferences. In this paper, we consider the problem of learning an ideal point representation of a user's preferences when the distance metric is an unknown Mahalanobis metric. Specifically, we present a novel approach to estimate the user's ideal point u and the Mahalanobis metric from paired comparisons of the form "item x_i is preferred to item x_j.'' This can be viewed as a special case of a more general metric learning problem where the location of some points are unknown a priori. We conduct extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets to exhibit the effectiveness of our algorithm.

paragraphs: The ideal point model represents a user and candidate items in a common feature space. Its central assumption is that items closer to the user’s ideal point are more preferred. This paper revisits how closeness is defined, arguing that the usual Euclidean distance excludes interactions between features and the user’s underlying preferences.

The authors instead treat distance as an unknown Mahalanobis metric and learn it together with the user’s ideal point. Their evidence consists of paired comparisons stating that one item is preferred to another. summary.tldr: Paired preference comparisons jointly identify a user’s ideal item and a distance metric that can capture feature interactions.

title: Simultaneous Preference and Metric Learning from Paired Comparisons

abstract: We propose a few-shot learning method for detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) samples from classes that are unseen during training while classifying samples from seen classes using only a few labeled examples. For detecting unseen classes while generalizing to new samples of known classes, we synthesize fake samples, i.e., OOD samples, but that resemble in-distribution samples, and use them along with real samples. Our approach is based on an extension of model-agnostic meta learning (MAML) and is denoted as OOD-MAML, which not only learns a model initialization but also the initial fake samples across tasks. The learned initial fake samples can be used to quickly adapt to new tasks to form task-specific fake samples with only one or a few gradient update steps using MAML. For testing, OOD-MAML converts a K-shot N-way classification task into N sub-tasks of K-shot OOD detection with respect to each class. The joint analysis of N sub-tasks facilitates simultaneous classification and OOD detection and, furthermore, offers an advantage, in that it does not require re-training when the number of classes for a test task differs from that for training tasks; it is sufficient to simply assume as many sub-tasks as the number of classes for the test task. We also demonstrate the effective performance of OOD-MAML over benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Few-shot classification must identify known classes from very few labeled examples, but it may also encounter samples belonging to unseen classes. OOD-MAML addresses both classification and out-of-distribution detection. This construction also accommodates a different number of test classes without retraining: the system uses a corresponding number of subtasks. Benchmark experiments demonstrate effective performance, supporting this combined approach to few-shot recognition and unfamiliar-class detection.
summary.tldr: OOD-MAML meta-learns model and synthetic-sample initializations to combine few-shot classification with detection of unseen classes.

title: OOD-MAML: Meta-Learning for Few-Shot Out-of-Distribution Detection and Classification

abstract: Progress in Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms goes hand-in-hand with the development of challenging environments that test the limits of current methods. While existing RL environments are either sufficiently complex or based on fast simulation, they are rarely both. Here, we present the NetHack Learning Environment (NLE), a scalable, procedurally generated, stochastic, rich, and challenging environment for RL research based on the popular single-player terminal-based roguelike game, NetHack. We argue that NetHack is sufficiently complex to drive long-term research on problems such as exploration, planning, skill acquisition, and language-conditioned RL, while dramatically reducing the computational resources required to gather a large amount of experience. We compare NLE and its task suite to existing alternatives, and discuss why it is an ideal medium for testing the robustness and systematic generalization of RL agents. We demonstrate empirical success for early stages of the game using a distributed Deep RL baseline and Random Network Distillation exploration, alongside qualitative analysis of various agents trained in the environment. NLE is open source and available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/nle.

The NetHack Learning Environment addresses that combination using the terminal-based roguelike game NetHack. It provides a scalable, procedurally generated, stochastic environment with a rich set of challenges for learning agents.

The authors argue that the game’s complexity can support sustained research on exploration, planning, skill acquisition, and language-conditioned reinforcement learning. The contribution is an open-source research platform that combines challenging behavior with efficient experience generation, along with baseline results showing how agents begin to engage with it.
summary.tldr: The NetHack Learning Environment offers complex, efficient RL tasks, with baseline agents demonstrating progress in the game’s early stages.

title: The NetHack Learning Environment

abstract: We study an online learning problem subject to the constraint of individual fairness, which requires that similar individuals are treated similarly. Unlike prior work on individual fairness, we do not assume the similarity measure among individuals is known, nor do we assume that such measure takes a certain parametric form. Instead, we leverage the existence of an auditor who detects fairness violations without enunciating the quantitative measure. In each round, the auditor examines the learner's decisions and attempts to identify a pair of individuals that are treated unfairly by the learner. We provide a general reduction framework that reduces online classification in our model to standard online classification, which allows us to leverage existing online learning algorithms to achieve sub-linear regret and number of fairness violations. Surprisingly, in the stochastic setting where the data are drawn independently from a distribution, we are also able to establish PAC-style fairness and accuracy generalization guarantees (Rothblum and Yona (2018)), despite only having access to a very restricted form of fairness feedback. Our fairness generalization bound qualitatively matches the uniform convergence bound of Rothblum and Yona (2018), while also providing a meaningful accuracy generalization guarantee. Our results resolve an open question by Gillen et al. (2018) by showing that online learning under an unknown individual fairness constraint is possible even without assuming a strong parametric form of the underlying similarity measure.

paragraphs: Individual fairness asks a learner to treat similar people similarly, but the relevant similarity measure may be unknown. This paper studies online learning without requiring that measure to be supplied or belong to a specified parametric family. Instead, it assumes access to an auditor who can identify unfairly treated pairs.

In each round, the auditor examines the learner's decisions and attempts to flag a violation. The authors build a reduction from classification with this feedback to standard online classification. This lets existing online learning algorithms achieve both sublinear regret and a sublinear number of fairness violations, meaning those quantities grow more slowly than the number of rounds.
