Its fairness bound qualitatively matches the referenced uniform-convergence result while adding a meaningful accuracy guarantee. The result establishes that an explicit quantitative similarity model is not required in this framework; the auditor's ability to detect violations supplies the crucial fairness information.
summary.tldr: Online learners can achieve accuracy and individual-fairness guarantees using an auditor's violation reports without knowing a similarity metric.

title: Metric-Free Individual Fairness in Online Learning

abstract: We consider online learning for episodic stochastically constrained Markov decision processes (CMDP), which plays a central role in ensuring the safety of reinforcement learning. Here the loss function can vary arbitrarily across the episodes, and both the loss received and the budget consumption are revealed at the end of each episode. Previous works solve this problem under the restrictive assumption that the transition model of the MDP is known a priori and establish regret bounds that depend polynomially on the cardinalities of the state space $\mathcal{S}$ and the action space $\mathcal{A}$. In this work, we propose a new \emph{upper confidence primal-dual} algorithm, which only requires the trajectories sampled from the transition model. In particular, we prove that the proposed algorithm achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(L|\mathcal{S}|\sqrt{|\mathcal{A}|T})$ upper bounds of both the regret and the constraint violation, where $L$ is the length of each episode. Our analysis incorporates a new high-probability drift analysis of Lagrange multiplier processes into the celebrated regret analysis of upper confidence reinforcement learning, which demonstrates the power of ``optimism in the face of uncertainty'' in constrained online learning.

The learner sees the incurred loss and budget consumption only after an episode ends. Unlike the earlier approaches discussed in the abstract, the proposed method does not require advance knowledge of the transition model.

The upper-confidence primal-dual algorithm instead uses trajectories sampled from the system. Its analysis combines optimistic reinforcement learning with a new high-probability treatment of the Lagrange multiplier process used in handling constraints. This connects uncertainty about the environment with the need to manage both performance and resource consumption.

The authors bound both regret and constraint violation by an expression proportional to episode length times the number of states times the square root of the product of action count and T, up to logarithmic factors. Bounding both quantities shows that learning performance and constraint management can be analyzed together despite unknown transitions and adversarial losses. A cumulative violation bound does not amount to a claim that every episode satisfies every constraint.
summary.tldr: An optimistic primal-dual learner bounds regret and constraint violations under changing losses without requiring a known transition model.

title: Upper Confidence Primal-Dual Reinforcement Learning for CMDP with Adversarial Loss

abstract: We propose an algorithm for tabular episodic reinforcement learning with constraints. We provide a modular analysis with strong theoretical guarantees for settings with concave rewards and convex constraints, and for settings with hard constraints (knapsacks). Most of the previous work in constrained reinforcement learning is limited to linear constraints, and the remaining work focuses on either the feasibility question or settings with a single episode. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed algorithm significantly outperforms these approaches in existing constrained episodic environments.

Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed algorithm significantly outperforms these approaches in existing constrained episodic environments.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with constraints asks an agent to pursue rewards while respecting additional requirements. This paper proposes an algorithm for the tabular episodic setting, where learning proceeds through episodes and the problem uses a table-based representation. Its focus is on broadening the kinds of objectives and constraints that can be treated with theoretical guarantees.

The analysis covers concave rewards together with convex constraints, as well as hard constraints described as knapsacks. These settings go beyond the linear constraints emphasized in much previous work. The authors also distinguish their scope from approaches centered on whether constraints can be satisfied at all or on problems involving only a single episode.

A modular analysis provides strong theoretical guarantees for these settings. Experiments in existing constrained episodic environments report substantial improvements over the compared approaches. Together, the analysis and experiments support the proposed algorithm as a way to address richer constrained learning problems, with the tabular episodic formulation defining the scope of the contribution.
summary.tldr: A tabular episodic reinforcement-learning algorithm handles concave rewards, convex constraints, and hard knapsack constraints with theoretical guarantees.

title: Constrained episodic reinforcement learning in concave-convex and knapsack settings

abstract: We describe a procedure for explaining neurons in deep representations by identifying compositional logical concepts that closely approximate neuron behavior. Compared to prior work that uses atomic labels as explanations, analyzing neurons compositionally allows us to more precisely and expressively characterize their behavior. We use this procedure to answer several questions on interpretability in models for vision and natural language processing. First, we examine the kinds of abstractions learned by neurons. In image classification, we find that many neurons learn highly abstract but semantically coherent visual concepts, while other polysemantic neurons detect multiple unrelated features; in natural language inference (NLI), neurons learn shallow lexical heuristics from dataset biases. Second, we see whether compositional explanations give us insight into model performance: vision neurons that detect human-interpretable concepts are positively correlated with task performance, while NLI neurons that fire for shallow heuristics are negatively correlated with task performance. Finally, we show how compositional explanations provide an accessible way for end users to produce simple "copy-paste" adversarial examples that change model behavior in predictable ways.

paragraphs: Explaining a neuron with a single concept label can miss much of what activates it. This paper instead searches for logical combinations of concepts that approximate a neuron's behavior. Compositional explanations offer a more expressive description, allowing the analysis to capture both coherent abstractions and neurons that respond to multiple unrelated features.

The authors apply the procedure to image classification and natural language inference. In vision, they find many neurons representing abstract but semantically coherent concepts, alongside polysemantic neurons that detect unrelated features. In natural language inference, they find neurons using shallow word-based heuristics associated with dataset biases. The explanations therefore reveal different kinds of learned behavior across the two settings.

The paper also relates these patterns to performance. Human-interpretable visual concepts correlate positively with task performance, while shallow language heuristics correlate negatively; these are associations rather than causal claims. Finally, the authors show that end users can use the explanations to construct simple copy-paste adversarial examples that alter model behavior predictably, making the explanations useful for probing model responses.
summary.tldr: Logical combinations of concepts explain neuron behavior more expressively and reveal patterns associated with performance and predictable adversarial responses.

title: Compositional Explanations of Neurons

abstract: The use of deep learning techniques has achieved significant progress for program synthesis from input-output examples. However, when the program semantics become more complex, it still remains a challenge to synthesize programs that are consistent with the specification. In this work, we propose SED, a neural program generation framework that incorporates synthesis, execution, and debugging stages. Instead of purely relying on the neural program synthesizer to generate the final program, SED first produces initial programs using the neural program synthesizer component, then utilizes a neural program debugger to iteratively repair the generated programs. The integration of the debugger component enables SED to modify the programs based on the execution results and specification, which resembles the coding process of human programmers. On Karel, a challenging input-output program synthesis benchmark, SED reduces the error rate of the neural program synthesizer itself by a considerable margin, and outperforms the standard beam search for decoding.

paragraphs: Program synthesis from input-output examples asks a model to produce code whose behavior matches a specification. Neural generators have made progress, but matching more complex program behavior remains difficult. Synthesize, Execute and Debug, or SED, adds a learned repair process to the initial generation step.

A neural synthesizer first proposes programs. Those programs are executed, and a neural debugger uses the execution results together with the specification to revise them iteratively. This gives the framework information about what a proposed program actually does, allowing later edits to respond to observed behavior. The overall sequence resembles the generate-test-revise cycle used in programming.

On the Karel input-output synthesis benchmark, SED considerably reduces the error rate of its neural synthesizer and outperforms standard beam-search decoding. These results support learned debugging as a useful part of the synthesis process on that benchmark. The contribution is an integrated framework in which execution feedback guides modifications, so the system can improve an initial candidate through repairs instead of depending entirely on its first generation stage.
summary.tldr: SED iteratively repairs generated programs using execution feedback, reducing synthesis errors and beating beam-search decoding on Karel.

title: Synthesize, Execute and Debug: Learning to Repair for Neural Program Synthesis

abstract: Single image super-resolution (SISR) deals with a fundamental problem of upsampling a low-resolution (LR) image to its high-resolution (HR) version. Last few years have witnessed impressive progress propelled by deep learning methods. However, one critical challenge faced by existing methods is to strike a sweet spot of deep model complexity and resulting SISR quality. This paper addresses this pain point by proposing a linearly-assembled pixel-adaptive regression network (LAPAR), which casts the direct LR to HR mapping learning into a linear coefficient regression task over a dictionary of multiple predefined filter bases. Such a parametric representation renders our model highly lightweight and easy to optimize while achieving state-of-the-art results on SISR benchmarks. Moreover, based on the same idea, LAPAR is extended to tackle other restoration tasks, e.g., image denoising and JPEG image deblocking, and again, yields strong performance.

paragraphs: Single-image super-resolution reconstructs a higher-resolution image from a lower-resolution input. Deep learning has improved reconstruction quality, but balancing that quality against model complexity remains a challenge. LAPAR addresses this tradeoff by changing the form of the prediction problem, using a structured representation for the image transformation.

Instead of learning the low-to-high-resolution mapping directly, the network predicts linear coefficients over a dictionary of predefined filter bases. These coefficients allow the filters to be assembled adaptively for individual pixels. Learning how to combine an existing set of bases provides a more constrained parameterization of the restoration operation.

The authors report that this representation produces a lightweight model that is easy to optimize while achieving state-of-the-art results on super-resolution benchmarks. They also extend the same idea to image denoising and JPEG deblocking, with strong reported performance. These extensions show that predicting combinations of predefined filters can support several restoration tasks, beyond the super-resolution problem that motivates the architecture.
summary.tldr: LAPAR predicts pixel-adaptive combinations of predefined filters to deliver lightweight, high-quality super-resolution and other image restoration.

title: LAPAR: Linearly-Assembled Pixel-Adaptive Regression Network for Single Image Super-resolution and Beyond

abstract: Reinforcement learning algorithms are highly sensitive to the choice of hyperparameters, typically requiring significant manual effort to identify hyperparameters that perform well on a new domain. In this paper, we take a step towards addressing this issue by using metagradients to automatically adapt hyperparameters online by meta-gradient descent (Xu et al., 2018). We apply our algorithm, Self-Tuning Actor-Critic (STAC), to self-tune all the differentiable hyperparameters of an actor-critic loss function, to discover auxiliary tasks, and to improve off-policy learning using a novel leaky V-trace operator. STAC is simple to use, sample efficient and does not require a significant increase in compute. Ablative studies show that the overall performance of STAC improved as we adapt more hyperparameters. When applied to the Arcade Learning Environment (Bellemare et al. 2012), STAC improved the median human normalized score in 200M steps from 243% to 364%. When applied to the DM Control suite (Tassa et al., 2018), STAC improved the mean score in 30M steps from 217 to 389 when learning with features, from 108 to 202 when learning from pixels, and from 195 to 295 in the Real-World Reinforcement Learning Challenge (Dulac-Arnold et al., 2020).

title: A Self-Tuning Actor-Critic Algorithm

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms can fail to generalize due to the gap between the simulation and the real world. One standard remedy is to use robust adversarial RL (RARL) that accounts for this gap during the policy training, by modeling the gap as an adversary against the training agent. In this work, we reexamine the effectiveness of RARL under a fundamental robust control setting: the linear quadratic (LQ) case. We first observe that the popular RARL scheme that greedily alternates agents’ updates can easily destabilize the system. Motivated by this, we propose several other policy-based RARL algorithms whose convergence behaviors are then studied both empirically and theoretically. We find: i) the conventional RARL framework (Pinto et al., 2017) can learn a destabilizing policy if the initial policy does not enjoy the robust stability property against the adversary; and ii) with robustly stabilizing initializations, our proposed double-loop RARL algorithm provably converges to the global optimal cost while maintaining robust stability on-the-fly. We also examine the stability and convergence issues of other variants of policy-based RARL algorithms, and then discuss several ways to learn robustly stabilizing initializations. From a robust control perspective, we aim to provide some new and critical angles about RARL, by identifying and addressing the stability issues in this fundamental LQ setting in continuous control. Our results make an initial attempt toward better theoretical understandings of policy-based RARL, the core approach in Pinto et al., 2017.

This paper examines that approach in linear quadratic control. It finds that a popular scheme based on greedily alternating agent updates can destabilize the system, making stability during learning a central concern.

The authors propose alternative policy-based algorithms and study their behavior theoretically and empirically. They show that the conventional framework can learn a destabilizing policy when the starting policy lacks robust stability against the adversary. Initialization therefore plays a concrete role in whether adversarial training maintains a controlled system.

For their double-loop algorithm, a robustly stabilizing initialization enables a stronger guarantee: convergence to the globally optimal cost while preserving robust stability throughout training. The paper also examines other algorithm variants and discusses ways to learn suitable initial policies. These results provide a conditional foundation for policy-based adversarial learning in the linear quadratic setting, connecting optimization progress with the system's stability along the training path.
summary.tldr: In linear quadratic control, a double-loop adversarial RL algorithm converges optimally while preserving stability when initialized with a robustly stabilizing policy.

title: On the Stability and Convergence of Robust Adversarial Reinforcement Learning: A Case Study on Linear Quadratic Systems

abstract: The ability to leverage large-scale hardware parallelism has been one of the key enablers of the accelerated recent progress in machine learning. Consequently, there has been considerable effort invested into developing efficient parallel variants of classic machine learning algorithms. However, despite the wealth of knowledge on parallelization, some classic machine learning algorithms often prove hard to parallelize efficiently while maintaining convergence. In this paper, we focus on efficient parallel algorithms for the key machine learning task of inference on graphical models, in particular on the fundamental belief propagation algorithm. We address the challenge of efficiently parallelizing this classic paradigm by showing how to leverage scalable relaxed schedulers, which reduce parallelization overheads, in this context. We investigate the overheads of relaxation analytically, and present an extensive empirical study, showing that our approach outperforms previous parallel belief propagation implementations both in terms of scalability and in terms of wall-clock convergence time, on a range of practical applications.

paragraphs: Belief propagation is a fundamental method for inference in graphical models, but making it run efficiently across parallel hardware is challenging. Distributing work is only part of the problem: coordination can add overhead, and the execution strategy must also account for convergence. This paper focuses on scheduling as a way to improve practical parallel performance.

The authors adapt scalable relaxed schedulers to belief propagation. These schedulers loosen scheduling requirements to reduce the coordination overhead associated with parallel execution. The paper analytically investigates the overheads introduced by relaxation, making the scheduling tradeoff part of the algorithmic analysis rather than judging the approach solely by how much work can run simultaneously.

An extensive empirical study compares the resulting approach with previous parallel belief-propagation implementations across practical applications. The reported improvements cover both scalability and wall-clock time to convergence. Those two outcomes matter together: using more parallel hardware is useful when it also reaches the inference result sooner. The findings support relaxed scheduling as an effective implementation strategy for the applications studied, without claiming that every graphical-model inference problem benefits equally.
summary.tldr: Relaxed scheduling improves the scalability and wall-clock convergence time of parallel belief propagation across the studied practical applications.

title: Scalable Belief Propagation via Relaxed Scheduling

abstract: Many real-world video-text tasks involve different levels of granularity, such as frames and words, clip and sentences or videos and paragraphs, each with distinct semantics. In this paper, we propose a Cooperative hierarchical Transformer (COOT) to leverage this hierarchy information and model the interactions between different levels of granularity and different modalities. The method consists of three major components: an attention-aware feature aggregation layer, which leverages the local temporal context (intra-level, e.g., within a clip), a contextual transformer to learn the interactions between low-level and high-level semantics (inter-level, e.g. clip-video, sentence-paragraph), and a cross-modal cycle-consistency loss to connect video and text. The resulting method compares favorably to the state of the art on several benchmarks while having few parameters.

paragraphs: Video and text describe events at several scales. Individual frames and words carry fine details, clips and sentences organize shorter events, and whole videos and paragraphs provide broader context. COOT is designed to learn representations that account for this hierarchy, including relationships within each medium and between the visual and textual descriptions.

Its architecture combines three components with distinct responsibilities. Attention-aware feature aggregation uses nearby temporal context within a level, such as within a clip. A contextual transformer models connections between lower-level and higher-level meaning, including clip-to-video and sentence-to-paragraph relationships. A cross-modal cycle-consistency loss provides a further training connection between video and text.

Together, these components make the organization of a video and its description part of the representation-learning problem. The method compares favorably with state-of-the-art approaches on several benchmarks while using few parameters. The stated result supports modeling several levels of meaning jointly: useful video-text correspondence can depend both on local details and on how those details fit into the larger sequence.
summary.tldr: COOT connects local and global video-text meaning through a hierarchical transformer, achieving favorable benchmark results with few parameters.

title: COOT: Cooperative Hierarchical Transformer for Video-Text Representation Learning

abstract: Existing deep learning real denoising methods require a large amount of noisy-clean image pairs for supervision. Nonetheless, capturing a real noisy-clean dataset is an unacceptable expensive and cumbersome procedure. To alleviate this problem, this work investigates how to generate realistic noisy images. Firstly, we formulate a simple yet reasonable noise model that treats each real noisy pixel as a random variable. This model splits the noisy image generation problem into two sub-problems: image domain alignment and noise domain alignment. Subsequently, we propose a novel framework, namely Pixel-level Noise-aware Generative Adversarial Network (PNGAN). PNGAN employs a pre-trained real denoiser to map the fake and real noisy images into a nearly noise-free solution space to perform image domain alignment. Simultaneously, PNGAN establishes a pixel-level adversarial training to conduct noise domain alignment. Additionally, for better noise fitting, we present an efficient architecture Simple Multi-scale Network (SMNet) as the generator. Qualitative validation shows that noise generated by PNGAN is highly similar to real noise in terms of intensity and distribution. Quantitative experiments demonstrate that a series of denoisers trained with the generated noisy images achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) results on four real denoising benchmarks.

paragraphs: Training image denoisers typically requires many paired noisy and clean images, but collecting realistic pairs is expensive and cumbersome. This paper explores generating realistic noisy images to ease that burden. Its starting noise model treats each noisy pixel as a random variable and separates the task into matching image content and matching noise.

The proposed Pixel-level Noise-aware Generative Adversarial Network, PNGAN, handles those two alignments differently. A pretrained real-image denoiser maps generated and real noisy images into a nearly noise-free space, where image alignment is performed. Pixel-level adversarial training addresses noise alignment. These findings support the usefulness of the synthesized data for denoising, alongside the reported visual resemblance of the noise.
summary.tldr: PNGAN separately aligns image content and pixel-level noise to generate training images that improve real-image denoising.

title: Learning to Generate Realistic Noisy Images via Pixel-level Noise-aware Adversarial Training

abstract: Decentralized optimization is emerging as a viable alternative for scalable distributed machine learning, but also introduces new challenges in terms of synchronization costs. To this end, several communication-reduction techniques, such as non-blocking communication, quantization, and local steps, have been explored in the decentralized setting. Due to the complexity of analyzing optimization in such a relaxed setting, this line of work often assumes \emph{global} communication rounds, which require additional synchronization. In this paper, we consider decentralized optimization in the simpler, but harder to analyze, \emph{asynchronous gossip} model, in which communication occurs in discrete, randomly chosen pairings among nodes. Perhaps surprisingly, we show that a variant of SGD called \emph{SwarmSGD} still converges in this setting, even if \emph{non-blocking communication}, \emph{quantization}, and \emph{local steps} are all applied \emph{in conjunction}, and even if the node data distributions and underlying graph topology are both \emph{heterogenous}. Our analysis is based on a new connection with multi-dimensional load-balancing processes. We implement this algorithm and deploy it in a super-computing environment, showing that it can outperform previous decentralized methods in terms of end-to-end training time, and that it can even rival carefully-tuned large-batch SGD for certain tasks.

paragraphs: Distributed training can lose time coordinating workers and exchanging model updates. Decentralized methods remove the need for a central coordinator, but their analyses often still assume global communication rounds. This paper studies asynchronous gossip, where communication happens through randomly selected pairs of nodes rather than synchronized rounds involving the whole system.

The proposed SwarmSGD combines three ways to reduce communication overhead: workers can communicate without blocking, send quantized updates, and take local optimization steps between exchanges. The authors prove convergence with all three mechanisms operating together, even when data distributions differ across nodes and the communication graph is heterogeneous. Their analysis draws a new connection to multidimensional load-balancing processes.

It can improve end-to-end training time over earlier decentralized methods and, on certain tasks, rival carefully tuned large-batch SGD. The contribution therefore links a convergence result for a relaxed communication setting with evidence that the same flexibility can translate into faster training in practice.
summary.tldr: SwarmSGD converges with asynchronous pairwise communication, quantized updates, and local steps, while showing practical training-time benefits.

title: Asynchronous Decentralized SGD with Quantized and Local Updates

abstract: Detecting customized moments and highlights from videos given natural language (NL) user queries is an important but under-studied topic. One of the challenges in pursuing this direction is the lack of annotated data. To address this issue, we present the Query-based Video Highlights (QVHighlights) dataset. It consists of over 10,000 YouTube videos, covering a wide range of topics, from everyday activities and travel in lifestyle vlog videos to social and political activities in news videos. Each video in the dataset is annotated with: (1) a human-written free-form NL query, (2) relevant moments in the video w.r.t. the query, and (3) five-point scale saliency scores for all query-relevant clips. This comprehensive annotation enables us to develop and evaluate systems that detect relevant moments as well as salient highlights for diverse, flexible user queries. We also present a strong baseline for this task, Moment-DETR, a transformer encoder-decoder model that views moment retrieval as a direct set prediction problem, taking extracted video and query representations as inputs and predicting moment coordinates and saliency scores end-to-end. While our model does not utilize any human prior, we show that it performs competitively when compared to well-engineered architectures. With weakly supervised pretraining using ASR captions, Moment-DETR substantially outperforms previous methods. Lastly, we present several ablations and visualizations of Moment-DETR. Data and code is publicly available at https://github.com/jayleicn/moment_detr.

paragraphs: Finding a video segment relevant to a written request and identifying its best highlights are related but distinct tasks. Progress has been constrained by limited annotated data. This paper introduces QVHighlights, a dataset of more than 10,000 YouTube videos covering topics from everyday activities and travel to news.

Each video has a freely written query, annotations marking relevant moments, and five-level saliency ratings for the relevant clips. Together, these labels support learning both where requested content occurs and which parts stand out. The paper also introduces Moment-DETR, a transformer encoder-decoder that takes video and query representations and directly predicts a set of temporal coordinates and saliency scores.

Moment-DETR is competitive with carefully engineered architectures without incorporating human priors into the model. With weakly supervised pretraining from automatic speech-recognition captions, it substantially outperforms previous methods. The qualification matters: the stronger reported result includes that pretraining. The dataset and model establish a shared setting for evaluating video retrieval and highlight selection against flexible user requests.
summary.tldr: QVHighlights and Moment-DETR support finding query-relevant video moments and ranking their highlights, with strong gains from caption-based pretraining.

title: Detecting Moments and Highlights in Videos via Natural Language Queries

abstract: We propose a novel end-to-end solution for video instance segmentation (VIS) based on transformers. Recently, the per-clip pipeline shows superior performance over per-frame methods leveraging richer information from multiple frames. However, previous per-clip models require heavy computation and memory usage to achieve frame-to-frame communications, limiting practicality.In this work, we propose Inter-frame Communication Transformers (IFC), which significantly reduces the overhead for information-passing between frames by efficiently encoding the context within the input clip.Specifically, we propose to utilize concise memory tokens as a means of conveying information as well as summarizing each frame scene.The features of each frame are enriched and correlated with other frames through exchange of information between the precisely encoded memory tokens.We validate our method on the latest benchmark sets and achieved state-of-the-art performance (AP 42.6 on YouTube-VIS 2019 val set using the offline inference) while having a considerably fast runtime (89.4 FPS). Our method can also be applied to near-online inference for processing a video in real-time with only a small delay.The code is available at https://github.com/sukjunhwang/IFC

paragraphs: Video instance segmentation benefits from processing multiple frames together, but exchanging information across frames can require substantial computation and memory. This paper introduces Inter-frame Communication Transformers, an end-to-end approach designed to retain the benefits of clip-level context while reducing the cost of that communication.

The method uses compact memory tokens to summarize each frame and carry information between frames. Exchanging information through these tokens enriches frame features and connects them to other frames in the clip. The communication mechanism therefore operates through concise scene summaries, making temporal context less expensive to encode.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on the evaluated benchmarks, including 42.6 average precision on the YouTube-VIS 2019 validation set with offline inference, alongside a reported runtime of 89.4 frames per second. The method also supports near-online inference, processing video in real time with a small delay. These results connect the architectural contribution to both segmentation quality and practical throughput, while distinguishing the reported offline accuracy result from the additional near-online operating mode.
summary.tldr: Compact memory tokens make communication between video frames more efficient while supporting strong instance-segmentation accuracy and fast inference.

title: Video Instance Segmentation using Inter-Frame Communication Transformers

abstract: "Monkey see monkey do" is an age-old adage, referring to naive imitation without a deep understanding of a system's underlying mechanics. Indeed, if a demonstrator has access to information unavailable to the imitator (monkey), such as a different set of sensors, then no matter how perfectly the imitator models its perceived environment (See), attempting to directly reproduce the demonstrator's behavior (Do) can lead to poor outcomes. Imitation learning in the presence of a mismatch between demonstrator and imitator has been studied in the literature under the rubric of causal imitation learning (Zhang et. al. 2020), but existing solutions are limited to single-stage decision-making. This paper investigates the problem of causal imitation learning in sequential settings, where the imitator must make multiple decisions per episode. We develop a graphical criterion that is both necessary and sufficient for determining the feasibility of causal imitation, providing conditions when an imitator can match a demonstrator's performance despite differing capabilities. Finally, we provide an efficient algorithm for determining imitability, and corroborate our theory with simulations.

paragraphs: Copying a demonstrator’s actions can fail when the demonstrator has information the learner cannot observe. Different sensors, for example, can produce different information even within the same environment. Accurately modeling the learner’s visible surroundings therefore may not be enough to reproduce the demonstrator’s performance through direct behavioral imitation.

This paper extends causal imitation learning from single decisions to sequential episodes containing multiple decisions. Its central question is when successful imitation is feasible despite differences between the demonstrator’s and learner’s capabilities. The authors develop a graphical criterion that is both necessary and sufficient for this feasibility question in the studied framework.

The criterion identifies when the learner can match the demonstrator’s performance despite the information mismatch. The paper also supplies an efficient algorithm for deciding imitability and uses simulations to support the theory. This shifts attention from simply improving how closely actions are copied to determining whether the available information and causal relationships permit successful imitation across an entire sequence of decisions.
summary.tldr: A necessary-and-sufficient graphical criterion determines when sequential imitation can match a demonstrator despite differences in available information.

title: Sequential Causal Imitation Learning with Unobserved Confounders

abstract: We consider a stochastic multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem with delayed impact of actions. In our setting, actions taken in the pastimpact the arm rewards in the subsequent future. This delayed impact of actions is prevalent in the real world. For example, the capability to pay back a loan for people in a certain social group might depend on historically how frequently that group has been approved loan applications. If banks keep rejecting loan applications to people in a disadvantaged group, it could create a feedback loop and further damage the chance of getting loans for people in that group. In this paper, we formulate this delayed and long-term impact of actions within the context of multi-armed bandits. We generalize the bandit setting to encode the dependency of this ``bias" due to the action history during learning. The goal is to maximize the collected utilities over time while taking into account the dynamics created by the delayed impacts of historical actions. We propose an algorithm that achieves a regret of $\tilde{O}(KT^{2/3})$ and show a matching regret lower bound of $\Omega(KT^{2/3})$, where $K$ is the number of arms and $T$ is the learning horizon. Our results complement the bandit literature by adding techniques to deal with actions with long-term impacts and have implications in designing fair algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decisions whose consequences change future rewards. In its bandit setting, an action does more than produce an immediate payoff: the history of chosen actions influences what later choices can yield. The lending example illustrates the concern, since repeated rejection of a group can affect its future ability to repay and reinforce disadvantage.

The authors formulate a stochastic multi-armed bandit model that explicitly includes this dependence on action history. The learner seeks to maximize utility over time while accounting for the dynamics its own decisions create. This changes the learning problem because the rewards available in the future depend partly on the policy followed in the past.

The proposed algorithm has regret bounded by roughly K times T to the two-thirds power, up to logarithmic factors, where K counts arms and T is the horizon. A lower bound matches that dependence without the hidden logarithmic factors. Together, the bounds characterize the difficulty of the formulated problem and provide techniques relevant to decision systems with long-term effects, including questions of fairness.
summary.tldr: A bandit model captures how past actions alter future rewards and admits an algorithm with regret matching a lower bound up to logarithmic factors.

title: Bandit Learning with Delayed Impact of Actions

abstract: Value factorization is a popular and promising approach to scaling up multi-agent reinforcement learning in cooperative settings, which balances the learning scalability and the representational capacity of value functions. However, the theoretical understanding of such methods is limited. In this paper, we formalize a multi-agent fitted Q-iteration framework for analyzing factorized multi-agent Q-learning. Based on this framework, we investigate linear value factorization and reveal that multi-agent Q-learning with this simple decomposition implicitly realizes a powerful counterfactual credit assignment, but may not converge in some settings. Through further analysis, we find that on-policy training or richer joint value function classes can improve its local or global convergence properties, respectively. Finally, to support our theoretical implications in practical realization, we conduct an empirical analysis of state-of-the-art deep multi-agent Q-learning algorithms on didactic examples and a broad set of StarCraft II unit micromanagement tasks.

paragraphs: Cooperative multi-agent learning must represent how joint behavior affects a shared outcome while remaining computationally manageable as agents are added. Value factorization addresses this tension by decomposing value functions. The paper develops a multi-agent fitted Q-iteration framework to analyze what such decompositions do and when the resulting learning process can converge.

For linear value factorization, the analysis reveals an implicit counterfactual credit-assignment mechanism. This helps explain how a simple decomposition can support reasoning about individual agents’ contributions to a collective result. However, the authors also show that the learning process may fail to converge in some settings.

Further analysis identifies two ways to improve convergence properties: on-policy training can help locally, while richer classes of joint value functions can help globally. The authors examine these theoretical implications empirically using illustrative examples and StarCraft II unit micromanagement tasks. The work therefore separates the usefulness of a decomposition for assigning credit from the conditions needed for reliable learning dynamics.
summary.tldr: Value factorization can implicitly assign credit among cooperating agents, but convergence depends on the training setup and joint value-function class.

title: Towards Understanding Cooperative Multi-Agent Q-Learning with Value Factorization

abstract: Many subfields of machine learning share a common stumbling block: evaluation. Advances in machine learning often evaporate under closer scrutiny or turn out to be less widely applicable than originally hoped. We conduct a meta-review of 107 survey papers from natural language processing, recommender systems, computer vision, reinforcement learning, computational biology, graph learning, and more, organizing the wide range of surprisingly consistent critique into a concrete taxonomy of observed failure modes. Inspired by measurement and evaluation theory, we divide failure modes into two categories: internal and external validity. Internal validity issues pertain to evaluation on a learning problem in isolation, such as improper comparisons to baselines or overfitting from test set re-use. External validity relies on relationships between different learning problems, for instance, whether progress on a learning problem translates to progress on seemingly related tasks.

paragraphs: This paper examines why reported machine learning advances sometimes weaken under closer examination or apply less broadly than expected. The authors review 107 survey papers spanning language processing, recommendation, vision, reinforcement learning, computational biology, graph learning, and other areas. They organize recurring criticisms into a taxonomy of evaluation failures.

The first category is internal validity: whether an evaluation supports its conclusions within the particular learning problem being studied. Examples include unfair comparisons with baseline methods and overfitting caused by repeated use of a test set. These problems affect how much confidence a reader should place in an apparent improvement on the evaluated task.

The second category is external validity: whether results on one learning problem carry over to other problems. Progress on a benchmark may not translate into progress on tasks that seem related. Separating these categories helps make evaluation criticism more precise, distinguishing weaknesses in a comparison itself from weaknesses in the broader conclusions drawn from that comparison.
summary.tldr: A review of 107 surveys organizes recurring machine learning evaluation failures around validity within tasks and generalization across tasks.

title: Are We Learning Yet? A Meta Review of Evaluation Failures Across Machine Learning

abstract: Dataset Condensation is a newly emerging technique aiming at learning a tiny dataset that captures the rich information encoded in the original dataset. As the size of datasets contemporary machine learning models rely on becomes increasingly large, condensation methods become a prominent direction for accelerating network training and reducing data storage. Despite numerous methods have been proposed in this rapidly growing field, evaluating and comparing different condensation methods is non-trivial and still remains an open issue. The quality of condensed dataset are often shadowed by many critical contributing factors to the end performance, such as data augmentation and model architectures. The lack of a systematic way to evaluate and compare condensation methods not only hinders our understanding of existing techniques, but also discourages practical usage of the synthesized datasets. This work provides the first large-scale standardized benchmark on Dataset Condensation. It consists of a suite of evaluations to comprehensively reflect the generability and effectiveness of condensation methods through the lens of their generated dataset. Leveraging this benchmark, we conduct a large-scale study of current condensation methods, and report many insightful findings that open up new possibilities for future development. The benchmark library, including evaluators, baseline methods, and generated datasets, is open-sourced to facilitate future research and application.

paragraphs: Dataset condensation learns a tiny synthetic dataset intended to preserve useful information from a much larger one. Such datasets could reduce storage requirements and accelerate network training. However, deciding which condensation method produces better data is difficult because the eventual model performance also depends on choices outside the condensation method itself.

DC-BENCH addresses this evaluation problem through a large-scale standardized benchmark. Its evaluation suite examines the effectiveness and generalizability of condensation methods through the datasets they generate. This focus matters because architecture and data augmentation can otherwise blur the distinction between a strong condensed dataset and a favorable training setup.

The authors use the benchmark to conduct a broad study of existing methods and report findings intended to inform further development. They also release a library containing evaluators, baseline methods, and generated datasets. The paper's central contribution is an organized basis for comparing condensation techniques and examining their outputs, making it easier to study a field where final training performance can reflect several interacting factors.
summary.tldr: DC-BENCH standardizes evaluation of dataset condensation so generated datasets can be assessed more systematically.

title: DC-BENCH: Dataset Condensation Benchmark

abstract: We consider the problem of controlling an unknown linear dynamical system under adversarially-changing convex costs and full feedback of both the state and cost function. We present the first computationally-efficient algorithm that attains an optimal $\sqrt{T}$-regret rate compared to the best stabilizing linear controller in hindsight, while avoiding stringent assumptions on the costs such as strong convexity. Our approach is based on a careful design of non-convex lower confidence bounds for the online costs, and uses a novel technique for computationally-efficient regret minimization of these bounds that leverages their particular non-convex structure.

We present the first computationally-efficient algorithm that attains an optimal $\sqrt{T}$-regret rate compared to the best stabilizing linear controller in hindsight, while avoiding stringent assumptions on the costs such as strong convexity. Our approach is based on a careful design of non-convex lower confidence bounds for the online costs, and uses a novel technique for computationally-efficient regret minimization of these bounds that leverages their particular non-convex structure.

paragraphs: This paper studies control of an unknown linear dynamical system when the cost of actions can change adversarially over time. The controller receives full feedback about both the system state and the cost function. Its performance is measured against the best stabilizing linear controller that could have been chosen with hindsight.

The authors present a computationally efficient algorithm with an optimal regret rate proportional to the square root of the time horizon T. Regret measures the accumulated performance gap relative to that hindsight comparator. The guarantee allows convex costs without requiring stronger conditions such as strong convexity, broadening the cost functions covered by this efficient control result.

The method carefully constructs lower confidence bounds for the online costs. Although these bounds are nonconvex, their particular structure allows a new efficient regret-minimization technique. The main contribution combines a favorable statistical rate with computational tractability under unknown dynamics. Its scope remains the stated setting of linear systems, convex changing costs, full feedback, and comparison with stabilizing linear controllers.
summary.tldr: An efficient adaptive controller achieves optimal square-root regret for unknown linear systems with adversarial convex costs and full feedback.

title: Rate-Optimal Online Convex Optimization in Adaptive Linear Control

abstract: Relative positional embeddings (RPE) have received considerable attention since RPEs effectively model the relative distance among tokens and enable length extrapolation. We propose KERPLE, a framework that generalizes relative position embedding for extrapolation by kernelizing positional differences. We achieve this goal using conditionally positive definite (CPD) kernels, a class of functions known for generalizing distance metrics. To maintain the inner product interpretation of self-attention, we show that a CPD kernel can be transformed into a PD kernel by adding a constant offset. This offset is implicitly absorbed in the Softmax normalization during self-attention. The diversity of CPD kernels allows us to derive various RPEs that enable length extrapolation in a principled way. Experiments demonstrate that the logarithmic variant achieves excellent extrapolation performance on three large language modeling datasets. Our implementation and pretrained checkpoints are released at~\url{https://github.com/chijames/KERPLE.git}.

paragraphs: Relative positional embeddings tell an attention model how far apart tokens are. They are also useful for length extrapolation, where a model handles sequences longer than those encountered during training. KERPLE develops a general framework for these embeddings by applying kernel functions to differences between token positions.

The construction uses conditionally positive definite kernels, a family of functions that generalizes distance measures. To preserve self-attention's interpretation in terms of inner products, the authors show that adding a constant offset transforms such a kernel into a positive definite one. Softmax normalization implicitly absorbs that offset, connecting the mathematical construction to the attention computation.

Different kernels within this family produce different relative positional embeddings, giving a principled way to derive alternatives. Experiments on three large language-modeling datasets show strong length extrapolation for the logarithmic variant. The result supports that particular variant empirically while the broader contribution is a framework for constructing positional representations. Together, the theory and experiments connect positional-distance modeling with the practical challenge of processing longer sequences.
summary.tldr: KERPLE derives relative positional embeddings from kernels, with a logarithmic variant showing strong length extrapolation.

title: KERPLE: Kernelized Relative Positional Embedding for Length Extrapolation

abstract: Two key challenges facing modern deep learning is mitigating deep networks vulnerability to adversarial attacks, and understanding deep learning's generalization capabilities. Towards the first issue, many defense strategies have been developed, with the most common being Adversarial Training (AT). Towards the second challenge, one of the dominant theories that has emerged is the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) -- a characterization of neural network behavior in the infinite-width limit. In this limit, the kernel is frozen and the underlying feature map is fixed. In finite-widths however, there is evidence that feature learning happens at the earlier stages of the training (kernel learning) before a second phase where the kernel remains fixed (lazy training). While prior work has aimed at studying adversarial vulnerability through the lens of the frozen infinite-width NTK, there is no work which studies adversarial robustness of NTK during training. In this work, we perform an empirical study of the evolution of the NTK under standard and adversarial training, aiming to disambiguate the effect of adversarial training on kernel learning and lazy training. We find under adversarial training, the NTK rapidly converges to a different kernel (and feature map) than standard training. This new kernel provides adversarial robustness, even when non-robust training is performed on top of it. Furthermore, we find that adversarial training on top of a fixed kernel can yield a classifier with $76.1\%$ robust accuracy under PGD attacks with $\varepsilon = 4/255$ on CIFAR-10.

Finite-width networks can instead learn features early in training before entering a phase where the kernel changes little. This paper examines how adversarial training affects that evolution.

The result is specific to that evaluation setting. Together, the findings distinguish the role of learning a kernel from the role of training a classifier using one, helping clarify how both stages can contribute to observed adversarial robustness.
summary.tldr: An empirical study finds that adversarial training rapidly learns a distinct neural tangent kernel that can itself support robustness.

title: Evolution of Neural Tangent Kernels under Benign and Adversarial Training

abstract: Unsupervised pretraining methods for object detection aim to learn object discrimination and localization ability from large amounts of images. Typically, recent works design pretext tasks that supervise the detector to predict the defined object priors. They normally leverage heuristic methods to produce object priors, \emph{e.g.,} selective search, which separates the prior generation and detector learning and leads to sub-optimal solutions. In this work, we propose a novel object detection pretraining framework that could generate object priors and learn detectors jointly by generating accurate object priors from the model itself. Specifically, region priors are extracted by attention maps from the encoder, which highlights foregrounds. Instance priors are the selected high-quality output bounding boxes of the detection decoder. By assuming objects as instances in the foreground, we can generate object priors with both region and instance priors. Moreover, our object priors are jointly refined along with the detector optimization. With better object priors as supervision, the model could achieve better detection capability, which in turn promotes the object priors generation. Our method improves the competitive approaches by \textbf{+1.3 AP}, \textbf{+1.7 AP} in 1\% and 10\% COCO low-data regimes object detection.

paragraphs: Unsupervised detector pretraining needs signals that teach a model where objects are and how to distinguish them. Earlier approaches often produce these object priors with separate heuristics, leaving prior generation disconnected from detector learning. This paper proposes generating the priors from the detector itself and improving both together.

The framework combines two sources of information. Under the assumption that objects are instances within the foreground, these signals jointly define the object priors. As detector optimization proceeds, the priors are refined too, creating a feedback process in which better supervision can improve detection and better detection can improve supervision.

In COCO low-data detection settings, the method improves over competitive approaches by 1.3 AP with 1% of the data and 1.7 AP with 10%. These results support jointly learning object priors and detection capabilities as a useful pretraining strategy when labeled data are limited.
summary.tldr: Jointly refining model-generated object priors and detector learning improves detection in the reported COCO low-data settings.

title: Unsupervised Object Detection Pretraining with Joint Object Priors Generation and Detector Learning

abstract: Energy-based models, a.k.a. energy networks, perform inference by optimizing an energy function, typically parametrized by a neural network. This allows one to capture potentially complex relationships between inputs andoutputs.To learn the parameters of the energy function, the solution to thatoptimization problem is typically fed into a loss function.The key challenge for training energy networks lies in computing loss gradients,as this typically requires argmin/argmax differentiation.In this paper, building upon a generalized notion of conjugate function,which replaces the usual bilinear pairing with a general energy function,we propose generalized Fenchel-Young losses, a natural loss construction forlearning energy networks. Our losses enjoy many desirable properties and theirgradients can be computed efficiently without argmin/argmax differentiation.We also prove the calibration of their excess risk in the case of linear-concaveenergies. We demonstrate our losses on multilabel classification and imitation learning tasks.

paragraphs: An energy network makes a prediction by optimizing an energy function that describes relationships between inputs and outputs. Training then evaluates that prediction with a loss. This creates a difficult gradient calculation: changing the network parameters changes the solution of the prediction-time optimization problem, and conventional training often needs to differentiate through that solution.

The paper introduces generalized Fenchel-Young losses to address this difficulty. Its mathematical starting point is a generalized conjugate function that replaces the usual bilinear pairing with a general energy function. The resulting losses are designed for learning energy networks, and their gradients can be computed efficiently without differentiating the argmin or argmax operation used to obtain a prediction.

The authors also prove an excess-risk calibration result for linear-concave energies, connecting the loss construction to predictive performance under that condition. They demonstrate the losses on multilabel classification and imitation learning. The contribution combines a more tractable training calculation with a conditional theoretical guarantee and examples in two application settings.
summary.tldr: Generalized Fenchel-Young losses enable efficient energy-network gradients without argmin or argmax differentiation, with calibration proved for linear-concave energies.

title: Learning Energy Networks with Generalized Fenchel-Young Losses

abstract: We consider the Continuum Bandit problem where the goal is to find the optimal action under an unknown reward function, with an additional monotonicity constraint (or, "markdown" constraint) that requires that the action sequence be non-increasing. This problem faithfully models a natural single-product dynamic pricing problem, called "markdown pricing", where the objective is to adaptively reduce the price over a finite sales horizon to maximize expected revenues. Jia et al '21 and Chen '21 independently showed a tight $T^{3/4}$ regret bound over $T$ rounds under *minimal* assumptions of unimodality and Lipschitzness in the reward (or, "revenue") function. This bound shows that the demand learning in markdown pricing is harder than unconstrained (i.e., without the monotonicity constraint) pricing under unknown demand which suffers regret only of the order of $T^{2/3}$ under the same assumptions (Kleinberg '04). However, in practice the demand functions are usually assumed to have certain functional forms (e.g. linear or exponential), rendering the demand-learning easier and suggesting lower regret bounds. We investigate two fundamental questions, assuming the underlying demand curve comes from a given parametric family: (1) Can we improve the $T^{3/4}$ regret bound for markdown pricing, under extra assumptions on the functional forms of the demand functions? (2) Is markdown pricing still harder than unconstrained pricing, under these additional assumptions? To answer these, we introduce a concept called markdown dimension that measures the complexity of the parametric family and present tight regret bounds under this framework, thereby completely settling the aforementioned questions.

paragraphs: Markdown pricing requires a seller to learn demand while only lowering, never raising, the price. This creates an irreversible aspect to exploration: a price reduction constrains later choices. The paper models this as a continuum bandit problem with a non-increasing action sequence and the goal of maximizing expected revenue over a finite horizon.

Under broad assumptions of unimodality and Lipschitz continuity, earlier results give regret of order T to the three-quarter power for markdown pricing, versus T to the two-thirds power without the constraint. The authors ask how that comparison changes when demand belongs to a specified parametric family, such as a linear or exponential family.

They introduce markdown dimension, a measure of the complexity of a parametric demand family, and establish tight regret bounds within this framework. These bounds resolve their questions about improved learning rates and the difficulty added by monotonicity under the framework's assumptions. The central insight is that the structure of the demand family matters when assessing the cost of learning with irreversible price reductions.
summary.tldr: Markdown dimension characterizes tight learning guarantees for dynamic pricing when prices can only decrease and demand is parametric.

title: Dynamic Pricing with Monotonicity Constraint under Unknown Parametric Demand Model

abstract: The need to learn from positive and unlabeled data, or PU learning, arises in many applications and has attracted increasing interest. While random forests are known to perform well on many tasks with positive and negative data, recent PU algorithms are generally based on deep neural networks, and the potential of tree-based PU learning is under-explored. In this paper, we propose new random forest algorithms for PU-learning. Key to our approach is a new interpretation of decision tree algorithms for positive and negative data as \emph{recursive greedy risk minimization algorithms}. We extend this perspective to the PU setting to develop new decision tree learning algorithms that directly minimizes PU-data based estimators for the expected risk. This allows us to develop an efficient PU random forest algorithm, PU extra trees. Our approach features three desirable properties: it is robust to the choice of the loss function in the sense that various loss functions lead to the same decision trees; it requires little hyperparameter tuning as compared to neural network based PU learning; it supports a feature importance that directly measures a feature's contribution to risk minimization. Our algorithms demonstrate strong performance on several datasets. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/puetpaper/PUExtraTrees}.

paragraphs: Positive-unlabeled learning addresses datasets containing confirmed positive examples and examples whose class is unknown. Random forests are well established when both positive and negative labels are available, but their use in this setting has received less attention. This paper develops decision trees and forests that learn directly from positive and unlabeled data.

The key step reinterprets ordinary decision-tree training as recursive greedy minimization of expected risk. The authors then replace the usual risk calculation with estimators suitable for positive-unlabeled data. This leads to new tree-learning algorithms and an efficient forest method called PU extra trees, connecting tree construction directly to the learning objective.

The approach has three stated advantages. Various loss functions produce the same trees, reducing sensitivity to that choice; it needs relatively little hyperparameter tuning compared with neural-network PU methods; and feature importance measures a feature’s contribution to risk reduction. Experiments show strong performance on several datasets. These findings make tree-based PU learning a practical option with an interpretation of feature importance grounded in the objective being optimized.
summary.tldr: PU extra trees adapts risk-minimizing decision-tree construction to positive-unlabeled data, with little tuning and objective-based feature importance.

title: Positive-Unlabeled Learning using Random Forests via Recursive Greedy Risk Minimization

abstract: Most people associate the term `hedging' exclusively with financial applications, particularly the use of financial derivatives. We argue that hedging is an activity that human and machine agents should engage in more broadly, even when the agent's value is not necessarily in monetary units. In this paper, we propose a decision-theoretic view of hedging based on augmenting a probabilistic graphical model -- specifically a Bayesian network or an influence diagram -- with a reward. Hedging is therefore posed as a particular kind of graph manipulation, and can be viewed as analogous to control/intervention and information gathering related analysis. Effective hedging occurs when a risk-averse agent finds opportunity to balance uncertain rewards in their current situation. We illustrate the concepts with examples and counter-examples, and conduct experiments to demonstrate the properties and applicability of the proposed computational tools that enable agents to proactively identify potential hedging opportunities in real-world situations.

In this paper, we propose a decision-theoretic view of hedging based on augmenting a probabilistic graphical model -- specifically a Bayesian network or an influence diagram -- with a reward. Hedging is therefore posed as a particular kind of graph manipulation, and can be viewed as analogous to control/intervention and information gathering related analysis. Effective hedging occurs when a risk-averse agent finds opportunity to balance uncertain rewards in their current situation. We illustrate the concepts with examples and counter-examples, and conduct experiments to demonstrate the properties and applicability of the proposed computational tools that enable agents to proactively identify potential hedging opportunities in real-world situations.

paragraphs: Hedging is usually associated with financial contracts, but the paper treats it as a broader decision problem. An agent may care about uncertain outcomes whose value is not monetary. For a risk-averse agent, a useful opportunity can arise when an additional reward helps balance the uncertain rewards already present in its situation.

The authors formalize this idea by adding a reward to a probabilistic graphical model, specifically a Bayesian network or an influence diagram. Hedging then becomes a particular operation on a graph representing uncertainty and decisions. This puts it alongside analyses of interventions and information gathering, while focusing on how rewards can be combined to manage uncertainty.

The paper develops examples and counter-examples to clarify the proposed concept and experiments to examine its computational tools. Those tools are intended to help agents actively identify potential hedging opportunities. The contribution is a general decision-theoretic formulation, together with demonstrations of its properties and applicability beyond the exclusively financial interpretation of hedging.
summary.tldr: The paper models hedging as adding rewards to probabilistic graphs so risk-averse agents can identify opportunities to balance uncertain outcomes.

title: Hedging as Reward Augmentation in Probabilistic Graphical Models

abstract: Time series synthesis is an important research topic in the field of deep learning, which can be used for data augmentation. Time series data types can be broadly classified into regular or irregular. However, there are no existing generative models that show good performance for both types without any model changes. Therefore, we present a general purpose model capable of synthesizing regular and irregular time series data. To our knowledge, we are the first designing a general purpose time series synthesis model, which is one of the most challenging settings for time series synthesis. To this end, we design a generative adversarial network-based method, where many related techniques are carefully integrated into a single framework, ranging from neural ordinary/controlled differential equations to continuous time-flow processes. Our method outperforms all existing methods.

The paper distinguishes regular and irregular time series and identifies a practical gap: existing generators had not shown good performance on both types without changes to the model. Its objective is a single framework that handles both.

The proposed approach is based on a generative adversarial network and integrates techniques for modeling time continuously. These include neural ordinary differential equations, neural controlled differential equations, and continuous time-flow processes. Combining them within one framework is central to the proposal, because the intended capability spans both regular and irregular observations.

The authors describe GT-GAN as a general-purpose synthesis model and report that it outperforms existing methods. The significance of this claim lies in the shared model across the two time-series categories: the framework is intended to avoid requiring a different model design for each. The paper's stated contribution therefore combines broader applicability within time-series synthesis with reported performance improvements.
summary.tldr: GT-GAN combines adversarial learning with continuous-time modeling to synthesize both regular and irregular time series using one framework.

title: GT-GAN: General Purpose Time Series Synthesis with Generative Adversarial Networks

abstract: We study the optimization problem associated with fitting two-layer ReLU neural networks with respect to the squared loss, where labels are generated by a target network. Use is made of the rich symmetry structure to develop a novel set of tools for studying the mechanism by which over-parameterization annihilates spurious minima through. Sharp analytic estimates are obtained for the loss and the Hessian spectrum at different minima, and it is shown that adding neurons can turn symmetric spurious minima into saddles through a local mechanism that does not generate new spurious minima; minima of smaller symmetry require more neurons. Using Cauchy's interlacing theorem, we prove the existence of descent directions in certain subspaces arising from the symmetry structure of the loss function. This analytic approach uses techniques, new to the field, from algebraic geometry, representation theory and symmetry breaking, and confirms rigorously the effectiveness of over-parameterization in making the associated loss landscape accessible to gradient-based methods. For a fixed number of neurons and inputs, the spectral results remain true under symmetry breaking perturbation of the target.

paragraphs: The paper investigates why adding neurons can make a neural network easier to optimize. Its setting is specific: a two-layer ReLU network trained with squared loss on labels generated by a target network. The analysis uses symmetries in this problem to examine undesirable local minima and how extra parameters change their surrounding loss geometry.

The authors derive precise estimates of loss values and Hessian spectra, which describe local curvature. They show that adding neurons can transform symmetric spurious minima into saddle points through a local mechanism that does not introduce new spurious minima. Minima with less symmetry require more added neurons for this transformation.

Using Cauchy's interlacing theorem, the analysis establishes directions of decreasing loss within particular symmetry-related subspaces. This gives a rigorous mechanism by which over-parameterization can help gradient-based optimization in the studied setting. For fixed numbers of neurons and inputs, the spectral conclusions also survive symmetry-breaking perturbations of the target, extending their relevance beyond an exactly symmetric target.
summary.tldr: Symmetry-based analysis shows how adding neurons can turn certain bad minima in two-layer ReLU networks into saddles.

title: Annihilation of Spurious Minima in Two-Layer ReLU Networks

abstract: The transferability of adversarial perturbations provides an effective shortcut for black-box attacks. Targeted perturbations have greater practicality but are more difficult to transfer between models. In this paper, we experimentally and theoretically demonstrated that neural networks trained on the same dataset have more consistent performance in High-Sample-Density-Regions (HSDR) of each class instead of low sample density regions. Therefore, in the target setting, adding perturbations towards HSDR of the target class is more effective in improving transferability. However, density estimation is challenging in high-dimensional scenarios. Further theoretical and experimental verification demonstrates that easy samples with low loss are more likely to be located in HSDR. Perturbations towards such easy samples in the target class can avoid density estimation for HSDR location. Based on the above facts, we verified that adding perturbations to easy samples in the target class improves targeted adversarial transferability of existing attack methods. A generative targeted attack strategy named Easy Sample Matching Attack (ESMA) is proposed, which has a higher success rate for targeted attacks and outperforms the SOTA generative method. Moreover, ESMA requires only $5\%$ of the storage space and much less computation time comparing to the current SOTA, as ESMA attacks all classes with only one model instead of seperate models for each class. Our code is available at https://github.com/gjq100/ESMA

paragraphs: A targeted adversarial attack tries to make a model predict a particular chosen class. Transferring such an attack between models is difficult. This paper investigates where models trained on the same dataset behave more consistently, finding theoretical and experimental support for greater consistency in regions with high sample density within each class.

That observation motivates perturbing inputs toward dense regions of the target class. Directly estimating density in high dimensions is challenging, so the authors study an alternative: easy examples with low loss. Their analysis and experiments indicate that these examples are more likely to lie in high-density regions, providing a practical target without explicit density estimation.

The authors show that targeting easy examples improves the transferability of existing attack methods and introduce Easy Sample Matching Attack, or ESMA. The reported generative attack exceeds the compared state-of-the-art method in targeted success rate. Because one model attacks all classes instead of using separate models per class, ESMA also requires only 5% of the storage and substantially less computation time in that comparison.
summary.tldr: Targeting low-loss examples improves adversarial transfer, and ESMA uses this strategy with one generative model for all classes.

title: Perturbation Towards Easy Samples Improves Targeted Adversarial Transferability

abstract: Collaborative learning techniques have the potential to enable training machine learning models that are superior to models trained on a single entity’s data. However, in many cases, potential participants in such collaborative schemes are competitors on a downstream task, such as firms that each aim to attract customers by providing the best recommendations. This can incentivize dishonest updates that damage other participants' models, potentially undermining the benefits of collaboration. In this work, we formulate a game that models such interactions and study two learning tasks within this framework: single-round mean estimation and multi-round SGD on strongly-convex objectives. For a natural class of player actions, we show that rational clients are incentivized to strongly manipulate their updates, preventing learning. We then propose mechanisms that incentivize honest communication and ensure learning quality comparable to full cooperation. Lastly, we empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of our incentive scheme on a standard non-convex federated learning benchmark. Our work shows that explicitly modeling the incentives and actions of dishonest clients, rather than assuming them malicious, can enable strong robustness guarantees for collaborative learning.

That competition may reward misleading updates that damage other participants’ results. This paper models such interactions as a game, making the incentives behind dishonest communication an explicit part of the learning problem.

The theoretical analysis covers single-round mean estimation and multi-round stochastic gradient descent on strongly convex objectives. For a natural class of available actions, the authors show that rational clients have incentives to manipulate updates strongly enough to prevent learning. They then design mechanisms that encourage honest communication and provide learning quality comparable to full cooperation within the studied framework.

The authors also demonstrate their incentive scheme on a standard non-convex federated-learning benchmark.
