The broader lesson is that understanding why participants might interfere can help construct robust collaboration rules. Here, honesty is encouraged through the structure of the interaction, and the guarantees depend on the modeled incentives and actions.
summary.tldr: Game-theoretic mechanisms encourage competing learners to communicate honestly and recover learning quality comparable to full cooperation in the analyzed settings.

title: Incentivizing Honesty among Competitors in Collaborative Learning and Optimization

abstract: Deep Neural Networks and Reinforcement Learning methods have empirically shown great promise in tackling challenging combinatorial problems. In those methods a deep neural network is used as a solution generator which is then trained by gradient-based methods (e.g., policy gradient) to successively obtain better solution distributions.In this work we introduce a novel theoretical framework for analyzing the effectiveness of such methods. We ask whether there exist generative models that (i) are expressive enough to generate approximately optimal solutions; (ii) have a tractable, i.e, polynomial in the size of the input, number of parameters; (iii) their optimization landscape is benign in the sense that it does not contain sub-optimal stationary points. Our main contribution is a positive answer to this question. Our result holds for a broad class of combinatorial problems including Max- and Min-Cut, Max-$k$-CSP, Maximum-Weight-Bipartite-Matching, and the Traveling Salesman Problem. As a byproduct of our analysis we introduce a novel regularization process over vanilla gradient descent and provide theoretical and experimental evidence that it helps address vanishing-gradient issues and escape bad stationary points.

paragraphs: Neural approaches to combinatorial optimization can learn to generate a distribution of candidate solutions and gradually improve it through gradient-based training. This paper develops a theoretical framework for understanding whether suitable solution generators can combine expressive power, manageable model size, and an optimization landscape without suboptimal stationary points.

The authors give a positive existence result: there are generative models that can represent approximately optimal solutions, use a number of parameters polynomial in input size, and satisfy the stated landscape property. The result covers a broad class of problems, including cut problems, constraint satisfaction, maximum-weight bipartite matching, and the Traveling Salesman Problem. The claim concerns these properties of suitable generators.

The analysis also produces a regularization process for ordinary gradient descent. Theoretical and experimental evidence indicates that it helps with vanishing gradients and escaping bad stationary points. Together, the results provide a framework for studying why learning distributions of solutions can be effective, while connecting that theory to a concrete intervention in the optimization procedure.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes the existence of compact, expressive combinatorial solution generators with benign landscapes and develops a regularizer that helps gradient optimization.

title: Optimizing Solution-Samplers for Combinatorial Problems: The Landscape of Policy-Gradient Method

abstract: Numerous studies have been conducted to investigate the properties of large-scale temporal graphs. Despite the ubiquity of these graphs in real-world scenarios, it's usually impractical for us to obtain the whole real-time graphs due to privacy concerns and technical limitations. In this paper, we introduce the concept of {\it Live Graph Lab} for temporal graphs, which enables open, dynamic and real transaction graphs from blockchains. Among them, Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) have become one of the most prominent parts of blockchain over the past several years. With more than \$40 billion market capitalization, this decentralized ecosystem produces massive, anonymous and real transaction activities, which naturally forms a complicated transaction network. However, there is limited understanding about the characteristics of this emerging NFT ecosystem from a temporal graph analysis perspective. To mitigate this gap, we instantiate a live graph with NFT transaction network and investigate its dynamics to provide new observations and insights. Specifically, through downloading and parsing the NFT transaction activities, we obtain a temporal graph with more than 4.5 million nodes and 124 million edges. Then, a series of measurements are presented to understand the properties of the NFT ecosystem. Through comparisons with social, citation, and web networks, our analyses give intriguing findings and point out potential directions for future exploration. Finally, we also study machine learning models in this live graph to enrich the current datasets and provide new opportunities for the graph community. The source codes and dataset are available at https://livegraphlab.github.io.

The abstract reports observations and future research directions from the comparisons without specifying individual structural findings.
summary.tldr: Live Graph Lab builds and studies a large temporal NFT transaction graph as an open resource for network analysis and graph learning.

title: Live Graph Lab: Towards Open, Dynamic and Real Transaction Graphs with NFT

abstract: Naturalistic stimuli evoke complex neural responses with spatial and temporal properties that differ across individuals. Current alignment methods focus on either spatial hyperalignment (assuming exact temporal correspondence) or temporal alignment (assuming exact spatial correspondence). Here, we propose a hybrid model, the Hyper-HMM, that simultaneously aligns both temporal and spatial features across brains. The model learns to linearly project voxels to a reduced-dimension latent space, in which timecourses are segmented into corresponding temporal events. This approach allows tracking of each individual's mental trajectory through an event sequence, and also allows for alignment with other feature spaces such as stimulus content. Using an fMRI dataset in which students watch videos of class lectures, we demonstrate that the Hyper-HMM can be used to map all participants and the semantic content of the videos into a common low-dimensional space, and that these mappings generalize to held-out data. Our model provides a new window into individual cognitive dynamics evoked by complex naturalistic stimuli.

title: Hyper-HMM: aligning human brains and semantic features in a common latent event space

abstract: The development of efficient machine learning models for molecular systems representation is becoming crucial in scientific research. We introduce TensorNet, an innovative O(3)-equivariant message-passing neural network architecture that leverages Cartesian tensor representations. By using Cartesian tensor atomic embeddings, feature mixing is simplified through matrix product operations. Furthermore, the cost-effective decomposition of these tensors into rotation group irreducible representations allows for the separate processing of scalars, vectors, and tensors when necessary. Compared to higher-rank spherical tensor models, TensorNet demonstrates state-of-the-art performance with significantly fewer parameters. For small molecule potential energies, this can be achieved even with a single interaction layer. As a result of all these properties, the model's computational cost is substantially decreased. Moreover, the accurate prediction of vector and tensor molecular quantities on top of potential energies and forces is possible. In summary, TensorNet's framework opens up a new space for the design of state-of-the-art equivariant models.

paragraphs: TensorNet is a message-passing neural network for molecular systems that respects O(3) symmetry, including rotations and reflections. Its central design choice is to represent atoms using Cartesian tensors. This gives the model structured geometric features while simplifying feature mixing through ordinary matrix products.

The architecture can efficiently separate these tensors into components corresponding to scalars, vectors, and tensors. Those components can then be processed separately when needed. The approach combines symmetry-aware representation with relatively simple operations, aiming to reduce the cost of learning molecular quantities without giving up geometric structure.

Compared with higher-rank spherical tensor models, TensorNet reports state-of-the-art performance with substantially fewer parameters and reduced computational cost. For small-molecule potential energies, that performance can be achieved with a single interaction layer. The framework also allows accurate prediction of vector and tensor molecular quantities alongside energies and forces. These findings present Cartesian tensor embeddings as an effective design option for efficient equivariant molecular models.
summary.tldr: TensorNet uses Cartesian tensor embeddings to achieve strong equivariant molecular predictions with fewer parameters and lower computational cost.

title: TensorNet: Cartesian Tensor Representations for Efficient Learning of Molecular Potentials

abstract: As society transitions towards an AI-based decision-making infrastructure, an ever-increasing number of decisions once under control of humans are now delegated to automated systems. Even though such developments make various parts of society more efficient, a large body of evidence suggests that a great deal of care needs to be taken to make such automated decision-making systems fair and equitable, namely, taking into account sensitive attributes such as gender, race, and religion. In this paper, we study a specific decision-making task called outcome control in which an automated system aims to optimize an outcome variable $Y$ while being fair and equitable. The interest in such a setting ranges from interventions related to criminal justice and welfare, all the way to clinical decision-making and public health. In this paper, we first analyze through causal lenses the notion of benefit, which captures how much a specific individual would benefit from a positive decision, counterfactually speaking, when contrasted with an alternative, negative one. We introduce the notion of benefit fairness, which can be seen as the minimal fairness requirement in decision-making, and develop an algorithm for satisfying it. We then note that the benefit itself may be influenced by the protected attribute, and propose causal tools which can be used to analyze this. Finally, if some of the variations of the protected attribute in the benefit are considered as discriminatory, the notion of benefit fairness may need to be strengthened, which leads us to articulating a notion of causal benefit fairness. Using this notion, we develop a new optimization procedure capable of maximizing $Y$ while ascertaining causal fairness in the decision process.

summary.tldr: The paper develops fairness constraints and outcome optimization around individual benefit and potentially discriminatory causal influences on that benefit.

title: Causal Fairness for Outcome Control

abstract: Conditional independence (CI) testing is a fundamental and challenging task in modern statistics and machine learning. Many modern methods for CI testing rely on powerful supervised learning methods to learn regression functions or Bayes predictors as an intermediate step; we refer to this class of tests as regression-based tests. Although these methods are guaranteed to control Type-I error when the supervised learning methods accurately estimate the regression functions or Bayes predictors of interest, their behavior is less understood when they fail due to misspecified inductive biases; in other words, when the employed models are not flexible enough or when the training algorithm does not induce the desired predictors. Then, we study the performance of regression-based CI tests under misspecified inductive biases. Namely, we propose new approximations or upper bounds for the testing errors of three regression-based tests that depend on misspecification errors. Moreover, we introduce the Rao-Blackwellized Predictor Test (RBPT), a regression-based CI test robust against misspecified inductive biases. Finally, we conduct experiments with artificial and real data, showcasing the usefulness of our theory and methods.

paragraphs: Conditional independence testing asks whether variables remain related after accounting for other information. Many modern tests first train predictive models, then use those predictions in a statistical test. Their guarantees against false positives depend on accurately learning the required regression functions or Bayes predictors. This paper examines what happens when that intermediate learning step goes wrong.

The failure can arise because the model family lacks sufficient flexibility or because training does not produce the desired predictor. The authors describe these problems as misspecified inductive biases. For three regression-based tests, they derive new approximations or upper bounds for testing errors that explicitly depend on prediction misspecification. This connects weaknesses in the learned predictor to the reliability of the subsequent statistical conclusion.

The paper also introduces the Rao-Blackwellized Predictor Test, designed to be robust against these misspecified biases. Experiments on artificial and real data demonstrate the usefulness of both the analysis and the proposed method. The contribution makes prediction error part of the testing analysis and offers a test intended to tolerate it more effectively.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes how misspecified predictors affect conditional independence tests and introduces a test robust to such misspecification.

title: Conditional independence testing under misspecified inductive biases

abstract: In this work, we study the low-rank MDPs with adversarially changed losses in the full-information feedback setting. In particular, the unknown transition probability kernel admits a low-rank matrix decomposition \citep{REPUCB22}, and the loss functions may change adversarially but are revealed to the learner at the end of each episode. We propose a policy optimization-based algorithm POLO, and we prove that it attains the $\widetilde{O}(K^{\frac{5}{6}}A^{\frac{1}{2}}d\ln(1+M)/(1-\gamma)^2)$ regret guarantee, where $d$ is rank of the transition kernel (and hence the dimension of the unknown representations), $A$ is the cardinality of the action space, $M$ is the cardinality of the model class that contains all the plausible representations, and $\gamma$ is the discounted factor. Notably, our algorithm is oracle-efficient and has a regret guarantee with no dependence on the size of potentially arbitrarily large state space. Furthermore, we also prove an $\Omega(\frac{\gamma^2}{1-\gamma} \sqrt{d A K})$ regret lower bound for this problem, showing that low-rank MDPs are statistically more difficult to learn than linear MDPs in the regret minimization setting. To the best of our knowledge, we present the first algorithm that interleaves representation learning, exploration, and exploitation to achieve the sublinear regret guarantee for RL with nonlinear function approximation and adversarial losses.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when the environment's transition model is unknown and losses can change adversarially between episodes. It assumes that transitions have a low-rank decomposition and that each episode's loss function is fully revealed afterward. This feedback setting gives the learner more information than observing only the losses of its chosen actions.

The proposed policy-optimization algorithm, POLO, interleaves learning a representation, exploring the environment, and exploiting what has been learned. Its regret bound grows as K^(5/6) with the number of episodes, alongside factors involving transition rank, action count, model-class size, and discounting. Because growth in K is sublinear, the bound gives diminishing average regret over sufficiently many episodes.

POLO is oracle-efficient, and its regret guarantee does not depend on the size of the state space, which may be arbitrarily large. A separate lower bound establishes that low-rank MDPs are statistically harder than linear MDPs in this regret setting. Together, the results show both the feasibility of learning under these assumptions and a meaningful difficulty introduced by the broader representation class.
summary.tldr: POLO achieves sublinear regret in unknown low-rank environments with adversarial losses and full-information feedback, without state-space-size dependence.

title: Learning Adversarial Low-rank Markov Decision Processes with Unknown Transition and Full-information Feedback

abstract: Temporal difference (TD) learning is often used to update the estimate of the value function which is used by RL agents to extract useful policies. In this paper, we focus on value function estimation in continual reinforcement learning. We propose to decompose the value function into two components which update at different timescales: a _permanent_ value function, which holds general knowledge that persists over time, and a _transient_ value function, which allows quick adaptation to new situations. We establish theoretical results showing that our approach is well suited for continual learning and draw connections to the complementary learning systems (CLS) theory from neuroscience. Empirically, this approach improves performance significantly on both prediction and control problems.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents use value estimates to guide their decisions, and temporal-difference learning is a common way to update those estimates. In continual learning, value estimation must support both knowledge that remains useful over time and adaptation to new situations. This paper addresses that tension by changing how the value function is represented.

The proposed representation has two components that update on different timescales. A permanent component stores general knowledge intended to persist, while a transient component adapts quickly to new circumstances. Together, they separate the roles of retaining useful information and responding to change within the agent's value estimation process.

The authors establish theoretical results supporting the approach's suitability for continual learning and connect it to complementary learning systems theory in neuroscience. Empirical evaluations show significant performance improvements in both prediction and control problems. This matters because the decomposition is relevant both to estimating values and to using those estimates for decisions. The evidence supports combining persistent and rapidly changing knowledge within one value-function framework.
summary.tldr: Splitting value estimates into persistent and rapidly adapting components improves continual reinforcement learning in prediction and control experiments.

title: Prediction and Control in Continual Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We propose a new algorithm for the problem of recovering data that adheres to multiple, heterogenous low-dimensional structures from linear observations. Focussing on data matrices that are simultaneously row-sparse and low-rank, we propose and analyze an iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) algorithm that is able to leverage both structures. In particular, it optimizes a combination of non-convex surrogates for row-sparsity and rank, a balancing of which is built into the algorithm. We prove locally quadratic convergence of the iterates to a simultaneously structured data matrix in a regime of minimal sample complexity (up to constants and a logarithmic factor), which is known to be impossible for a combination of convex surrogates. In experiments, we show that the IRLS method exhibits favorable empirical convergence, identifying simultaneously row-sparse and low-rank matrices from fewer measurements than state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: A matrix can have several simplifying structures at once: only a few rows may be nonzero, while its rows and columns also obey a low-rank structure. This paper studies recovery of such matrices from linear observations. The aim is to exploit both forms of structure together when measurements are limited.

The proposed method uses iteratively reweighted least squares, repeatedly solving weighted fitting problems. Its objective combines nonconvex approximations to row sparsity and rank, with a balancing mechanism built into the algorithm. This joint treatment is intended to use the information supplied by both structures rather than relying on just one.

The authors prove locally quadratic convergence in a regime with nearly minimal sample complexity, allowing constants and a logarithmic factor. The local qualification matters: the result describes convergence near the structured solution. The abstract states that combining convex surrogates cannot achieve this sample regime. Experiments also show favorable convergence and recovery from fewer measurements than the state-of-the-art methods compared.
summary.tldr: A nonconvex reweighted least-squares method jointly exploits row sparsity and low rank, with local quadratic convergence at nearly minimal sample complexity.

title: Recovering Simultaneously Structured Data via Non-Convex Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares

abstract: Diffusion models have recently achieved great success in the synthesis of high-quality images and videos. However, the existing denoising techniques in diffusion models are commonly based on step-by-step noise predictions, which suffers from high computation cost, resulting in a prohibitive latency for interactive applications. In this paper, we propose AdaptiveDiffusion to relieve this bottleneck by adaptively reducing the noise prediction steps during the denoising process. Our method considers the potential of skipping as many noise prediction steps as possible while keeping the final denoised results identical to the original full-step ones. Specifically, the skipping strategy is guided by the third-order latent difference that indicates the stability between timesteps during the denoising process, which benefits the reusing of previous noise prediction results. Extensive experiments on image and video diffusion models demonstrate that our method can significantly speed up the denoising process while generating identical results to the original process, achieving up to an average 2-5x speedup without quality degradation. The code is available at https://github.com/UniModal4Reasoning/AdaptiveDiffusion

paragraphs: Diffusion generation repeatedly predicts noise while progressively denoising an image or video. These repeated predictions make generation expensive and can create excessive latency for interactive use. AdaptiveDiffusion seeks to reduce that cost by deciding during generation when a previous noise prediction can be reused instead of computing a new one.

The skipping decision is guided by a third-order difference in the latent sequence, which the method uses as an indicator of stability across timesteps. When the sequence is sufficiently stable according to this strategy, reusing a previous prediction can avoid another prediction step. The method is training-free and aims to skip as many such computations as possible while preserving the output of the full-step process.

Experiments on image and video diffusion models report outputs identical to the original process, without quality degradation, and average speedups in the reported two-to-five-fold range. This evidence supports adaptive reuse as a way to reduce denoising latency in the evaluated models. The output-preservation result is an experimental finding, rather than a stated universal guarantee for every diffusion model and generated sample.
summary.tldr: AdaptiveDiffusion skips noise predictions based on latent stability, reporting faster generation with unchanged outputs in image and video experiments.

title: Training-Free Adaptive Diffusion with Bounded Difference Approximation Strategy

abstract: This paper studies the challenging task of makeup transfer, which aims to apply diverse makeup styles precisely and naturally to a given facial image. Due to the absence of paired data, current methods typically synthesize sub-optimal pseudo ground truths to guide the model training, resulting in low makeup fidelity. Additionally, different makeup styles generally have varying effects on the person face, but existing methods struggle to deal with this diversity. To address these issues, we propose a novel Self-supervised Hierarchical Makeup Transfer (SHMT) method via latent diffusion models. Following a "decoupling-and-reconstruction" paradigm, SHMT works in a self-supervised manner, freeing itself from the misguidance of imprecise pseudo-paired data. Furthermore, to accommodate a variety of makeup styles, hierarchical texture details are decomposed via a Laplacian pyramid and selectively introduced to the content representation. Finally, we design a novel Iterative Dual Alignment (IDA) module that dynamically adjusts the injection condition of the diffusion model, allowing the alignment errors caused by the domain gap between content and makeup representations to be corrected. Extensive quantitative and qualitative analyses demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at https://github.com/Snowfallingplum/SHMT.

paragraphs: Makeup transfer aims to apply a makeup style precisely and naturally to a facial image. Training is difficult because paired examples are unavailable, leading existing methods to rely on imperfect synthetic targets. Different makeup styles also affect facial appearance in different ways, creating a need to accommodate variation in texture and style.

SHMT uses latent diffusion with a self-supervised decoupling-and-reconstruction approach, avoiding dependence on imprecise pseudo-paired training targets. It decomposes texture details hierarchically through a Laplacian pyramid and selectively introduces those details into the content representation. This gives the method a mechanism for handling makeup styles with differing effects on the face.

An Iterative Dual Alignment module dynamically adjusts the diffusion model's conditioning to correct alignment errors arising from differences between the content and makeup representations. Quantitative and qualitative analyses demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The components address complementary parts of the task: obtaining training supervision, representing varied texture details, and improving alignment as the diffusion model applies the makeup.
summary.tldr: SHMT combines self-supervised latent diffusion, hierarchical texture details, and iterative alignment to improve makeup transfer without pseudo-paired supervision.

title: SHMT: Self-supervised Hierarchical Makeup Transfer via Latent Diffusion Models

abstract: Evaluating policies using off-policy data is crucial for applying reinforcement learning to real-world problems such as healthcare and autonomous driving. Previous methods for *off-policy evaluation* (OPE) generally suffer from high variance or irreducible bias, leading to unacceptably high prediction errors. In this work, we introduce STAR, a framework for OPE that encompasses a broad range of estimators -- which include existing OPE methods as special cases -- that achieve lower mean squared prediction errors. STAR leverages state abstraction to distill complex, potentially continuous problems into compact, discrete models which we call *abstract reward processes* (ARPs). Predictions from ARPs estimated from off-policy data are provably consistent (asymptotically correct). Rather than proposing a specific estimator, we present a new framework for OPE and empirically demonstrate that estimators within STAR outperform existing methods. The best STAR estimator outperforms baselines in all twelve cases studied, and even the median STAR estimator surpasses the baselines in seven out of the twelve cases.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a policy would perform using data collected under a different policy. This is valuable when directly testing a new policy is difficult. Existing estimators can face a tradeoff between unstable predictions caused by high variance and systematic errors that remain even as more data become available.

The paper introduces STAR, a framework that simplifies complex state spaces into compact, discrete models called abstract reward processes. These abstractions let the framework work with problems whose original states may be continuous. STAR encompasses multiple estimators, including existing approaches as special cases, rather than prescribing a single estimation procedure.

The authors prove that predictions from abstract reward processes estimated using off-policy data are consistent, meaning they become correct asymptotically. Their experiments also examine practical prediction error: the best STAR estimator beats the baselines in all twelve studied cases, while the median STAR estimator does so in seven. These findings support the framework's usefulness while distinguishing its long-run correctness guarantee from its observed finite-data performance.
summary.tldr: STAR uses compact state abstractions to support consistent off-policy evaluation and empirically reduce prediction error.

title: Abstract Reward Processes: Leveraging State Abstraction for Consistent Off-Policy Evaluation

abstract: We study a dynamic pricing problem for third-party platform service fees under strategic, far-sighted customers. In each time period, the platform sets a service fee based on historical data, observes the resulting transaction quantities, and collects revenue. The platform also monitors equilibrium prices influenced by both demand and supply. The objective is to maximize total revenue over a time horizon $T$. Our problem incorporates three practical challenges: (a) initially, the platform lacks knowledge of the demand side beforehand, necessitating a balance between exploring (learning the demand curve) and exploiting (maximizing revenue) simultaneously; (b) since only equilibrium prices and quantities are observable, traditional Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) estimators would be biased and inconsistent; (c) buyers are rational and strategic, seeking to maximize their consumer surplus and potentially misrepresenting their preferences. To address these challenges, we propose novel algorithmic solutions. Our approach involves: (i) a carefully designed active randomness injection to balance exploration and exploitation effectively; (ii) using non-i.i.d. actions as instrumental variables (IV) to consistently estimate demand; (iii) a low-switching cost design that promotes nearly truthful buyer behavior. We show an expected regret bound of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}} (\sqrt{T}\wedge\sigma_S^{-2})$ and demonstrate its optimality, up to logarithmic factors, with respect to both the time horizon $T$ and the randomness in supply $\sigma_S$. Despite its simplicity, our model offers valuable insights into the use of actions as estimation instruments, the benefits of low-switching pricing policies in mitigating strategic buyer behavior, and the role of supply randomness in facilitating exploration which leads to a phase transition of policy performance.

paragraphs: The paper studies a platform that repeatedly sets service fees to maximize revenue while learning demand. It observes transaction quantities and equilibrium prices shaped by both buyers and sellers. This creates two complications: ordinary least squares produces biased, inconsistent demand estimates, and forward-looking buyers may strategically misrepresent their preferences to improve their own outcomes.

The proposed algorithms combine deliberate random variation, instrumental-variable estimation, and a pricing design with low switching costs. The platform's actions serve as instruments for consistently estimating demand, even though those actions are not independent and identically distributed. The low-switching design encourages nearly truthful buyer behavior, while randomness helps balance gathering information with earning revenue.

The authors prove an expected regret bound, ignoring logarithmic factors, given by the smaller of the square root of the time horizon and the inverse square of supply randomness. They show this dependence is optimal up to logarithmic factors. The result identifies a change between performance regimes: randomness already present in supply can facilitate exploration and alter how the revenue shortfall scales.
summary.tldr: The paper develops provably efficient service-fee policies that learn demand through pricing actions while accounting for strategic buyers and supply randomness.

title: Dynamic Service Fee Pricing under Strategic Behavior: Actions as Instruments and Phase Transition

abstract: Existing Maximum-Entropy (MaxEnt) Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods for continuous action spaces are typically formulated based on actor-critic frameworks and optimized through alternating steps of policy evaluation and policy improvement. In the policy evaluation steps, the critic is updated to capture the soft Q-function. In the policy improvement steps, the actor is adjusted in accordance with the updated soft Q-function. In this paper, we introduce a new MaxEnt RL framework modeled using Energy-Based Normalizing Flows (EBFlow). This framework integrates the policy evaluation steps and the policy improvement steps, resulting in a single objective training process. Our method enables the calculation of the soft value function used in the policy evaluation target without Monte Carlo approximation. Moreover, this design supports the modeling of multi-modal action distributions while facilitating efficient action sampling. To evaluate the performance of our method, we conducted experiments on the MuJoCo benchmark suite and a number of high-dimensional robotic tasks simulated by Omniverse Isaac Gym. The evaluation results demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance compared to widely-adopted representative baselines.

paragraphs: Maximum-entropy reinforcement learning methods for continuous actions commonly alternate between evaluating a policy and improving it. A critic learns the soft Q-function, and an actor then adjusts its behavior using that estimate. This paper proposes an energy-based normalizing-flow framework that integrates these two steps into a single training objective.

The framework also changes how quantities needed for learning and action selection are computed. It can calculate the soft value function used in the policy-evaluation target without a Monte Carlo approximation. Its action distribution can contain multiple modes, allowing several distinct action regions to receive high probability, while still supporting efficient sampling.

The authors evaluate the method on MuJoCo and on high-dimensional robotic tasks simulated in Omniverse Isaac Gym. They report better performance than widely used representative baselines. The contribution combines a unified learning objective with a flexible action distribution and direct soft-value calculation. Together, these properties offer an alternative to the alternating actor-critic formulation in the continuous-control settings studied, with the empirical comparisons supporting the effectiveness of that combination.
summary.tldr: An energy-based normalizing flow unifies maximum-entropy policy evaluation and improvement while supporting multimodal actions and direct soft-value calculation.

title: Maximum Entropy Reinforcement Learning via Energy-Based Normalizing Flow

abstract: We explore uncertainty quantification in large language models (LLMs), with the goal to identify when uncertainty in responses given a query is large. We simultaneously consider both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainties, where the former comes from the lack of knowledge about the ground truth (such as about facts or the language), and the latter comes from irreducible randomness (such as multiple possible answers). In particular, we derive an information-theoretic metric that allows to reliably detect when only epistemic uncertainty is large, in which case the output of the model is unreliable. This condition can be computed based solely on the output of the model obtained simply by some special iterative prompting based on the previous responses. Such quantification, for instance, allows to detect hallucinations (cases when epistemic uncertainty is high) in both single- and multi-answer responses. This is in contrast to many standard uncertainty quantification strategies (such as thresholding the log-likelihood of a response) where hallucinations in the multi-answer case cannot be detected. We conduct a series of experiments which demonstrate the advantage of our formulation. Further, our investigations shed some light on how the probabilities assigned to a given output by an LLM can be amplified by iterative prompting, which might be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Uncertainty in a language-model response can have different causes. Epistemic uncertainty reflects missing knowledge about the truth, while aleatoric uncertainty can arise because several answers are possible. This paper aims to distinguish these sources so that uncertainty caused by a knowledge gap can be identified even when legitimate answer variation is also present.

The authors derive an information-theoretic metric for detecting high epistemic uncertainty. It can be computed using only model outputs from a special iterative prompting process, in which earlier responses inform later prompts. The approach therefore obtains its signal through repeated interaction with the model and supports analysis of both single-answer and multiple-answer responses.

Experiments demonstrate advantages over standard uncertainty strategies, including response log-likelihood thresholding, which the authors identify as unable to detect hallucinations in the multiple-answer case. The work also explores how iterative prompting can amplify the probability assigned to an output. Its central contribution is a way to separate unreliable knowledge from uncertainty that accompanies a range of possible answers.
summary.tldr: An output-only metric uses iterative prompting to distinguish uncertainty from missing knowledge from uncertainty due to multiple possible answers.

title: To Believe or Not to Believe Your LLM: Iterative Prompting for Estimating Epistemic Uncertainty

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a range of scientific tasks including mathematics, physics, and chemistry. Despite their successes, the effectiveness of LLMs in handling complex statistical tasks remains systematically under-explored. To bridge this gap, we introduce StatQA, a new benchmark designed for statistical analysis tasks. StatQA comprises 11,623 examples tailored to evaluate LLMs' proficiency in specialized statistical tasks and their applicability assessment capabilities, particularly for hypothesis testing methods. We systematically experiment with representative LLMs using various prompting strategies and show that even state-of-the-art models such as GPT-4o achieve a best performance of only 64.83%, indicating significant room for improvement. Notably, while open-source LLMs (e.g. LLaMA-3) show limited capability, those fine-tuned ones exhibit marked improvements, outperforming all in-context learning-based methods (e.g. GPT-4o). Moreover, our comparative human experiments highlight a striking contrast in error types between LLMs and humans: LLMs primarily make applicability errors, whereas humans mostly make statistical task confusion errors. This divergence highlights distinct areas of proficiency and deficiency, suggesting that combining LLM and human expertise could lead to complementary strengths, inviting further investigation into their collaborative potential. Our source code and data are available at https://statqa.github.io/.

paragraphs: Statistical analysis requires more than recognizing the name of a procedure: a model must also determine whether that procedure applies to the problem. This paper introduces StatQA to evaluate both specialized statistical tasks and judgments about method applicability, with particular attention to hypothesis testing. The benchmark contains 11,623 examples.

The authors test representative language models with several prompting strategies. GPT-4o reaches a best reported performance of 64.83%, showing substantial remaining difficulty on the benchmark. Open-source models such as LLaMA-3 initially show limited capability, but fine-tuned models improve markedly and outperform all the evaluated approaches that rely on examples supplied in context.

Comparisons with human participants reveal a difference in the kinds of mistakes made. Models mainly choose methods where they do not apply, while humans more often confuse the statistical task itself. These findings distinguish procedural knowledge from knowing when to use it. They also motivate investigating human–model collaboration, although complementary error patterns alone do not demonstrate that such collaboration will improve results.
summary.tldr: StatQA finds substantial weaknesses in language models’ statistical judgments, especially deciding when a method applies, while fine-tuning improves performance.

title: Are Large Language Models Good Statisticians?

abstract: Pretrained language models can encode a large amount of knowledge and utilize it for various reasoning tasks, yet they can still struggle to learn novel factual knowledge effectively from finetuning on limited textual demonstrations. In this work, we show that the reason for this deficiency is that language models are biased to learn word co-occurrence statistics instead of true factual associations. We identify the differences between two forms of knowledge representation in language models: knowledge in the form of co-occurrence statistics is encoded in the middle layers of the transformer model and does not generalize well to reasoning scenarios beyond simple question answering, while true factual associations are encoded in the lower layers and can be freely utilized in various reasoning tasks. Based on these observations, we propose two strategies to improve the learning of factual associations in language models. We show that training on text with implicit rather than explicit factual associations can force the model to learn factual associations instead of co-occurrence statistics, significantly improving the generalization of newly learned knowledge. We also propose a simple training method to actively forget the learned co-occurrence statistics, which unblocks and enhances the learning of factual associations when training on plain narrative text. On both synthetic and real-world corpora, the two proposed strategies improve the generalization of the knowledge learned during finetuning to reasoning scenarios such as indirect and multi-hop question answering.

paragraphs: This paper studies why language models can struggle to learn new facts from limited fine-tuning text. The authors identify a bias toward learning which words appear together rather than learning factual relationships that remain useful across different reasoning tasks. A model may consequently answer a straightforward question without applying the same knowledge successfully in a more indirect setting.

The study distinguishes two forms of representation. It associates co-occurrence statistics with middle transformer layers and factual associations with lower layers. In the reported analysis, the former transfer poorly beyond simple question answering, whereas the latter support varied reasoning tasks. This distinction motivates changes to how new knowledge is taught.

One strategy trains on text where factual associations are implicit, encouraging the model to learn the underlying relationship. Another actively makes the model forget learned co-occurrence statistics during training on narrative text. On synthetic and real-world corpora, both strategies improve the transfer of newly learned knowledge to indirect and multi-hop questions. The findings connect how knowledge is represented with whether fine-tuning produces reusable reasoning capabilities.
summary.tldr: Two training strategies improve factual generalization by reducing language models’ reliance on word co-occurrence statistics.

title: Co-occurrence is not Factual Association in Language Models

abstract: Recent works show that assembling multiple off-the-shelf large language models (LLMs) can harness their complementary abilities. To achieve this, routing is a promising method, which learns a router to select the most suitable LLM for each query. However, existing routing models are ineffective when multiple LLMs perform well for a query. To address this problem, in this paper, we propose a method called query-based Router by Dual Contrastive learning (RouterDC). The RouterDC model, which consists of an encoder and LLM embeddings, is trained by two proposed contrastive losses (sample-LLM and sample-sample losses). Experimental results show that RouterDC is effective in assembling LLMs and largely outperforms individual top-performing LLMs as well as existing routing methods on both in-distribution (+2.76\%) and out-of-distribution (+1.90\%) tasks. The source code is available at https://github.com/shuhao02/RouterDC.

paragraphs: RouterDC studies how to choose an appropriate language model for each incoming query from a collection of existing models. Different models have complementary abilities, so a good router can make the collection more useful than any one member. The paper focuses on a difficulty for existing routers: several models may all perform well on the same query.

The proposed router consists of an encoder and learned embeddings for the available language models. Training uses two contrastive objectives, one relating samples to models and another relating samples to samples. This dual structure makes both query-model relationships and relationships among queries part of the routing representation, addressing the ambiguity created when a query has several capable model choices.

The authors report that RouterDC outperforms individual top-performing models and existing routing approaches. Reported gains are 2.76% on in-distribution tasks and 1.90% on out-of-distribution tasks. These results support query-dependent model selection as a way to combine complementary strengths, with the dual contrastive training objective providing the paper's specific mechanism for learning that selection.
summary.tldr: RouterDC learns query-to-model routing with two contrastive losses, improving the performance of assembled language models on familiar and shifted task distributions.

title: RouterDC: Query-Based Router by Dual Contrastive Learning for Assembling Large Language Models

abstract: Audio deepfake detection (ADD) is crucial to combat the misuse of speech synthesized by generative AI models. Existing ADD models suffer from generalization issues to unseen attacks, with a large performance discrepancy between in-domain and out-of-domain data. Moreover, the black-box nature of existing models limits their use in real-world scenarios, where explanations are required for model decisions. To alleviate these issues, we introduce a new ADD model that explicitly uses the Style-LInguistics Mismatch (SLIM) in fake speech to separate them from real speech. SLIM first employs self-supervised pretraining on only real samples to learn the style-linguistics dependency in the real class. The learned features are then used in complement with standard pretrained acoustic features (e.g., Wav2vec) to learn a classifier on the real and fake classes. When the feature encoders are frozen, SLIM outperforms benchmark methods on out-of-domain datasets while achieving competitive results on in-domain data. The features learned by SLIM allow us to quantify the (mis)match between style and linguistic content in a sample, hence facilitating an explanation of the model decision.

paragraphs: Audio deepfake detectors often lose effectiveness on synthesis attacks they have not encountered during training. Their decisions can also be difficult to explain. SLIM addresses both issues by examining the relationship between speaking style and linguistic content. The proposed signal is a mismatch between these aspects of speech that can help distinguish fabricated audio from real recordings.

The method first uses self-supervised pretraining on real speech alone to learn dependencies between style and language. It then combines these learned features with standard pretrained acoustic features, such as Wav2vec representations, to train a classifier on real and fake samples. The mismatch features thus complement the broader acoustic information available to the detector.

With feature encoders frozen, SLIM outperforms benchmark methods on out-of-domain datasets while remaining competitive on in-domain data. Its learned features also quantify how closely style and linguistic content match in a sample, providing a basis for explaining a decision. The findings support this explicit relationship as both a generalization signal and an interpretable component of the evaluated detector.
summary.tldr: SLIM learns style-language dependencies in real speech to improve deepfake detection on unfamiliar data and help explain its decisions.

title: SLIM: Style-Linguistics Mismatch Model for Generalized Audio Deepfake Detection

abstract: Assistive agents should make humans' lives easier. Classically, such assistance is studied through the lens of inverse reinforcement learning, where an assistive agent (e.g., a chatbot, a robot) infers a human's intention and then selects actions to help the human reach that goal. This approach requires inferring intentions, which can be difficult in high-dimensional settings. We build upon prior work that studies assistance through the lens of empowerment: an assistive agent aims to maximize the influence of the human's actions such that they exert a greater control over the environmental outcomes and can solve tasks in fewer steps. We lift the major limitation of prior work in this area—scalability to high-dimensional settings—with contrastive successor representations. We formally prove that these representations estimate a similar notion of empowerment to that studied by prior work and provide a ready-made mechanism for optimizing it. Empirically, our proposed method outperforms prior methods on synthetic benchmarks, and scales to Overcooked, a cooperative game setting. Theoretically, our work connects ideas from information theory, neuroscience, and reinforcement learning, and charts a path for representations to play a critical role in solving assistive problems. Our code is available at https://github.com/vivekmyers/empowerment_successor_representations.

paragraphs: Assistive agents are often designed to infer a person's intention and then help achieve it. That inference can be difficult in high-dimensional environments. This paper instead builds on empowerment: assistance aims to increase how much influence the person's actions have over environmental outcomes, giving them greater control and helping them complete tasks in fewer steps.

The technical contribution uses contrastive successor representations to make this approach scalable. These representations support both estimating an empowerment-related quantity and optimizing it. The authors formally establish that the estimated quantity corresponds to a notion of empowerment similar to the one studied in earlier work. This provides a mathematical connection between the learned representation and the assistance objective.

Experiments show improvements over prior methods on synthetic benchmarks and demonstrate scaling to the cooperative game Overcooked. The results support representation learning as a practical route to empowerment-based assistance in more complex settings. The approach's defining choice is to make human actions more effective without first requiring an inferred reward function that specifies the human's intended goal.
summary.tldr: Contrastive successor representations help assistive agents increase human control without first inferring human rewards.

title: Learning to Assist Humans without Inferring Rewards

abstract: Despite many recent works on Mixture of Experts (MoEs) for resource-efficient Transformer language models, existing methods mostly focus on MoEs for feedforward layers. Previous attempts at extending MoE to the self-attention layer fail to match the performance of the parameter-matched baseline. Our novel SwitchHead is an effective MoE method for the attention layer that successfully reduces both the compute and memory requirements, achieving wall-clock speedup, while matching the language modeling performance of the baseline Transformer. Our novel MoE mechanism allows SwitchHead to compute up to 8 times fewer attention matrices than the standard Transformer. SwitchHead can also be combined with MoE feedforward layers, resulting in fully-MoE "SwitchAll" Transformers. For our 262M parameter model trained on C4, SwitchHead matches the perplexity of standard models with only 44% compute and 27% memory usage. Zero-shot experiments on downstream tasks confirm the performance of SwitchHead, e.g., achieving more than 3.5% absolute improvements on BliMP compared to the baseline with an equal compute resource.

paragraphs: SwitchHead brings mixture-of-experts computation to Transformer attention. Much prior work applies this idea to feedforward layers, while earlier attention extensions struggled to match parameter-matched Transformer baselines. The paper presents an attention mechanism that reduces compute and memory requirements while matching baseline language modeling performance and delivering measured execution speedups.

The mechanism can compute up to eight times fewer attention matrices than a standard Transformer. It can also be combined with mixture-of-experts feedforward layers to create the authors’ SwitchAll models. This expands the scope of expert-based efficiency improvements beyond a single type of Transformer layer and makes attention itself a target for resource savings.

For a 262-million-parameter model trained on C4, SwitchHead matches standard-model perplexity using 44% of the compute and 27% of the memory. Zero-shot downstream evaluations also support its performance; on BliMP, it improves by more than 3.5 absolute percentage points against an equal-compute baseline. These results distinguish the benefits of maintaining quality with fewer resources from improving quality under a matched compute budget.
summary.tldr: SwitchHead applies mixture-of-experts attention to reduce Transformer compute and memory while preserving reported language modeling quality.

title: SwitchHead: Accelerating Transformers with Mixture-of-Experts Attention

abstract: While traditional federated learning (FL) typically focuses on a star topology where clients are directly connected to a central server, real-world distributed systems often exhibit hierarchical architectures. Hierarchical FL (HFL) has emerged as a promising solution to bridge this gap, leveraging aggregation points at multiple levels of the system. However, existing algorithms for HFL encounter challenges in dealing with multi-timescale model drift, i.e., model drift occurring across hierarchical levels of data heterogeneity. In this paper, we propose a multi-timescale gradient correction (MTGC) methodology to resolve this issue. Our key idea is to introduce distinct control variables to (i) correct the client gradient towards the group gradient, i.e., to reduce client model drift caused by local updates based on individual datasets, and (ii) correct the group gradient towards the global gradient, i.e., to reduce group model drift caused by FL over clients within the group. We analytically characterize the convergence behavior of MTGC under general non-convex settings, overcoming challenges associated with couplings between correction terms. We show that our convergence bound is immune to the extent of data heterogeneity, confirming the stability of the proposed algorithm against multi-level non-i.i.d. data. Through extensive experiments on various datasets and models, we validate the effectiveness of MTGC in diverse HFL settings. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/wenzhifang/MTGC.

paragraphs: Federated learning systems can have several aggregation levels, with clients organized into groups before their updates reach a global model. Different datasets can cause individual clients to drift away from their group’s direction, while groups also drift away from the global direction. These effects occur across multiple update timescales, complicating training in hierarchical systems.

Multi-Timescale Gradient Correction addresses the two sources of drift with separate control variables. One corrects client gradients toward the group gradient. Another corrects group gradients toward the global gradient. This design explicitly accounts for the hierarchy instead of treating data differences as a single source of disagreement.

The authors analyze convergence for general non-convex objectives while handling interactions between the correction terms. Their convergence bound does not depend on the extent of data heterogeneity, providing theoretical support for stability across differing client and group datasets. Experiments on multiple datasets and models also support the method’s effectiveness. The contribution combines a correction mechanism matched to the system structure with an analysis of how its coupled updates converge.
summary.tldr: Separate corrections for client and group gradients stabilize hierarchical federated learning, with a convergence bound independent of data heterogeneity.

title: Hierarchical Federated Learning with Multi-Timescale Gradient Correction

abstract: Solving Olympiad-level mathematical problems represents a significant advancement in machine intelligence and automated reasoning. Current machine learning methods, however, struggle to solve Olympiad-level problems beyond Euclidean plane geometry due to a lack of large-scale, high-quality datasets. The challenge is even greater in algebraic systems, which involve infinite reasoning spaces within finite conditions. To address these issues, we propose *AIPS*, an *Algebraic Inequality Proving System* capable of autonomously generating complex inequality theorems and effectively solving Olympiad-level inequality problems without requiring human demonstrations. During proof search in a mixed reasoning manner, a value curriculum learning strategy on generated datasets is implemented to improve proving performance, demonstrating strong mathematical intuitions. On a test set of 20 International Mathematical Olympiad-level inequality problems, AIPS successfully solved 10, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, AIPS automatically generated a vast array of non-trivial theorems without human intervention, some of which have been evaluated by professional contestants and deemed to reach the level of the International Mathematical Olympiad. Notably, one theorem was selected as a competition problem in a major city's 2024 Mathematical Olympiad.All the materials are available at [sites.google.com/view/aips2](https://sites.google.com/view/aips2)

paragraphs: Automated reasoning about algebraic inequalities faces a large space of possible reasoning steps and a shortage of high-quality training examples. AIPS addresses both issues by generating its own complex inequality theorems and learning to prove challenging problems without human demonstrations. Its target is Olympiad-level algebraic inequality reasoning.

The system combines a mixed reasoning approach to proof search with value curriculum learning on generated datasets. This links autonomous problem generation to improvement in proving performance. The generated material supplies training opportunities in a domain where the abstract identifies limited datasets as a major obstacle to existing machine learning methods.

On a test set of 20 problems at International Mathematical Olympiad level, AIPS solves 10 and outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods. It also generates many non-trivial theorems, some judged by professional contestants to reach that level. One generated theorem was selected for a major city's 2024 Mathematical Olympiad. These results demonstrate both solving ability on the tested problems and the potential of autonomous theorem generation.
summary.tldr: AIPS generates its own inequality theorems and solves 10 of 20 Olympiad-level test problems without human demonstrations.

title: Proving Olympiad Algebraic Inequalities without Human Demonstrations

abstract: We present a novel algorithm that efficiently computes near-optimal deterministic policies for constrained reinforcement learning (CRL) problems. Our approach combines three key ideas: (1) value-demand augmentation, (2) action-space approximate dynamic programming, and (3) time-space rounding. Our algorithm constitutes a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) for any time-space recursive (TSR) cost criteria. A TSR criteria requires the cost of a policy to be computable recursively over both time and (state) space, which includes classical expectation, almost sure, and anytime constraints. Our work answers three open questions spanning two long-standing lines of research: polynomial-time approximability is possible for 1) anytime-constrained policies, 2) almost-sure-constrained policies, and 3) deterministic expectation-constrained policies.

paragraphs: Constrained reinforcement learning seeks good decisions while respecting requirements on policy costs. This paper focuses on deterministic policies, which select an action without randomizing the choice. The authors present an algorithm that efficiently finds near-optimal policies for a broad family of constraints, addressing whether useful approximation is possible within polynomial computation time.

The method combines value-demand augmentation, approximate dynamic programming over actions, and rounding across time and state space. Its guarantee applies to time-space recursive cost criteria: the cost must be calculable recursively across both time and states. The abstract identifies expectation constraints, almost-sure constraints, and anytime constraints as members of this family.

For these criteria, the algorithm is a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme. This means its computation scales polynomially with problem size and the inverse approximation tolerance. The result answers three stated open questions about polynomial-time approximation: anytime-constrained policies, almost-sure-constrained policies, and deterministic policies under expectation constraints. Its significance is an efficient approximation guarantee spanning these constraint types, subject to the recursive cost structure.
summary.tldr: A fully polynomial-time approximation scheme computes near-optimal deterministic policies for constraints whose costs admit time-space recursion.

title: Deterministic Policies for Constrained Reinforcement Learning in Polynomial Time

abstract: Video editing is an emerging task, in which most current methods adopt the pre-trained text-to-image (T2I) diffusion model to edit the source video in a zero-shot manner. Despite extensive efforts, maintaining the temporal consistency of edited videos remains challenging due to the lack of temporal constraints in the regular T2I diffusion model. To address this issue, we propose COrrespondence-guided Video Editing (COVE), leveraging the inherent diffusion feature correspondence to achieve high-quality and consistent video editing. Specifically, we propose an efficient sliding-window-based strategy to calculate the similarity among tokens in the diffusion features of source videos, identifying the tokens with high correspondence across frames. During the inversion and denoising process, we sample the tokens in noisy latent based on the correspondence and then perform self-attention within them. To save the usage of GPU memory and accelerate the editing process, we further introduce the temporal-dimensional token merging strategy, which can effectively reduce the redundancy. COVE can be seamlessly integrated into the pre-trained T2I diffusion model without the need for extra training or optimization. Extensive experiment results demonstrate that COVE achieves the start-of-the-art performance in various video editing scenarios, outperforming existing methods both quantitatively and qualitatively. The source code will be released.

paragraphs: COVE tackles temporal consistency when using a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model to edit video. Such models can edit individual images, but their ordinary formulation lacks constraints connecting successive frames. The paper uses correspondences already present in diffusion features to connect related content across a video's frames during editing.

A sliding-window procedure compares feature tokens from the source video and identifies strongly corresponding tokens across frames. During inversion and denoising, COVE uses these correspondences to sample tokens from the noisy latent representation and perform self-attention among them. This gives the editing process a way to coordinate content associated with matching parts of different frames.

The method also merges tokens along the temporal dimension to reduce redundant computation, lower GPU memory use, and accelerate editing. It integrates with pretrained text-to-image diffusion models without additional training or optimization. Across the evaluated editing scenarios, the authors report state-of-the-art results in both quantitative and qualitative comparisons, supporting correspondence-guided attention as a practical mechanism for improving consistency.
summary.tldr: COVE uses diffusion-feature correspondences across frames to improve video-editing consistency without extra training or optimization.

title: COVE: Unleashing the Diffusion Feature Correspondence for Consistent Video Editing

abstract: Revealing the underlying causal mechanisms in the real world is the key to the development of science. Despite the progress in the past decades, traditional causal discovery approaches (CDs) mainly rely on high-quality measured variables, usually given by human experts, to find causal relations. The lack of well-defined high-level variables in many real-world applications has already been a longstanding roadblock to a broader application of CDs. To this end, this paper presents Causal representatiOn AssistanT (COAT) that introduces large language models (LLMs) to bridge the gap. LLMs are trained on massive observations of the world and have demonstrated great capability in extracting key information from unstructured data. Therefore, it is natural to employ LLMs to assist with proposing useful high-level factors and crafting their measurements. Meanwhile, COAT also adopts CDs to find causal relations among the identified variables as well as to provide feedback to LLMs to iteratively refine the proposed factors. We show that LLMs and CDs are mutually beneficial and the constructed feedback provably also helps with the factor proposal. We construct and curate several synthetic and real-world benchmarks including analysis of human reviews and diagnosis of neuropathic and brain tumors, to comprehensively evaluate COAT. Extensive empirical results confirm the effectiveness and reliability of COAT with significant improvements.

paragraphs: Causal discovery methods usually begin with measured variables that experts have already defined. In many applications, deciding what those variables should represent is itself a major obstacle. COAT addresses that earlier stage by using language models to propose meaningful high-level factors from unstructured information and help design ways to measure them.

The framework pairs this language-based work with causal discovery algorithms. Once factors have been proposed, causal discovery estimates relationships among them and sends feedback to the language model. The model then refines its factors, creating an iterative exchange between defining the variables and analyzing their relationships. The authors provide a theoretical result showing that the constructed feedback also helps the factor-proposal process.

Evaluation uses curated synthetic and real-world benchmarks, including human reviews and diagnosis involving neuropathic conditions and brain tumors. The reported experiments show significant improvements and support COAT's effectiveness and reliability. The broader contribution is a workflow that connects extracting candidate concepts from messy data with the structured analysis needed to investigate causal relationships.
summary.tldr: COAT combines language-model factor proposals with causal-discovery feedback to iteratively improve the variables used for causal analysis.

title: Discovery of the Hidden World with Large Language Models

abstract: Accurate estimation of human pose and the pose of interacting objects, like a hockey stick, is crucial for action recognition and performance analysis, particularly in sports. Existing methods capture the object along with the human in the bounding boxes, assuming all keypoints are visible within the bounding box. This necessitates larger bounding boxes to capture the object, introducing unnecessary visual features and hindering performance in real-world cluttered environments. We propose a simple image and text-based multimodal solution TokenCLIPose that addresses this limitation. Our approach focuses solely on human keypoints within the bounding box, treating objects as unseen. TokenCLIPose leverages the rich semantic representations endowed by language for inducing keypoint-specific context, even for occluded keypoints. We evaluate the performance of TokenCLIPose on a real-world Ice-Hockey dataset, and demonstrate its generalizability through zero-shot transfer to a smaller Lacrosse dataset. Additionally, we showcase its flexibility on CrowdPose, a popular occlusion benchmark with keypoints within the bounding box. Our method significantly improves over state-of-the-art approaches on all three datasets, with gains of 4.36\%, 2.35\%, and 3.8\%, respectively.

paragraphs: Estimating a person's pose together with an interacting object is useful for understanding sports actions. Existing methods often enlarge the image crop to include the object, such as a hockey stick. That also brings in background clutter. TokenCLIPose instead works with a crop focused on the person and treats the interacting object as unseen.

The model combines image information with language-derived context for individual keypoints. Language representations help supply semantic information when a keypoint is occluded or lies outside the crop. This changes the information available for prediction: the method can use relationships expressed through language without requiring every relevant point to be directly visible inside a larger bounding box.

The authors evaluate TokenCLIPose on Ice-Hockey, test zero-shot transfer to a smaller Lacrosse dataset, and assess occlusion handling on CrowdPose. Reported gains over state-of-the-art approaches are 4.36%, 2.35%, and 3.8%, respectively. These results support the method across sports-specific out-of-crop prediction and a benchmark where the keypoints remain within the bounding box but may be occluded.
summary.tldr: TokenCLIPose uses language-derived keypoint context to predict human and interacting-object poses from person-focused image crops.

title: Seeing Beyond the Crop: Using Language Priors for Out-of-Bounding Box Keypoint Prediction

abstract: When artificial agents are jointly trained to perform collaborative tasks using a communication channel, they develop opaque goal-oriented communication protocols. Good task performance is often considered sufficient evidence that meaningful communication is taking place, but existing empirical results show that communication strategies induced by common objectives can be counterintuitive whilst solving the task nearly perfectly. In this work, we identify a goal-agnostic prerequisite to meaningful communication, which we term semantic consistency, based on the idea that messages should have similar meanings across instances. We provide a formal definition for this idea, and use it to compare the two most common objectives in the field of emergent communication: discrimination and reconstruction. We prove, under mild assumptions, that semantically inconsistent communication protocols can be optimal solutions to the discrimination task, but not to reconstruction. We further show that the reconstruction objective encourages a stricter property, spatial meaningfulness, which also accounts for the distance between messages. Experiments with emergent communication games validate our theoretical results. These findings demonstrate an inherent advantage of distance-based communication goals, and contextualize previous empirical discoveries.

paragraphs: Agents trained together can develop communication protocols that solve a task well yet remain difficult to interpret. This paper asks what makes such communication meaningful beyond successful coordination. It introduces semantic consistency: the requirement that messages carry similar meanings across instances, framed independently of the particular task goal.

The authors formalize that property and compare two common training objectives, discrimination and reconstruction. Under mild assumptions, they prove that semantically inconsistent protocols can be optimal for discrimination but cannot be optimal for reconstruction. This shows that task success alone has different implications depending on the objective used to train communication.

Reconstruction also encourages a stronger property called spatial meaningfulness, which takes distances between messages into account. Experiments with emergent communication games support the theoretical results. The findings give a reason to favor distance-based communication goals when consistent meaning matters, while keeping the theoretical comparison tied to its assumptions. They also help explain why earlier experiments could observe counterintuitive protocols despite nearly perfect task performance.
summary.tldr: Under mild assumptions, reconstruction objectives rule out semantically inconsistent optimal communication protocols that discrimination objectives can permit.

title: Semantics and Spatiality of Emergent Communication

abstract: With the widespread application of Large Language Models (LLMs) to various domains, concerns regarding the trustworthiness of LLMs in safety-critical scenarios have been raised, due to their unpredictable tendency to hallucinate and generate misinformation. Existing LLMs do not have an inherent functionality to provide the users with an uncertainty/confidence metric for each response it generates, making it difficult to evaluate trustworthiness. Although several studies aim to develop uncertainty quantification methods for LLMs, they have fundamental limitations, such as being restricted to classification tasks, requiring additional training and data, considering only lexical instead of semantic information, and being prompt-wise but not response-wise. A new framework is proposed in this paper to address these issues. Semantic density extracts uncertainty/confidence information for each response from a probability distribution perspective in semantic space. It has no restriction on task types and is "off-the-shelf" for new models and tasks. Experiments on seven state-of-the-art LLMs, including the latest Llama 3 and Mixtral-8x22B models, on four free-form question-answering benchmarks demonstrate the superior performance and robustness of semantic density compared to prior approaches.

paragraphs: A language model’s answer does not inherently come with a dependable measure of uncertainty. Existing approaches can be restricted to classification, require extra training, focus on wording rather than meaning, or assign confidence to an entire prompt instead of a particular answer. Semantic density is proposed to address these obstacles through response-level confidence measurement.

The framework interprets uncertainty using a probability-distribution perspective in semantic space, where the relevant information concerns meaning. It produces a confidence measure for each response and is presented as usable with new models and tasks without additional task-specific training or data. The method is not restricted to a particular task type, allowing evaluation on freely generated answers.

Experiments cover seven language models, including Llama 3 and Mixtral-8x22B, across four free-form question-answering benchmarks. The authors report better performance and robustness than prior approaches. These results support semantic density as a practical confidence-estimation method in the tested settings, with its response-level focus allowing different answers to the same prompt to receive their own uncertainty assessments.
summary.tldr: Semantic density estimates confidence for individual LLM responses from their meaning, without requiring additional training.

title: Semantic Density: Uncertainty Quantification for Large Language Models through Confidence Measurement in Semantic Space

abstract: Data curation is an essential component of large-scale pretraining. In this work, we demonstrate that jointly prioritizing batches of data is more effective for learning than selecting examples independently. Multimodal contrastive objectives expose the dependencies between data and thus naturally yield criteria for measuring the joint learnability of a batch. We derive a simple and tractable algorithm for selecting such batches, which significantly accelerate training beyond individually-prioritized data points. As performance improves by selecting from large super-batches, we also leverage recent advances in model approximation to reduce the computational overhead of scoring. As a result, our approach—multimodal contrastive learning with joint example selection (JEST)—surpasses state-of-the-art pretraining methods with up to 13× fewer iterations and 10× less computation. Essential to the performance of JEST is the ability to steer the data selection process towards the distribution of smaller, well-curated datasets via pretrained reference models, exposing data curation as a new dimension for neural scaling laws.
