paragraphs: Training-data selection often evaluates examples separately, but examples can affect one another’s usefulness within a batch. This paper studies that interaction in multimodal contrastive learning. It shows that selecting groups of examples according to their joint learnability can accelerate training more effectively than prioritizing each example independently.

The proposed method, JEST, derives a tractable batch-selection algorithm from the dependencies exposed by the contrastive objective. It selects training batches from larger candidate super-batches. Because scoring larger pools adds computational work, the method also uses model approximation to reduce that overhead. Pretrained reference models guide selection toward the distribution of smaller, carefully curated datasets.

The authors report surpassing leading pretraining methods with up to 13 times fewer iterations and 10 times less computation. These are reported best-case reductions, rather than fixed savings for every training run. The reference models’ guidance is essential to the stated performance, showing how a relatively small curated dataset can shape the use of a larger collection and make data selection an additional factor in scaling model training.
summary.tldr: JEST jointly selects multimodal training batches, reporting strong pretraining results with up to 10 times less computation.

title: Data curation via joint example selection further accelerates multimodal learning

abstract: Online bipartite matching is a fundamental problem in online optimization, extensively studied both in its integral and fractional forms due to its theoretical significance and practical applications, such as online advertising and resource allocation. Motivated by recent progress in learning-augmented algorithms, we study online bipartite fractional matching when the algorithm is given advice in the form of a suggested matching in each iteration. We develop algorithms for both the vertex-weighted and unweighted variants that provably dominate the naive ``coin flip'' strategy of randomly choosing between the advice-following and advice-free algorithms. Moreover, our algorithm for the vertex-weighted setting extends to the AdWords problem under the small bids assumption, yielding a significant improvement over the seminal work of Mahdian, Nazerzadeh, and Saberi (EC 2007, TALG 2012). Complementing our positive results, we establish a hardness bound on the robustness-consistency tradeoff that is attainable by any algorithm. We empirically validate our algorithms through experiments on synthetic and real-world data.

paragraphs: This paper studies online fractional matching, where allocation decisions arrive sequentially and can divide assignments fractionally. The algorithm receives advice in the form of a suggested matching at each iteration. The central question is how to benefit from useful advice while retaining protection when that advice is unreliable.

The authors develop algorithms for both unweighted and vertex-weighted matching. Their guarantees improve on a simple randomized strategy that chooses between following advice and using an algorithm that ignores it. The vertex-weighted approach also extends to the AdWords allocation problem under the small bids assumption, where the paper reports a significant improvement over prior work.

The theoretical analysis includes a hardness bound on the achievable trade-off between consistency with helpful advice and robustness to poor advice. This establishes a constraint on what any algorithm can accomplish, alongside the proposed positive results. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data support the methods empirically. Together, the results explain how advice can be integrated more effectively and where fundamental limits remain.
summary.tldr: New online fractional matching algorithms improve the use of advice while establishing limits on the robustness–consistency trade-off.

title: Learning-Augmented Online Bipartite Fractional Matching

abstract: This work presents a novel framework for few-shot 3D part segmentation. Recent advances have demonstrated the significant potential of 2D foundation models for low-shot 3D part segmentation. However, it is still an open problem that how to effectively aggregate 2D knowledge from foundation models to 3D. Existing methods either ignore geometric structures for 3D feature learning or neglects the high-quality grouping clues from SAM, leading to under-segmentation and inconsistent part labels. We devise a novel SAM segment graph-based propagation method, named SegGraph, to explicitly learn geometric features encoded within SAM's segmentation masks. Our method encodes geometric features by modeling mutual overlap and adjacency between segments while preserving intra-segment semantic consistency. We construct a segment graph, conceptually similar to an atlas, where nodes represent segments and edges capture their spatial relationships (overlap/adjacency). Each node adaptively modulates 2D foundation model features, which are then propagated via a graph neural network to learn global geometric structures. To enforce intra-segment semantic consistency, we map segment features to 3D points with a novel view-direction-weighted fusion attenuating contributions from low-quality segments. Extensive experiments on PartNet-E demonstrate that our method outperforms all competing baselines by at least 6.9% mIoU. Further analysis reveals that SegGraph achieves particularly strong performance on small components and part boundaries, demonstrating its superior geometric understanding.

paragraphs: Few-shot 3D part segmentation aims to label object parts with limited annotated examples. Two-dimensional foundation models offer useful visual knowledge, but transferring it into 3D requires preserving geometry and coherent groupings. SegGraph addresses failures such as merged parts and inconsistent labels by explicitly modeling relationships among segments produced by SAM.

The method builds a graph whose nodes are segments and whose edges describe overlap or adjacency. Each node adaptively adjusts features from a 2D foundation model, and a graph neural network propagates information to learn broader geometric structure. The resulting segment features are mapped to 3D points through fusion weighted by viewing direction, reducing contributions from low-quality segments while maintaining consistency within segments.

On PartNet-E, the authors report outperforming every compared baseline by at least 6.9% mIoU, a measure of segmentation overlap. Further analysis shows particularly strong results on small parts and boundaries. These findings support explicitly connecting segment groupings and spatial relationships when transferring 2D model knowledge into detailed 3D part labels.
summary.tldr: SegGraph connects SAM segments through overlap and adjacency graphs to improve few-shot 3D part segmentation, especially for small parts and boundaries.

title: SegGraph: Leveraging Graphs of SAM Segments for Few-Shot 3D Part Segmentation

abstract: Estimating heterogeneous treatment effects (HTEs) is crucial for personalized decision-making. However, this task is challenging in survival analysis, which includes time-to-event data with censored outcomes (e.g., due to study dropout). In this paper, we propose a toolbox of orthogonal survival learners to estimate HTEs from time-to-event data under censoring. Our learners have three main advantages: (i) we show that learners from our toolbox are guaranteed to be orthogonal and thus robust with respect to nuisance estimation errors; (ii) our toolbox allows for incorporating a custom weighting function, which can lead to robustness against different types of low overlap, and (iii) our learners are \emph{model-agnostic} (i.e., they can be combined with arbitrary machine learning models). We instantiate the learners from our toolbox using several weighting functions and, as a result, propose various neural orthogonal survival learners. Some of these coincide with existing survival learners (including survival versions of the DR- and R-learner), while others are novel and further robust w.r.t. low overlap regimes specific to the survival setting (i.e., survival overlap and censoring overlap). We then empirically verify the effectiveness of our learners for HTE estimation in different low-overlap regimes through numerical experiments. In sum, we provide practitioners with a large toolbox of learners that can be used for randomized and observational studies with censored time-to-event data.

paragraphs: This paper develops methods for estimating how treatment effects differ between people when outcomes describe the time until an event. Such data are often censored: a study may stop observing someone before the event occurs, for example after dropout. That incomplete observation makes personalized treatment-effect estimation more challenging.

The proposed toolbox constructs orthogonal survival learners. Orthogonality makes their estimates robust to errors in auxiliary quantities estimated along the way. The framework also accepts custom weighting functions, which can provide robustness when overlap is low. It is model-agnostic, so practitioners can combine the learners with different machine-learning models.

The authors instantiate several neural learners using different weights. Some recover existing survival adaptations of DR- and R-learners, while others add robustness to survival-specific overlap problems involving survival and censoring. Numerical experiments support their effectiveness across different low-overlap regimes. The contribution is a flexible collection of estimators for randomized and observational studies, with weighting choices that address different challenges posed by censored event-time data.
summary.tldr: A model-agnostic toolbox estimates heterogeneous treatment effects from censored event-time data with orthogonality and customizable overlap-sensitive weighting.

title: Orthogonal Survival Learners for Estimating Heterogeneous Treatment Effects from Time-to-Event Data

abstract: Pre-training has proven effective in addressing data scarcity and performance limitations in solving PDE problems with neural operators. However, challenges remain due to the heterogeneity of PDE datasets in equation types, which leads to high errors in mixed training. Additionally, dense pre-training models that scale parameters by increasing network width or depth incur significant inference costs. To tackle these challenges, we propose a novel **M**ixture-**o**f-**E**xperts **P**re-training **O**perator **T**ransformer (**MoE-POT**), a sparse-activated architecture that scales parameters efficiently while controlling inference costs. Specifically, our model adopts a layer-wise router-gating network to dynamically select 4 routed experts from 16 expert networks during inference, enabling the model to focus on equation-specific features. Meanwhile, we also integrate 2 shared experts, aiming to capture common properties of PDE and reduce redundancy among routed experts. The final output is computed as the weighted average of the results from all activated experts. We pre-train models with parameters from 30M to 0.5B on 6 public PDE datasets. Our model with 90M activated parameters achieves up to a 40\% reduction in zero-shot error compared with existing models with 120M activated parameters. Additionally, we conduct interpretability analysis, showing that dataset types can be inferred from router-gating network decisions, which validates the rationality and effectiveness of the MoE architecture.

paragraphs: Pre-training neural PDE solvers on multiple datasets can help with limited data, but different equation types can interfere with one another during mixed training. Simply enlarging a dense model also increases inference costs. MoE-POT addresses both issues using a mixture of experts that increases total model capacity while activating only selected parts for a given input.

At each layer, a routing network selects four of sixteen routed experts. Two additional shared experts are intended to capture properties common across PDEs and reduce duplication among the specialized experts. The activated experts' results are combined through a weighted average. This structure gives the model separate resources for equation-specific information and common mathematical behavior.

The authors pre-train models ranging from 30 million to 500 million parameters on six public PDE datasets. A model with 90 million activated parameters reduces zero-shot error by up to 40% compared with existing models using 120 million activated parameters. Dataset types can also be inferred from routing decisions, supporting the interpretation that the routing network learns meaningful distinctions among the datasets.
summary.tldr: MoE-POT routes PDE inputs among specialized and shared experts, improving reported zero-shot accuracy with fewer activated parameters.

title: Mixture-of-Experts Operator Transformer for Large-Scale PDE Pre-Training

abstract: As one of the state-of-the-art parameter-efficient fine-tuning~(PEFT) methods, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) enables model optimization with reduced computational cost through trainable low-rank matrix. However, the low-rank nature makes it prone to produce a decrease in the representation ability, leading to suboptimal performance. In order to break this limitation, we propose RidgeLoRA, a lightweight architecture like LoRA that incorporates novel architecture and matrix ridge enhanced full-rank approximation, to match the performance of full-rank training, while eliminating the need for high memory and a large number of parameters to restore the rank of matrices. We provide a rigorous mathematical derivation to prove that RidgeLoRA has a better upper bound on the representations than vanilla LoRA. Furthermore, extensive experiments across multiple domains demonstrate that RidgeLoRA achieves better performance than other LoRA variants, and can even match or surpass full-rank training.

In order to break this limitation, we propose RidgeLoRA, a lightweight architecture like LoRA that incorporates novel architecture and matrix ridge enhanced full-rank approximation, to match the performance of full-rank training, while eliminating the need for high memory and a large number of parameters to restore the rank of matrices. paragraphs: Low-Rank Adaptation reduces the cost of fine-tuning by learning compact matrix updates. That low-rank restriction can also reduce representational ability and lead to weaker performance. RidgeLoRA aims to preserve the lightweight character of LoRA while approximating the capabilities of full-rank training more closely.

The method combines a new architecture with a matrix-ridge-enhanced full-rank approximation. Its design avoids requiring high memory usage and large numbers of parameters simply to restore matrix rank. The authors also provide a mathematical derivation establishing a better upper bound on representations than standard LoRA. This theoretical result addresses the representation limitation that motivates the architecture, alongside the empirical investigation of its practical behavior.

Across experiments in multiple domains, RidgeLoRA performs better than other LoRA variants and can match or surpass full-rank training. These are reported experimental outcomes, rather than a claim that every adaptation task will favor RidgeLoRA. The findings indicate that a lightweight adaptation architecture can recover substantial representational flexibility while retaining the efficiency motivation behind low-rank fine-tuning.
summary.tldr: RidgeLoRA adds a matrix-ridge-enhanced approximation to lightweight adaptation, with experiments showing performance that can rival full-rank training.

title: RidgeLoRA: Matrix Ridge Enhanced Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models

abstract: A long-standing goal in AI is to develop agents capable of solving diverse tasks across a range of environments, including those never seen during training. Two dominant paradigms address this challenge: (i) reinforcement learning (RL), which learns policies via trial and error, and (ii) optimal control, which plans actions using a known or learned dynamics model. However, their comparative strengths in the offline setting—where agents must learn from reward-free trajectories—remain underexplored. In this work, we systematically evaluate RL and control-based methods on a suite of navigation tasks, using offline datasets of varying quality. On the RL side, we consider goal-conditioned and zero-shot methods. On the control side, we train a latent dynamics model using the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) and employ it for planning. We investigate how factors such as data diversity, trajectory quality, and environment variability influence the performance of these approaches. Our results show that model-free RL benefits most from large amounts of high-quality data, whereas model-based planning generalizes better to unseen layouts and is more data-efficient, while achieving trajectory stitching performance comparable to leading model-free methods. Notably, planning with a latent dynamics model proves to be a strong approach for handling suboptimal offline data and adapting to diverse environments.

paragraphs: This study compares ways to learn useful behavior from previously collected trajectories that lack rewards. It focuses on navigation and varies dataset quality, diversity, and environmental conditions. The central question is how reinforcement-learning methods compare with planning methods when agents must make use of this fixed, reward-free experience.

The reinforcement-learning side includes goal-conditioned and zero-shot approaches. For the control-based approach, the authors train a latent dynamics model using a Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture, or JEPA, and then use that learned model to plan actions. This places learning a representation of environmental dynamics at the center of action selection.

The experiments find that model-free reinforcement learning benefits most from abundant high-quality data. Planning with learned latent dynamics is more data-efficient and generalizes better to unseen layouts in the evaluated navigation tasks. It also matches leading model-free approaches in trajectory stitching, the ability to combine useful portions of recorded behavior. These findings support latent-model planning as a strong option when offline trajectories are suboptimal or agents must adapt across varied environments.
summary.tldr: In reward-free offline navigation experiments, latent-dynamics planning uses data efficiently and generalizes well to unfamiliar layouts.

title: Learning from Reward-Free Offline Data: A Case for Planning with Latent Dynamics Models

abstract: Projection-free first-order methods, e.g., the celebrated Frank-Wolfe (FW) algorithms, have emerged as powerful tools for optimization over simple convex sets such as polyhedra, because of their scalability, fast convergence, and iteration-wise feasibility without costly projections. However, extending these methods effectively to general compact convex sets remains challenging and largely open, as FW methods rely on expensive linear optimization oracles (LOO), while penalty-based methods often struggle with poor feasibility. We tackle this open challenge by presenting **Hom-PGD**, a novel projection-free method without expensive (optimization) oracles. Our method constructs a homeomorphism between the convex constraint set and a unit ball, transforming the original problem into an equivalent ball-constrained formulation, thus enabling efficient gradient-based optimization while preserving the original problem structure. We prove that Hom-PGD attains *optimal* convergence rates matching gradient descent with constant step-size to find an $\epsilon$-approximate (stationary) solution: $\mathcal{O}(\log (1/\epsilon))$ for strongly convex objectives, $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1})$ for convex objectives, and $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ for non-convex objectives. Meanwhile, Hom-PGD enjoys a low per-iteration complexity of $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$, without expensive oracles like LOO or projection, where $n$ is the input size. Our framework further extends to certain non-convex sets, broadening its applicability in practical optimization scenarios with complex constraints. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate that Hom-PGD achieves comparable convergence rates to state-of-the-art projection-free methods, while significantly reducing per-iteration runtime (up to 5 orders of magnitude faster) and thus the total problem-solving time.

title: Fast Projection-Free Approach (without Optimization Oracle) for Optimization over Compact Convex Set

abstract: With AI advancement and increasing circuit complexity, efficient chip design through Electronic Design Automation (EDA) is critical. Fast and accurate congestion prediction in chip layout and routing can significantly enhance automated design performance. Existing congestion modeling methods are limited by **(i)** ineffective processing and fusion of multi-view circuit data information, and **(ii)** insufficient reliability and interpretability in the prediction process. To address these challenges, We propose **M**ulti-view **I**nterpretable **H**ypergraph for **C**hip (**MIHC**), a trustworthy 'multi-view hypergraph neural network'-based framework that **(i)** processes both graph and image information in unified hypergraph representations, capturing topological and geometric circuit data, and **(ii)** implements a novel subgraph Information Bottleneck mechanism identifying critical congestion-correlated regions to guide predictions. This represents the first attempt to incorporate such interpretability into congestion prediction through informative graph reasoning. Experiments show our model reduces NMAE by 16.67% and 8.57% in cell-based and grid-based predictions on ISPD2015, and 5.26% and 2.44% on CircuitNet-N28, respectively, compared to state-of-the-art methods. Rigorous cross-design generalization experiments further validate our method’s capability to handle entirely unseen circuit designs.

title: MIHC: Multi-View Interpretable Hypergraph Neural Networks with Information Bottleneck for Chip Congestion Prediction

abstract: Euclidean diffusion models have achieved remarkable success in generative modeling across diverse domains, and they have been extended to manifold cases in recent advances. Instead of explicitly utilizing the structure of special manifolds as studied in previous works, in this paper we investigate direct sampling of the Euclidean diffusion models for general manifold-structured data. We reveal the multiscale singularity of the score function in the ambient space, which hinders the accuracy of diffusion-generated samples. We then present an elaborate theoretical analysis of the singularity structure of the score function by decomposing it along the tangential and normal directions of the manifold. To mitigate the singularity and improve the sampling accuracy, we propose two novel methods: (1) Niso-DM, which reduces the scale discrepancies in the score function by utilizing a non-isotropic noise, and (2) Tango-DM, which trains only the tangential component of the score function using a tangential-only loss function. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our methods achieve superior performance on distributions over various manifolds with complex geometries.

paragraphs: Some data occupy a curved, lower-dimensional structure inside a larger space. This paper studies how ordinary Euclidean diffusion models can sample such manifold-structured data directly. The authors identify a source of inaccurate generation: the score function used by diffusion develops singular behavior at multiple scales in the surrounding space.

Their theoretical analysis separates the score into directions tangent to the manifold and directions normal to it. Tangential directions follow the data's underlying structure, while normal directions point away from it. This decomposition exposes the structure of the singularity and motivates two methods aimed at improving the accuracy of generated samples.

Niso-DM uses non-isotropic noise, allowing different directions to receive different noise scales, to reduce scale discrepancies in the score function. Tango-DM instead trains only its tangential component through a corresponding loss. Numerical experiments report superior performance on distributions supported by manifolds with varied, complex geometries. The work connects a geometric analysis of sampling error to two concrete changes in diffusion modeling.
summary.tldr: Two diffusion methods improve sampling of manifold data by addressing score-function singularities through directional noise or tangential-only training.

title: Improving the Euclidean Diffusion Generation of Manifold Data by Mitigating Score Function Singularity

abstract: Series Section Electron Microscopy (ssEM) has emerged as a pivotal technology for deciphering nanoscale biological architectures. Three-dimensional (3D) registration is a critical step in ssEM, tasked with rectifying axial misalignments and nonlinear distortions introduced during serial sectioning. The core scientific challenge lies in achieving distortion mitigation without erasing the natural morphological deformations of biological tissues, thereby enabling faithful reconstruction of 3D ultrastructural organization. In this study, we present a paradigm-shifting optimization framework that rethinks 3D registration through the lens of manifold trajectory optimization. We propose the first continuous trajectory dynamics formulation for 3D registration and introduce a novel optimization strategy. Specifically, we introduce a dual optimization objective that inherently balances global trajectory smoothness with local structural preservation, while developing a solver that combines Gauss-Seidel iteration with Neural ODEs to systematically integrate biophysical priors with data-driven deformation compensation. A key strength of our method is its fully unsupervised training, which avoids reliance on ground truth and suits ssEM scenarios where annotations are difficult to obtain. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets spanning diverse tissue types demonstrate our method's superior performance in structural restoration accuracy and cross-tissue robustness.

The difficult part is preserving genuine biological shape changes while removing preparation artifacts. This paper formulates registration as continuous trajectory optimization, treating consistency across sections and preservation of local structure as linked objectives.

summary.tldr: An unsupervised Neural ODE registration framework balances smooth reconstruction with preservation of local tissue structure in serial electron microscopy.

title: Unsupervised Trajectory Optimization for 3D Registration in Serial Section Electron Microscopy using Neural ODEs

abstract: Clinical reasoning in medicine is a hypothesis-driven process where physicians refine diagnoses from limited information through targeted history, physical examination, and diagnostic investigations. In contrast, current medical benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) primarily assess knowledge recall through single-turn questions, where complete clinical information is provided upfront. To address this gap, we introduce VivaBench, a multi-turn benchmark that evaluates sequential clinical reasoning in LLM agents. Our dataset consists of 1762 physician-curated clinical vignettes structured as interactive scenarios that simulate a $ \textit{viva voce}$ (oral) examination in medical training, requiring agents to actively probe for relevant findings, select appropriate investigations, and synthesize information across multiple steps to reach a diagnosis. While current LLMs demonstrate competence in diagnosing conditions from well-described clinical presentations, their performance degrades significantly when required to navigate iterative diagnostic reasoning under uncertainty in our evaluation. Our analysis identified several failure modes that mirror common cognitive errors in clinical practice, including: (1) fixation on initial hypotheses, (2) inappropriate investigation ordering, (3) premature diagnostic closure, and (4) failing to screen for critical conditions. These patterns reveal fundamental limitations in how current LLMs reason and make decisions under uncertainty. Through VivaBench, we provide a standardized benchmark for evaluating conversational medical AI systems for real-world clinical decision support. Beyond medical applications, we contribute to the larger corpus of research on agentic AI by demonstrating how sequential reasoning trajectories can diverge in complex decision-making environments.

summary.tldr: VivaBench reveals substantial weaknesses when language models must gather evidence and reason through clinical cases over multiple turns.

title: Simulating Viva Voce Examinations to Evaluate Clinical Reasoning in Large Language Models

abstract: Although today's pretrained discriminative vision-language models (e.g., CLIP) have demonstrated strong perception abilities, such as zero-shot image classification, they also suffer from the bag-of-words problem and spurious bias. To mitigate these problems, some pioneering studies leverage powerful generative models (e.g., pretrained diffusion models) to realize generalizable image classification, dubbed Diffusion Classifier (DC). Specifically, by randomly sampling a Gaussian noise, DC utilizes the differences of denoising effects with different category conditions to classify categories. Unfortunately, an inherent and notorious weakness of existing DCs is noise instability: different random sampled noises lead to significant performance changes. To achieve stable classification performance, existing DCs always ensemble the results of hundreds of sampled noises, which significantly reduces the classification speed. To this end, we firstly explore the role of noise in DC, and conclude that: there are some ``good noises'' that can relieve the instability. Meanwhile, we argue that these good noises should meet two principles: 1) Frequency Matching: noise should destroy the specific frequency signals; 2) Spatial Matching: noise should destroy the specific spatial areas. Regarding both principles, we propose a novel Noise Optimization method to learn matching (i.e., good) noise for DCs: NoOp. For frequency matching, NoOp first optimizes a dataset-specific noise: Given a dataset and a timestep $t$, optimize one randomly initialized parameterized noise. For Spatial Matching, NoOp trains a Meta-Network that adopts an image as input and outputs image-specific noise offset. The sum of optimized noise and noise offset will be used in DC to replace random noise. Extensive ablations on various datasets demonstrated the effectiveness of NoOp. It is worth noting that our noise optimization is orthogonal to existing optimization methods (e.g., prompt tuning), our NoOP can even benefit from these methods to further boost performance.

The authors also report that noise optimization is complementary to approaches such as prompt tuning and can benefit from combining with them.
summary.tldr: NoOp learns dataset-level noise and image-specific adjustments to address instability in diffusion-based image classification.

title: Noise Matters: Optimizing Matching Noise for Diffusion Classifiers

abstract: Targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) is a widely used debiasing algorithm for plug-in estimation. While its statistical guarantees, such as double robustness and asymptotic efficiency, are well-studied, the convergence properties of TMLE as an iterative optimization scheme have remained underexplored. To bridge this gap, we study TMLE’s iterative updates through an optimization-theoretic lens, establishing global convergence under standard assumptions and regularity conditions. We begin by providing the first complete characterization of different stopping criteria and their relationship to convergence in TMLE. Next, we provide geometric insights. We show that each submodel induces a smooth, non-selfintersecting path (homotopy) through the probability simplex. We then analyze the solution space of the estimating equation and loss landscape. We show that all valid solutions form a submanifold of the statistical model, with the difference in dimension (i.e., codimension) exactly matching the dimension of the target parameter. Building on these geometric insights, we deliver the first strict proof of TMLE’s convergence from an optimization viewpoint, as well as explicit sufficient criteria under which TMLE terminates in a single update. As a by-product, we discover an unidentified overshooting phenomenon wherein the algorithm can surpass feasible roots to the estimating equation along a homotopy path, highlighting a promising avenue for designing enhanced debias algorithms.

Its statistical properties are well studied, but this paper examines a different question: how its iterative updates converge as an optimization procedure. The authors establish global convergence under standard assumptions and regularity conditions, connecting the algorithm’s movement through models with its stopping rules.

The analysis characterizes different stopping criteria and their relationship to convergence. Geometrically, each submodel traces a smooth path without self-intersections through the probability simplex. They also identify an overshooting phenomenon: an update can pass feasible roots along its path. This observation suggests opportunities to improve debiasing algorithms, while the single-update result applies when its stated sufficient conditions hold.
summary.tldr: An optimization and geometric analysis establishes conditional TMLE convergence, sufficient one-update criteria, and a previously unidentified overshooting phenomenon.

title: Targeted Maximum Likelihood Learning: An Optimization Perspective

abstract: Out-of-town trip recommendation aims to generate a sequence of Points of Interest (POIs) for users traveling from their hometowns to previously unvisited regions based on personalized itineraries, e.g., origin, destination, and trip duration. Modeling the complex user preferences--which often exhibit a two-fold nature of static and dynamic interests--is critical for effective recommendations. However, the sparsity of out-of-town check-in data presents significant challenges in capturing such user preferences. Meanwhile, existing methods often conflate the static and dynamic preferences, resulting in suboptimal performance. In this paper, we for the first time systematically study the problem of out-of-town trip recommendation. A novel framework SPOT-Trip is proposed to explicitly learns the dual static-dynamic user preferences. Specifically, to handle scarce data, we construct a POI attribute knowledge graph to enrich the semantic modeling of users’ hometown and out-of-town check-ins, enabling the static preference modeling through attribute relation-aware aggregation. Then, we employ neural ordinary differential equations (ODEs) to capture the continuous evolution of latent dynamic user preferences and innovatively combine a temporal point process to describe the instantaneous probability of each preference behavior. Further, a static-dynamic fusion module is proposed to merge the learned static and dynamic user preferences. Extensive experiments on real data offer insight into the effectiveness of the proposed solutions, showing that SPOT-Trip achieves performance improvement by up to 17.01%.

paragraphs: Recommending a trip to an unfamiliar region requires selecting a sequence of places that fits a traveler's itinerary and interests. Out-of-town check-ins are sparse, making those interests difficult to infer. SPOT-Trip distinguishes relatively stable preferences from preferences that evolve over time, addressing the paper's concern that existing methods mix these signals together.

For stable interests, the framework builds a knowledge graph of place attributes and uses relations among those attributes to enrich hometown and out-of-town check-ins. For changing interests, neural ordinary differential equations model the continuous evolution of latent preferences. A temporal point process complements this representation by describing the instantaneous probability of preference-related behavior.

A fusion module combines the static and dynamic representations to support trip recommendation. Experiments on real data report performance gains of up to 17.01%. The approach matters because it gives sparse observations two complementary interpretations: evidence about enduring interests and evidence about evolving behavior. The reported results support explicitly modeling and then combining these two sources of personalization for the evaluated trip-recommendation problem.
summary.tldr: SPOT-Trip combines knowledge-graph-based stable preferences with continuously evolving interests to improve out-of-town itinerary recommendations.

title: SPOT-Trip: Dual-Preference Driven Out-of-Town Trip Recommendation

abstract: This paper addresses the problem of weakly supervised cross-view localization, where the goal is to estimate the pose of a ground camera relative to a satellite image with noisy ground truth annotations. A common approach to bridge the cross-view domain gap for pose estimation is Bird’s-Eye View (BEV) synthesis. However, existing methods struggle with height ambiguity due to the lack of depth information in ground images and satellite height maps. Previous solutions either assume a flat ground plane or rely on complex models, such as cross-view transformers. We propose BevSplat, a novel method that resolves height ambiguity by using feature-based Gaussian primitives. Each pixel in the ground image is represented by a 3D Gaussian with semantic and spatial features, which are synthesized into a BEV feature map for relative pose estimation. We validate our method on the widely used KITTI and VIGOR datasets, which include both pinhole and panoramic query images. Experimental results show that BevSplat significantly improves localization accuracy over prior approaches.

paragraphs: BevSplat estimates a ground camera's pose relative to a satellite image using noisy ground-truth annotations. These two views describe the same place from very different perspectives. A common strategy is to turn the ground image into a bird's-eye representation, creating a more comparable view for localization.

The difficulty is deciding how image content should be placed vertically when depth information and satellite height maps are unavailable. Earlier approaches either assume flat ground or use complex models to bridge the views. BevSplat represents each ground-image pixel as a three-dimensional Gaussian carrying semantic and spatial features. The findings support feature-based Gaussian primitives as an effective way to address height ambiguity in weakly supervised cross-view localization.
summary.tldr: BevSplat uses feature-bearing 3D Gaussians to address height ambiguity and improve camera localization against satellite imagery.

title: BevSplat: Resolving Height Ambiguity via Feature-Based Gaussian Primitives for Weakly-Supervised Cross-View Localization

abstract: Pre-trained encoders for offline feature extraction followed by multiple instance learning (MIL) aggregators have become the dominant paradigm in computational pathology (CPath), benefiting cancer diagnosis and prognosis. However, performance limitations arise from the absence of encoder fine-tuning for downstream tasks and disjoint optimization with MIL. While slide-level supervised end-to-end (E2E) learning is an intuitive solution to this issue, it faces challenges such as high computational demands and suboptimal results. These limitations motivate us to revisit E2E learning. We argue that prior work neglects inherent E2E optimization challenges, leading to performance disparities compared to traditional two-stage methods. In this paper, we pioneer the elucidation of optimization challenge caused by sparse-attention MIL and propose a novel MIL called ABMILX. ABMILX mitigates this problem through global correlation-based attention refinement and multi-head mechanisms. With the efficient multi-scale random patch sampling strategy, an E2E trained ResNet with ABMILX surpasses SOTA foundation models under the two-stage paradigm across multiple challenging benchmarks, while remaining computationally efficient ($<$ 10 RTX3090 GPU hours). We demonstrate the potential of E2E learning in CPath and calls for greater research focus in this area. The code is https://github.com/DearCaat/E2E-WSI-ABMILX.

paragraphs: Computational pathology commonly processes a slide in two stages: a pretrained encoder extracts patch features, then a multiple-instance learning model combines them into a slide-level prediction. This separates feature extraction from the downstream task. Training both parts together could improve coordination, but earlier end-to-end approaches have faced high computational costs and disappointing results.

The authors identify an optimization difficulty associated with sparse attention in multiple-instance learning. Their proposed aggregator, ABMILX, addresses it through attention refinement based on global correlations and multiple attention heads. They combine this with random patch sampling at multiple scales, allowing the encoder and aggregator to learn jointly from slide-level supervision while keeping computation manageable.

Across multiple challenging benchmarks, the resulting ResNet-based system surpasses state-of-the-art foundation models used in the two-stage setup. The authors report a computational cost below ten RTX3090 GPU hours. These findings suggest that earlier end-to-end results partly reflected optimization challenges, and that addressing those challenges can make joint training both competitive and efficient in computational pathology.
summary.tldr: ABMILX improves end-to-end pathology training by addressing sparse-attention optimization, outperforming two-stage foundation-model systems on several benchmarks.

title: Revisiting End-to-End Learning with Slide-level Supervision in Computational Pathology

abstract: Accurate attribution for multiple platforms is critical for evaluating performance-based advertising. However, existing attribution methods rely heavily on the heuristic methods, e.g., Last-Click Mechanism (LCM) which always allocates the attribution to the platform with the latest report, lacking theoretical guarantees for attribution accuracy. In this work, we propose a novel theoretical model for the advertising attribution problem, in which we aim to design the optimal dominant strategy incentive compatible (DSIC) mechanisms and evaluate their performance. We first show that LCM is not DSIC and performs poorly in terms of accuracy and fairness. To address this limitation, we introduce the Peer-Validated Mechanism (PVM), a DSIC mechanism in which a platform's attribution depends solely on the reports of other platforms. We then examine the accuracy of PVM across both homogeneous and heterogeneous settings, and provide provable accuracy bounds for each case. Notably, we show that PVM is the optimal DSIC mechanism in the homogeneous setting. Finally, numerical experiments are conducted to show that PVM consistently outperforms LCM in terms of attribution accuracy and fairness.

paragraphs: Advertising attribution assigns credit to platforms involved in an advertising outcome. The paper studies how to assign that credit when platforms supply reports that may affect their own attribution. It formalizes the problem using mechanism design, bringing incentives into an evaluation often based on rules such as giving all credit to the latest report.

The authors show that, within their model, this last-click rule does not make truthful reporting a dominant strategy and performs poorly on accuracy and fairness. They propose the Peer-Validated Mechanism, where each platform’s attribution depends exclusively on other platforms’ reports. They prove that this mechanism is dominant strategy incentive compatible: truthful reporting is a best strategy regardless of what other platforms report.

The analysis provides accuracy bounds for both homogeneous and heterogeneous settings. The stronger optimality result applies specifically to the homogeneous setting, where the mechanism is optimal among incentive-compatible alternatives of the stated kind. Numerical experiments also find better accuracy and fairness than last-click attribution. Together, these results connect attribution quality with the incentives created by the credit-allocation rule.
summary.tldr: A peer-validated attribution mechanism encourages truthful reporting and is provably optimal among DSIC mechanisms in the paper’s homogeneous setting.

title: Beyond Last-Click: An Optimal Mechanism for Ad Attribution

abstract: The exponential growth of data-driven systems and AI technologies has intensified the demand for high-quality web-sourced datasets. While existing datasets have proven valuable, conventional web data collection approaches face significant limitations in terms of human effort and scalability. Current data collecting solutions fall into two categories: wrapper-based methods that struggle with adaptability and reproducibility, and large language model (LLM)-based approaches that incur substantial computational and financial costs. To address these challenges, we propose AutoData, a novel multi-agent system for Automated web Data collection, that requires minimal human intervention, i.e., only necessitating a natural language instruction specifying the desired dataset. In addition, AutoData is designed for a robust multi-agent architecture, featuring a novel oriented message hypergraph coordinated by a central task manager, to efficiently organize agents across research and development squads. Besides, we introduce a novel hypergraph cache system to advance the multi-agent collaboration process that enables efficient automated data collection and mitigates the token cost issues prevalent in existing LLM-based systems. Moreover, we introduce Instruct2DS, a new benchmark dataset supporting live data collection from web sources across three domains: academic, finance, and sports. Comprehensive evaluations over Instruct2DS and three existing benchmark datasets demonstrate AutoData's superior performance compared to baseline methods. Case studies on challenging tasks such as picture book collection and paper extraction from surveys further validate its applicability.

paragraphs: Building a dataset from the web often requires substantial human work. Existing collection systems also face a tradeoff: site-specific wrappers struggle with adaptability and reproducibility, while language-model-based approaches can incur considerable computational and financial costs. AutoData addresses this problem with a multi-agent system that starts from a natural-language description of the desired dataset.

A central task manager coordinates agents organized into research and development squads. Their communication follows an oriented message hypergraph, providing an explicit structure for organizing collaboration. A separate hypergraph cache supports that collaboration and reduces the token costs associated with language-model-based collection. Together, these components are designed to automate collection with minimal human intervention.

The authors also introduce Instruct2DS, a benchmark for live collection across academic, financial, and sports sources. Evaluations on this benchmark and three existing datasets show better performance than the compared baseline methods. Case studies involving picture books and extracting papers from surveys further demonstrate applicability to challenging collection requests. The contribution combines an automated collection system with a benchmark for assessing such systems.
summary.tldr: AutoData coordinates specialized agents and cached collaboration to collect web datasets from natural-language instructions with minimal human intervention.

title: AutoData: A Multi-Agent System for Open Web Data Collection

abstract: Regularized Multinomial Logistic regression has emerged as one of the most common methods for performing data classification and analysis. With the advent of large-scale data it is common to find scenarios where the number of possible multinomial outcomes is large (in the order of thousands to tens of thousands). In such cases, the computational cost of training logistic models or even simply iterating through all the model parameters is prohibitively expensive. In this paper, we propose a training method for large-scale multinomial logistic models that breaks this bottleneck by enabling parallel optimization of the likelihood objective. Our experiments on large-scale datasets showed an order of magnitude reduction in training time.

paragraphs: Multinomial logistic regression is used for classification problems with multiple possible outcomes. The paper focuses on regularized models with thousands or tens of thousands of outcomes. At that scale, the computational burden can become severe: even passing through all of the model parameters can be prohibitively expensive.

The authors propose a training method that allows the likelihood objective to be optimized in parallel. This addresses the bottleneck within the training computation itself. Its importance comes from the size of the outcome space, which can make a familiar classification model difficult to train even before considering more elaborate modeling choices.

Experiments on large-scale datasets show an order-of-magnitude reduction in training time. That result provides empirical support for using parallel optimization to make these large logistic models more practical. The paper’s stated contribution centers on computational efficiency: it offers a way to train models whose parameter scale otherwise makes ordinary optimization too costly, with the reported speed improvement demonstrated on the evaluated datasets.
summary.tldr: Parallel likelihood optimization reduces training time by an order of magnitude in experiments with large-scale multinomial logistic models.

title: Distributed training of Large-scale Logistic models

abstract: In this paper, we claim that some of the non-support vectors (non-SVs) that have no influence on the classifier can be screened out prior to the training phase in pathwise SVM computation scenario, in which one is asked to train a sequence (or path) of SVM classifiers for different regularization parameters. Based on a recently proposed framework so-called safe screening rule, we derive a rule for screening out non-SVs in advance, and discuss how we can exploit the advantage of the rule in pathwise SVM computation scenario. Experiments indicate that our approach often substantially reduce the total pathwise computation cost.

paragraphs: Pathwise support vector machine computation trains a sequence of classifiers using different regularization parameters. Repeating training across this sequence can be costly. The paper asks whether some observations can be identified in advance as non-support vectors, meaning they have no influence on the relevant classifier.

The authors derive a rule within the safe-screening framework to remove some of these observations before training. The safety requirement is central: screening is meant to identify points that can be excluded without affecting the classifier. The paper also explains how to take advantage of the rule when computing a path of SVM solutions.

Experiments indicate that this approach often substantially reduces total pathwise computation cost. The claim concerns screening some non-support vectors, with substantial savings occurring often in the evaluated setting. The contribution is a way to avoid unnecessary training work across a sequence of related problems by establishing in advance that certain observations do not contribute to a solution.
summary.tldr: Safe screening removes some non-support vectors before pathwise SVM training and often substantially reduces total computation.

title: Safe Screening of Non-Support Vectors in Pathwise SVM Computation

abstract: Domain adaptation arises in supervised learning when the training (source domain) and test (target domain) data have different distributions. Let X and Y denote the features and target, respectively, previous work on domain adaptation considers the covariate shift situation where the distribution of the features P(X) changes across domains while the conditional distribution P(Y|X) stays the same. To reduce domain discrepancy, recent methods try to find invariant components \mathcalT(X) that have similar P(\mathcalT(X)) by explicitly minimizing a distribution discrepancy measure. However, it is not clear if P(Y|\mathcalT(X)) in different domains is also similar when P(Y|X) changes. Furthermore, transferable components do not necessarily have to be invariant. If the change in some components is identifiable, we can make use of such components for prediction in the target domain. In this paper, we focus on the case where P(X|Y) and P(Y) both change in a causal system in which Y is the cause for X. Under appropriate assumptions, we aim to extract conditional transferable components whose conditional distribution P(\mathcalT(X)|Y) is invariant after proper location-scale (LS) transformations, and identify how P(Y) changes between domains simultaneously. We provide theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation on both synthetic and real-world data to show the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation learns from a source distribution for use on a different target distribution. This paper questions whether making feature distributions look similar is enough when the relationship between features and labels also changes. It emphasizes that useful transferable components may change across domains, provided those changes can be identified.

The authors consider a causal setting in which the label Y causes the features X, and both the label distribution and the distribution of features conditional on labels change. Under appropriate assumptions, they seek components whose conditional distributions become invariant after suitable location and scale transformations. They simultaneously identify changes in the label distribution.

This approach makes transfer depend on understanding structured changes, rather than only suppressing differences between domains. A component can remain useful if its change can be accounted for through the proposed transformations. The paper provides theoretical analysis and evaluations on synthetic and real-world data supporting the method’s effectiveness within this setting. Its assumptions about causal direction and transformable conditional distributions are central to the formulation.
summary.tldr: Under causal and transformation assumptions, the method transfers features by identifying conditional distribution changes alongside label-distribution shifts.

title: Domain Adaptation with Conditional Transferable Components

abstract: Domain adaptation is an important open problem in deep reinforcement learning (RL). In many scenarios of interest data is hard to obtain, so agents may learn a source policy in a setting where data is readily available, with the hope that it generalises well to the target domain. We propose a new multi-stage RL agent, DARLA (DisentAngled Representation Learning Agent), which learns to see before learning to act. DARLA’s vision is based on learning a disentangled representation of the observed environment. Once DARLA can see, it is able to acquire source policies that are robust to many domain shifts – even with no access to the target domain. DARLA significantly outperforms conventional baselines in zero-shot domain adaptation scenarios, an effect that holds across a variety of RL environments (Jaco arm, DeepMind Lab) and base RL algorithms (DQN, A3C and EC).

paragraphs: DARLA addresses the difficulty of transferring a reinforcement-learning policy from a setting with available training data to a different target setting. This matters when collecting target-domain data is difficult. The paper focuses on zero-shot adaptation, where the agent must transfer without access to the target domain.

The proposed agent separates learning to perceive the environment from learning to act within it. Its visual stage learns a disentangled representation of observations, organizing the representation around separable aspects of the environment. Once this stage is established, the agent learns a source policy using that representation. The authors report that the resulting policies are robust to many domain shifts.

DARLA significantly outperforms conventional baselines in the reported zero-shot adaptation experiments. The effect appears across Jaco arm and DeepMind Lab environments and across several underlying reinforcement-learning algorithms. This breadth supports the usefulness of the representation-learning stage across the tested settings, while the stated robustness remains to many shifts rather than every possible change in environment.
summary.tldr: DARLA learns a disentangled visual representation before a policy, improving zero-shot transfer across the environments and learning algorithms tested.

title: DARLA: Improving Zero-Shot Transfer in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Many studies in biomedical and health sciences involve small sample sizes due to logistic or financial constraints. Often, identifying weak (but scientifically interesting) associations between a set of predictors and a response necessitates pooling datasets from multiple diverse labs or groups. While there is a rich literature in statistical machine learning to address distributional shifts and inference in multi-site datasets, it is less clear when such pooling is guaranteed to help (and when it does not) – independent of the inference algorithms we use. In this paper, we present a hypothesis test to answer this question, both for classical and high dimensional linear regression. We precisely identify regimes where pooling datasets across multiple sites is sensible, and how such policy decisions can be made via simple checks executable on each site before any data transfer ever happens. With a focus on Alzheimer’s disease studies, we present empirical results showing that in regimes suggested by our analysis, pooling a local dataset with data from an international study improves power.

paragraphs: Small studies may lack enough data to detect weak but scientifically interesting associations. Pooling data from several laboratories can increase the available evidence, but differences between sites complicate the decision. This paper asks when pooling helps regression, seeking guidance that is independent of the particular inference algorithm used.

The authors develop a hypothesis test for both classical and high-dimensional linear regression. Their analysis identifies regimes in which combining datasets is sensible. It also translates that decision into simple checks that each site can perform locally, before any data is transferred, making the pooling question actionable at the planning stage.

Empirical results focus on Alzheimer's disease studies. In regimes indicated by the analysis, combining a local dataset with an international study improves statistical power. The conditional nature of this finding is central: the paper provides a way to assess pooling, rather than treating additional data as automatically beneficial. Its contribution links a theoretical decision rule with evidence that the identified regimes can improve the detection of associations.
summary.tldr: Local hypothesis checks identify when pooling datasets can benefit regression, with improved power demonstrated in the indicated Alzheimer's-study regimes.

title: When can Multi-Site Datasets be Pooled for Regression? Hypothesis Tests, $\ell_2$-consistency and Neuroscience Applications

abstract: Dropout, a stochastic regularisation technique for training of neural networks, has recently been reinterpreted as a specific type of approximate inference algorithm for Bayesian neural networks. The main contribution of the reinterpretation is in providing a theoretical framework useful for analysing and extending the algorithm. We show that the proposed framework suffers from several issues; from undefined or pathological behaviour of the true posterior related to use of improper priors, to an ill-defined variational objective due to singularity of the approximating distribution relative to the true posterior. Our analysis of the improper log uniform prior used in variational Gaussian dropout suggests the pathologies are generally irredeemable, and that the algorithm still works only because the variational formulation annuls some of the pathologies. To address the singularity issue, we proffer Quasi-KL (QKL) divergence, a new approximate inference objective for approximation of high-dimensional distributions. We show that motivations for variational Bernoulli dropout based on discretisation and noise have QKL as a limit. Properties of QKL are studied both theoretically and on a simple practical example which shows that the QKL-optimal approximation of a full rank Gaussian with a degenerate one naturally leads to the Principal Component Analysis solution.

The analysis suggests that the problems associated with the improper log-uniform prior in variational Gaussian dropout are generally irredeemable. The authors argue that the variational formulation suppresses some pathologies, explaining why the algorithm can still work. They separately address the singularity issue by proposing Quasi-KL divergence, an approximate inference objective for high-dimensional distributions.

The proposed objective thus addresses a specific mathematical issue, rather than repairing every problem identified in Bayesian dropout.
summary.tldr: The paper exposes flaws in Bayesian dropout interpretations and introduces Quasi-KL to address singular variational approximations.

title: Variational Bayesian dropout: pitfalls and fixes

abstract: We present a new approach and a novel architecture, termed WSNet, for learning compact and efficient deep neural networks. Existing approaches conventionally learn full model parameters independently and then compress them via ad hoc processing such as model pruning or filter factorization. Alternatively, WSNet proposes learning model parameters by sampling from a compact set of learnable parameters, which naturally enforces parameter sharing throughout the learning process. We demonstrate that such a novel weight sampling approach (and induced WSNet) promotes both weights and computation sharing favorably. By employing this method, we can more efficiently learn much smaller networks with competitive performance compared to baseline networks with equal numbers of convolution filters. Specifically, we consider learning compact and efficient 1D convolutional neural networks for audio classification. Extensive experiments on multiple audio classification datasets verify the effectiveness of WSNet. Combined with weight quantization, the resulted models are up to 180x smaller and theoretically up to 16x faster than the well-established baselines, without noticeable performance drop.

paragraphs: WSNet builds compact neural networks by learning a small parameter set from which model weights are sampled. This enforces parameter sharing throughout training. The paper contrasts that construction with approaches that first learn full sets of independent parameters and later compress them through procedures such as pruning or filter factorization.

Weight sampling supports both weight sharing and computation sharing. The authors investigate this design in one-dimensional convolutional networks for audio classification, comparing against baseline networks with the same number of convolution filters. This comparison shows how a network can retain its filter count while reducing the independently learned parameters used to define those filters.

Experiments on multiple audio-classification datasets show competitive performance for much smaller networks. When combined with weight quantization, the resulting models are up to 180 times smaller and theoretically up to 16 times faster than established baselines, without a noticeable performance drop. The speed figure is a theoretical result, while the classification experiments support the practical value of learning compact, shared parameters from the outset.
summary.tldr: WSNet learns shared weights from a compact parameter pool, producing audio classifiers up to 180 times smaller when combined with quantization.

title: WSNet: Compact and Efficient Networks Through Weight Sampling

abstract: The current trend of pushing CNNs deeper with convolutions has created a pressing demand to achieve higher compression gains on CNNs where convolutions dominate the computation and parameter amount (e.g., GoogLeNet, ResNet and Wide ResNet). Further, the high energy consumption of convolutions limits its deployment on mobile devices. To this end, we proposed a simple yet effective scheme for compressing convolutions though applying k-means clustering on the weights, compression is achieved through weight-sharing, by only recording $K$ cluster centers and weight assignment indexes. We then introduced a novel spectrally relaxed $k$-means regularization, which tends to make hard assignments of convolutional layer weights to $K$ learned cluster centers during re-training. We additionally propose an improved set of metrics to estimate energy consumption of CNN hardware implementations, whose estimation results are verified to be consistent with previously proposed energy estimation tool extrapolated from actual hardware measurements. We finally evaluated Deep $k$-Means across several CNN models in terms of both compression ratio and energy consumption reduction, observing promising results without incurring accuracy loss. The code is available at https://github.com/Sandbox3aster/Deep-K-Means

paragraphs: Convolutional layers can account for much of a neural network's computation and parameter storage, creating pressure to reduce both model size and energy use. This paper targets those layers through weight sharing. It clusters convolutional weights so that many weights can be represented by the same learned value.

The compressed representation stores K cluster centers together with indexes indicating which center each weight uses. During retraining, a new spectrally relaxed k-means regularizer encourages weights toward harder assignments to these centers. This makes the training procedure support the shared-weight representation that will ultimately provide compression.

The authors also propose metrics for estimating energy consumption in CNN hardware implementations. Their estimates agree with an existing estimation tool derived from hardware measurements, providing support for that evaluation approach. Across several CNN models, they report promising compression and estimated energy reductions without accuracy loss in the evaluated cases. The work therefore links a concrete parameter-sharing scheme with retraining and an assessment of its potential hardware energy benefits.
summary.tldr: Deep k-Means compresses convolutional weights through clustering and retraining, with reported compression and energy benefits without accuracy loss.

title: Deep k-Means: Re-Training and Parameter Sharing with Harder Cluster Assignments for Compressing Deep Convolutions

abstract: In the fair classification setup, we recast the links between fairness and predictability in terms of probability metrics. We analyze repair methods based on mapping conditional distributions to the Wasserstein barycenter. We propose a Random Repair which yields a tradeoff between minimal information loss and a certain amount of fairness.

We analyze repair methods based on mapping conditional distributions to the Wasserstein barycenter. We propose a Random Repair which yields a tradeoff between minimal information loss and a certain amount of fairness.

paragraphs: This paper studies fair classification through the relationship between fairness and predictability. It expresses that relationship using probability metrics, which provide a way to compare distributions. This places the analysis at the level of distributions and their differences, giving a mathematical language for examining how a repair changes the classification setting.

The authors analyze repair procedures that map conditional distributions to a Wasserstein barycenter. The barycenter serves as a shared distributional destination for those mappings. This makes the repair question concrete: the analysis concerns how conditional distributions are transformed toward that common reference, rather than treating fairness as an unspecified adjustment to a classifier.

The proposed Random Repair is designed to trade minimal information loss against a certain amount of fairness. Its stated contribution is that trade-off, rather than an unconditional promise of perfect fairness while preserving all information. The approach matters because it puts the preservation of information and the amount of fairness into the same repair problem, making both part of the method's objective.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes distributional repairs for fair classification and proposes Random Repair to trade information loss against a degree of fairness.

title: Obtaining Fairness using Optimal Transport Theory

abstract: Human perception is structured around objects which form the basis for our higher-level cognition and impressive systematic generalization abilities. Yet most work on representation learning focuses on feature learning without even considering multiple objects, or treats segmentation as an (often supervised) preprocessing step. Instead, we argue for the importance of learning to segment and represent objects jointly. We demonstrate that, starting from the simple assumption that a scene is composed of multiple entities, it is possible to learn to segment images into interpretable objects with disentangled representations. Our method learns – without supervision – to inpaint occluded parts, and extrapolates to scenes with more objects and to unseen objects with novel feature combinations. We also show that, due to the use of iterative variational inference, our system is able to learn multi-modal posteriors for ambiguous inputs and extends naturally to sequences.

paragraphs: This paper argues that learning visual representations should include discovering the separate objects in a scene. Instead of treating segmentation as a supervised preprocessing stage, it learns segmentation and object representations together. The starting assumption is simply that a scene contains multiple entities.

Using that structure, the method learns without supervision to divide images into interpretable objects with disentangled representations. It also learns to fill in occluded portions of objects. These capabilities connect identifying an object's visible region with representing aspects of the object beyond what is directly visible in the image.

Iterative variational inference also allows it to learn multimodal posterior distributions for ambiguous inputs, so its inferred representation can account for multiple possible interpretations. The approach extends naturally to sequences. Together, these findings show that joint object discovery and representation learning can support several forms of generalization under the paper's multi-entity scene assumption.
summary.tldr: Iterative variational inference jointly discovers and represents objects without supervision, supporting occlusion completion, ambiguity, and demonstrated generalization.

title: Multi-Object Representation Learning with Iterative Variational Inference

abstract: For learning tasks where the data (or losses) may be heavy-tailed, algorithms based on empirical risk minimization may require a substantial number of observations in order to perform well off-sample. In pursuit of stronger performance under weaker assumptions, we propose a technique which uses a cheap and robust iterative estimate of the risk gradient, which can be easily fed into any steepest descent procedure. Finite-sample risk bounds are provided under weak moment assumptions on the loss gradient. The algorithm is simple to implement, and empirical tests using simulations and real-world data illustrate that more efficient and reliable learning is possible without prior knowledge of the loss tails.

paragraphs: When data or losses have heavy tails, unusually large observations can make learning from a finite sample difficult. Algorithms that minimize average training loss may then need many observations to perform well on new data. This paper targets that problem by changing how the direction of improvement is estimated during learning.

The proposed technique constructs a computationally inexpensive, robust estimate of the risk gradient through an iterative procedure. That estimate can be supplied to a steepest descent method. The intervention is therefore at the level of the information used to choose an update: the method seeks a reliable gradient estimate under weaker statistical assumptions.

The authors provide finite-sample risk bounds under weak moment assumptions on the loss gradient. Simulations and experiments on real data illustrate that learning can become more efficient and reliable without knowing the loss tails beforehand. Together, the theory and experiments support robust gradient estimation as a practical route to better generalization when ordinary sample averages are difficult to estimate reliably.
summary.tldr: Robust estimates of the risk gradient can improve learning with heavy-tailed data under weak moment assumptions, without prior knowledge of the loss tails.

title: Better generalization with less data using robust gradient descent

abstract: Contextual multi-armed bandit (MAB) algorithms have been shown promising for maximizing cumulative rewards in sequential decision tasks such as news article recommendation systems, web page ad placement algorithms, and mobile health. However, most of the proposed contextual MAB algorithms assume linear relationships between the reward and the context of the action. This paper proposes a new contextual MAB algorithm for a relaxed, semiparametric reward model that supports nonstationarity. The proposed method is less restrictive, easier to implement and faster than two alternative algorithms that consider the same model, while achieving a tight regret upper bound. We prove that the high-probability upper bound of the regret incurred by the proposed algorithm has the same order as the Thompson sampling algorithm for linear reward models. The proposed and existing algorithms are evaluated via simulation and also applied to Yahoo! news article recommendation log data.

paragraphs: Contextual bandit algorithms repeatedly choose actions using contextual information, aiming to accumulate reward over time. Many methods assume that an action's context has a linear relationship with its reward. This paper relaxes that modeling requirement through a semiparametric reward model that also supports nonstationarity, allowing the reward setting to change over time.

The proposed algorithm is described as less restrictive, simpler to implement, and faster than two alternative algorithms for the same model. Its theoretical contribution concerns regret, the accumulated performance gap used to evaluate sequential decisions. The authors prove a tight high-probability upper bound with the same order as the bound for Thompson sampling under linear reward models.

That comparison matters because it pairs a more flexible reward model with a regret guarantee of the same order as one available in the linear setting. It does not mean the algorithms make identical decisions or achieve identical rewards. The authors evaluate their method and existing algorithms in simulations and apply them to Yahoo! news recommendation logs, connecting the analysis to a recommendation application.
summary.tldr: A semiparametric contextual bandit algorithm supports nonstationary rewards while matching the regret-bound order of linear-model Thompson sampling.

title: Contextual Multi-armed Bandit Algorithm for Semiparametric Reward Model

abstract: This work generalizes graph neural networks (GNNs) beyond those based on the Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) algorithm, graph Laplacians, and diffusions. Our approach, denoted Relational Pooling (RP), draws from the theory of finite partial exchangeability to provide a framework with maximal representation power for graphs. RP can work with existing graph representation models and, somewhat counterintuitively, can make them even more powerful than the original WL isomorphism test. Additionally, RP allows architectures like Recurrent Neural Networks and Convolutional Neural Networks to be used in a theoretically sound approach for graph classification. We demonstrate improved performance of RP-based graph representations over state-of-the-art methods on a number of tasks.
