The paper derives the framework from finite partial exchangeability and describes it as having maximal representation power for graphs. Its central concern is how much information a graph representation can distinguish and retain.

The framework can incorporate existing graph representation models and increase their expressive power. In particular, the authors show that it can make such models more powerful than the original Weisfeiler-Lehman isomorphism test. Relational Pooling also provides a theoretically sound way to use recurrent and convolutional neural networks for graph classification, broadening the range of architectures available for the task.

The authors report improved performance over state-of-the-art methods across several tasks. These experiments complement the expressiveness argument: the framework offers both a theoretical expansion of representational capability and observed benefits in evaluated applications. Its importance lies in treating graph representation as a general framework that can strengthen existing models and accommodate other neural architectures.
summary.tldr: Relational Pooling expands graph representation power and enables existing neural architectures to support principled graph classification.

title: Relational Pooling for Graph Representations

abstract: This paper investigates the impact of pre-existing offline data on online learning, in the context of dynamic pricing. We study a single-product dynamic pricing problem over a selling horizon of T periods. The demand in each period is determined by the price of the product according to a linear demand model with unknown parameters. We assume that the seller already has some pre-existing offline data before the start of the selling horizon. The seller wants to utilize both the pre-existing offline data and the sequential online data to minimize the regret of the online learning process. We characterize the joint effect of the size, location and dispersion of the offline data on the optimal regret of the online learning process. Our results reveal surprising transformations of the optimal regret rate with respect to the size of the offline data, which we refer to as phase transitions. In addition, our results demonstrate that the location and dispersion of the offline data also have an intrinsic effect on the optimal regret, and we quantify this effect via the inverse-square law.

paragraphs: This paper studies how historical data changes the difficulty of learning prices during a selling period. The setting has one product and a horizon of T periods. Demand follows a linear relationship with price, but the parameters are unknown. The seller begins with offline observations and then collects additional data through sequential pricing decisions.

The objective is to minimize regret during online learning. The authors characterize how three properties of the offline data jointly affect the best achievable regret: its size, its location, and its dispersion. This makes the analysis sensitive to the price levels represented in the historical observations and how broadly those observations are spread, alongside their quantity.

The results show phase transitions, meaning that the optimal regret rate changes its behavior as the amount of offline data varies. They also quantify the effect of data location and dispersion through an inverse-square law. Within the stated linear-demand setting, the findings show why the value of historical data cannot be summarized by sample count alone: where the data come from also shapes the subsequent learning problem.
summary.tldr: Under a linear demand model, historical data's quantity, location, and dispersion jointly determine optimal online pricing regret.

title: Online Pricing with Offline Data: Phase Transition and Inverse Square Law

abstract: We provide an improved analysis of normalized SGD showing that adding momentum provably removes the need for large batch sizes on non-convex objectives. Then, we consider the case of objectives with bounded second derivative and show that in this case a small tweak to the momentum formula allows normalized SGD with momentum to find an $\epsilon$-critical point in $O(1/\epsilon^{3.5})$ iterations, matching the best-known rates without accruing any logarithmic factors or dependence on dimension. We provide an adaptive learning rate schedule that automatically improves convergence rates when the variance in the gradients is small. Finally, we show that our method is effective when employed on popular large scale tasks such as ResNet-50 and BERT pretraining, matching the performance of the disparate methods used to get state-of-the-art results on both tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies normalized stochastic gradient descent, focusing on how momentum changes its convergence behavior on nonconvex objectives. The authors provide an improved analysis showing that adding momentum removes the need for large batch sizes. The result gives theoretical support to a modification of the optimizer rather than simply reporting a favorable training curve.

For objectives with bounded second derivative, a small change to the momentum formula yields an O(1/epsilon^3.5) iteration bound for reaching an epsilon-critical point. This is a point with a sufficiently small gradient, rather than necessarily a global optimum. The bound matches the best-known rates described in the paper without logarithmic factors or dependence on dimension.

The authors also introduce an adaptive learning-rate schedule whose convergence rate improves automatically when gradient variance is small. Experiments on ResNet-50 and BERT pretraining show performance matching the different methods used to obtain state-of-the-art results on those tasks. Together, the results connect momentum's theoretical benefit with effectiveness across two distinct large-scale learning applications.
summary.tldr: Momentum strengthens normalized SGD's convergence guarantees, removes a large-batch requirement, and performs effectively on ResNet-50 and BERT pretraining.

title: Momentum Improves Normalized SGD

abstract: Due to the high communication cost in distributed and federated learning problems, methods relying on compression of communicated messages are becoming increasingly popular. While in other contexts the best performing gradient-type methods invariably rely on some form of acceleration/momentum to reduce the number of iterations, there are no methods which combine the benefits of both gradient compression and acceleration. In this paper, we remedy this situation and propose the first \emph{accelerated compressed gradient descent (ACGD)} methods. In the single machine regime, we prove that ACGD enjoys the rate $O\Big((1+\omega)\sqrt{\frac{L}{\mu}}\log \frac{1}{\epsilon}\Big)$ for $\mu$-strongly convex problems and $O\Big((1+\omega)\sqrt{\frac{L}{\epsilon}}\Big)$ for convex problems, respectively, where $\omega$ is the compression parameter. Our results improve upon the existing non-accelerated rates $O\Big((1+\omega)\frac{L}{\mu}\log \frac{1}{\epsilon}\Big)$ and $O\Big((1+\omega)\frac{L}{\epsilon}\Big)$, respectively, and recover the optimal rates of accelerated gradient descent as a special case when no compression ($\omega=0$) is applied. We further propose a distributed variant of ACGD (called ADIANA) and prove the convergence rate $\widetilde{O}\Big(\omega+\sqrt{\frac{L}{\mu}}+\sqrt{\big(\frac{\omega}{n}+\sqrt{\frac{\omega}{n}}\big)\frac{\omega L}{\mu}}\Big)$, where $n$ is the number of devices/workers and $\widetilde{O}$ hides the logarithmic factor $\log \frac{1}{\epsilon}$. This improves upon the previous best result $\widetilde{O}\Big(\omega + \frac{L}{\mu}+\frac{\omega L}{n\mu} \Big)$ achieved by the DIANA method of Mishchenko et al. (2019). Finally, we conduct several experiments on real-world datasets which corroborate our theoretical results and confirm the practical superiority of our accelerated methods.

paragraphs: Distributed and federated learning can spend substantial effort communicating updates between workers. Compressing those updates reduces message size, while acceleration aims to reduce the number of optimization iterations. This paper develops accelerated compressed gradient descent, or ACGD, to combine these two benefits within algorithms supported by convergence guarantees.

For a single machine, the authors prove improved rates for convex and strongly convex problems. In the strongly convex case, acceleration replaces a linear dependence on the ratio of smoothness to strong convexity with a square-root dependence, while retaining a factor reflecting compression. For convex problems, it similarly improves the dependence on the target accuracy. Without compression, the bounds recover optimal accelerated gradient descent rates.

The paper also introduces ADIANA, a distributed version whose convergence bound accounts for compression and the number of workers. Its bound improves on the previous DIANA result. Experiments on real-world datasets support the theoretical improvements and report practical advantages for the accelerated methods.
summary.tldr: ACGD and its distributed variant combine gradient compression with acceleration to improve convergence guarantees and practical optimization performance.

title: Acceleration for Compressed Gradient Descent in Distributed and Federated Optimization

abstract: Communication overhead hinders the scalability of large-scale distributed training. Gossip SGD, where each node averages only with its neighbors, is more communication-efficient than the prevalent parallel SGD. However, its convergence rate is reversely proportional to quantity $1-\beta$ which measures the network connectivity. On large and sparse networks where $1-\beta \to 0$, Gossip SGD requires more iterations to converge, which offsets against its communication benefit. This paper introduces Gossip-PGA, which adds Periodic Global Averaging to accelerate Gossip SGD. Its transient stage, i.e., the iterations required to reach asymptotic linear speedup stage, improves from $\Omega(\beta^4 n^3/(1-\beta)^4)$ to $\Omega(\beta^4 n^3 H^4)$ for non-convex problems. The influence of network topology in Gossip-PGA can be controlled by the averaging period $H$. Its transient-stage complexity is also superior to local SGD which has order $\Omega(n^3 H^4)$. Empirical results of large-scale training on image classification (ResNet50) and language modeling (BERT) validate our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Distributed training must balance communication costs against progress toward a solution. Gossip SGD reduces communication by having each worker average only with its neighbors. On large, sparsely connected networks, however, information spreads slowly, and the extra iterations needed for convergence can offset the communication savings.

Gossip-PGA adds occasional averaging across all workers to these local exchanges. Its key control is the period H between global averages. The analysis focuses on the transient stage before training reaches the regime of asymptotic linear speedup. For nonconvex problems, the stated transient-stage expression changes from Ω(β⁴n³/(1−β)⁴) to Ω(β⁴n³H⁴), where 1−β measures network connectivity.

This change makes the influence of network topology controllable through the averaging schedule. The paper also reports a better transient-stage complexity than local SGD, whose stated order is Ω(n³H⁴). Experiments using ResNet50 for image classification and BERT for language modeling support the theoretical findings. The contribution is a way to retain neighborhood communication while periodically correcting the slow coordination caused by sparse networks.
summary.tldr: Occasional global averaging accelerates Gossip SGD and makes its sensitivity to sparse network connectivity controllable through the averaging period.

title: Accelerating Gossip SGD with Periodic Global Averaging

abstract: Counterfactual explanations are usually generated through heuristics that are sensitive to the search’s initial conditions. The absence of guarantees of performance and robustness hinders trustworthiness. In this paper, we take a disciplined approach towards counterfactual explanations for tree ensembles. We advocate for a model-based search aiming at "optimal" explanations and propose efficient mixed-integer programming approaches. We show that isolation forests can be modeled within our framework to focus the search on plausible explanations with a low outlier score. We provide comprehensive coverage of additional constraints that model important objectives, heterogeneous data types, structural constraints on the feature space, along with resource and actionability restrictions. Our experimental analyses demonstrate that the proposed search approach requires a computational effort that is orders of magnitude smaller than previous mathematical programming algorithms. It scales up to large data sets and tree ensembles, where it provides, within seconds, systematic explanations grounded on well-defined models solved to optimality.

paragraphs: Counterfactual explanations identify changes to an input that would produce a different model outcome. Heuristic searches can depend on where they start and lack guarantees about solution quality. This paper formulates explanation search for tree ensembles as a mathematical optimization problem with explicit objectives and constraints.

The authors develop efficient mixed-integer programming approaches and incorporate isolation forests to favor plausible explanations with low outlier scores. Their framework also supports different data types, structural restrictions on the feature space, resource limits, and actionability requirements. These constraints let the optimization reflect which proposed changes are permitted or practical within the chosen model.

In experiments, the approach requires orders of magnitude less computational effort than previous mathematical programming methods. It scales to large datasets and tree ensembles, producing explanations within seconds and solving the specified models to optimality. Here optimality is grounded in the defined objective and constraints. The contribution is a systematic, configurable search procedure whose explanations can be assessed against an explicit model of what makes a counterfactual desirable.
summary.tldr: Efficient mixed-integer optimization produces optimal tree-ensemble counterfactuals under explicit plausibility, structural, and actionability constraints.

title: Optimal Counterfactual Explanations in Tree Ensembles

abstract: Linear layers in neural networks (NNs) trained by gradient descent can be expressed as a key-value memory system which stores all training datapoints and the initial weights, and produces outputs using unnormalised dot attention over the entire training experience. While this has been technically known since the 1960s, no prior work has effectively studied the operations of NNs in such a form, presumably due to prohibitive time and space complexities and impractical model sizes, all of them growing linearly with the number of training patterns which may get very large. However, this dual formulation offers a possibility of directly visualising how an NN makes use of training patterns at test time, by examining the corresponding attention weights. We conduct experiments on small scale supervised image classification tasks in single-task, multi-task, and continual learning settings, as well as language modelling, and discuss potentials and limits of this view for better understanding and interpreting how NNs exploit training patterns. Our code is public.

paragraphs: A linear layer trained by gradient descent can be expressed as a memory of its training experience and initial weights. In this dual form, outputs arise through unnormalized dot-product attention over stored training information. The paper revisits this known mathematical view as a tool for understanding neural-network predictions.

The attraction is interpretability: examining the attention weights offers a way to visualize how a network uses training patterns at test time. The practical difficulty is that the representation's size, time cost, and space cost grow linearly with the number of training patterns. That growth has hindered direct study of networks in this form.

The authors investigate small-scale supervised image classification in single-task, multitask, and continual-learning settings, as well as language modeling. They discuss both the potential and limits of using the dual view to interpret reliance on training patterns. The contribution is an experimental exploration of a mathematically grounded connection between predictions and training experience, with the scaling burden remaining an explicit part of that perspective.
summary.tldr: The paper explores a dual representation of trained linear layers as attention over training experience to help interpret test-time predictions.

title: The Dual Form of Neural Networks Revisited: Connecting Test Time Predictions to Training Patterns via Spotlights of Attention

abstract: Recent works put much effort into tensor network structure search (TN-SS), aiming to select suitable tensor network (TN) structures, involving the TN-ranks, formats, and so on, for the decomposition or learning tasks. In this paper, we consider a practical variant of TN-SS, dubbed TN permutation search (TN-PS), in which we search for good mappings from tensor modes onto TN vertices (core tensors) for compact TN representations. We conduct a theoretical investigation of TN-PS and propose a practically-efficient algorithm to resolve the problem. Theoretically, we prove the counting and metric properties of search spaces of TN-PS, analyzing for the first time the impact of TN structures on these unique properties. Numerically, we propose a novel meta-heuristic algorithm, in which the searching is done by randomly sampling in a neighborhood established in our theory, and then recurrently updating the neighborhood until convergence. Numerical results demonstrate that the new algorithm can reduce the required model size of TNs in extensive benchmarks, implying the improvement in the expressive power of TNs. Furthermore, the computational cost for the new algorithm is significantly less than that in (Li and Sun, 2020).

Numerically, we propose a novel meta-heuristic algorithm, in which the searching is done by randomly sampling in a neighborhood established in our theory, and then recurrently updating the neighborhood until convergence. Furthermore, the computational cost for the new algorithm is significantly less than that in (Li and Sun, 2020).

paragraphs: Tensor networks represent large tensors using interconnected smaller core tensors. Choosing a suitable structure matters for compact representations. This paper focuses on a particular structural choice: how tensor modes are assigned to network vertices. It calls this problem tensor network permutation search and studies how to find useful assignments efficiently.

The theoretical analysis establishes counting and metric properties of the permutation search spaces. It also examines how the tensor network’s structure changes these properties. Using that foundation, the authors define neighborhoods for search and propose a meta-heuristic that samples randomly within a neighborhood, then repeatedly updates the neighborhood until convergence.

Across extensive numerical benchmarks, the algorithm reduces the model size needed for tensor network representations. The authors interpret this as evidence of improved expressive power through better assignments of modes to cores. The method also requires significantly less computation than the prior search method compared in the paper. The contribution connects search-space theory to a practical procedure for finding more compact tensor networks.
summary.tldr: A theoretically grounded local-sampling search finds tensor-mode assignments that reduce tensor network model size in the reported benchmarks.

title: Permutation Search of Tensor Network Structures via Local Sampling

abstract: Visualizing optimization landscapes has resulted in many fundamental insights in numeric optimization, specifically regarding novel improvements to optimization techniques. However, visualizations of the objective that reinforcement learning optimizes (the "reward surface") have only ever been generated for a small number of narrow contexts. This work presents reward surfaces and related visualizations of 27 of the most widely used reinforcement learning environments in Gym for the first time. We also explore reward surfaces in the policy gradient direction and show for the first time that many popular reinforcement learning environments have frequent "cliffs" (sudden large drops in expected reward). We demonstrate that A2C often "dives off" these cliffs into low reward regions of the parameter space while PPO avoids them, confirming a popular intuition for PPO’s improved performance over previous methods. We additionally introduce a highly extensible library that allows researchers to easily generate these visualizations in the future. Our findings provide new intuition to explain the successes and failures of modern RL methods, and our visualizations concretely characterize several failure modes of reinforcement learning agents in novel ways.

This paper expands these visualizations to 27 widely used Gym environments, moving beyond the narrow settings previously explored.

The comparison provides evidence about update behavior in the studied environments, showing how the surrounding reward landscape can help explain differences between reinforcement learning methods.
summary.tldr: Reward-surface visualizations reveal abrupt reward cliffs that A2C often crosses and PPO avoids in the studied reinforcement learning environments.

title: Cliff Diving: Exploring Reward Surfaces in Reinforcement Learning Environments

abstract: Learning representations of algorithms is an emerging area of machine learning, seeking to bridge concepts from neural networks with classical algorithms. Several important works have investigated whether neural networks can effectively reason like algorithms, typically by learning to execute them. The common trend in the area, however, is to generate targeted kinds of algorithmic data to evaluate specific hypotheses, making results hard to transfer across publications, and increasing the barrier of entry. To consolidate progress and work towards unified evaluation, we propose the CLRS Algorithmic Reasoning Benchmark, covering classical algorithms from the Introduction to Algorithms textbook. Our benchmark spans a variety of algorithmic reasoning procedures, including sorting, searching, dynamic programming, graph algorithms, string algorithms and geometric algorithms. We perform extensive experiments to demonstrate how several popular algorithmic reasoning baselines perform on these tasks, and consequently, highlight links to several open challenges. Our library is readily available at https://github.com/deepmind/clrs.

Individual studies often generate specialized data to test a particular hypothesis. That practice makes results difficult to compare across publications and creates additional work for researchers entering the field.

The CLRS benchmark provides a shared collection of tasks drawn from algorithms in Introduction to Algorithms. It spans sorting, searching, dynamic programming, graph processing, string processing, and geometry. This breadth gives researchers a common basis for studying learned algorithm execution across different kinds of procedures, instead of relying solely on isolated task-specific evaluations.

The authors run extensive experiments with several popular algorithmic-reasoning baselines and use their performance to highlight connections to open challenges. They also release a library for using the benchmark. The main contribution is a common evaluation resource: it helps organize evidence about what models can do across algorithm families and reduces the need for each study to construct its own evaluation setup.
summary.tldr: CLRS provides a shared benchmark spanning classical algorithms to make neural algorithmic-reasoning evaluations easier to compare.

title: The CLRS Algorithmic Reasoning Benchmark

abstract: This paper studies the algorithmic stability and generalizability of decentralized stochastic gradient descent (D-SGD). We prove that the consensus model learned by D-SGD is $\mathcal{O}{(m/N\unaryplus1/m\unaryplus\lambda^2)}$-stable in expectation in the non-convex non-smooth setting, where $N$ is the total sample size of the whole system, $m$ is the worker number, and $1\unaryminus\lambda$ is the spectral gap that measures the connectivity of the communication topology. These results then deliver an $\mathcal{O}{(1/N\unaryplus{({(m^{-1}\lambda^2)}^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}\unaryplus m^{\unaryminus\alpha})}/{N^{1\unaryminus\frac{\alpha}{2}}})}$ in-average generalization bound, which is non-vacuous even when $\lambda$ is closed to $1$, in contrast to vacuous as suggested by existing literature on the projected version of D-SGD. Our theory indicates that the generalizability of D-SGD has a positive correlation with the spectral gap, and can explain why consensus control in initial training phase can ensure better generalization. Experiments of VGG-11 and ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet justify our theory. To our best knowledge, this is the first work on the topology-aware generalization of vanilla D-SGD. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/Raiden-Zhu/Generalization-of-DSGD}.

paragraphs: Decentralized stochastic gradient descent distributes training across communicating workers. This paper examines how the pattern of connections between those workers affects stability and generalization. The analysis concerns the consensus model and allows an optimization setting that is both non-convex and non-smooth.

The authors derive an expected stability bound involving total sample size, worker count, and a spectral quantity measuring network connectivity. They then obtain an average generalization bound that remains informative even when the spectral gap is small. Earlier analysis of a projected version of the algorithm had suggested uninformative bounds in this weakly connected regime.

The theory indicates a positive relationship between generalization and the spectral gap, and explains why controlling consensus early in training can improve generalization. Experiments with VGG-11 and ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet support the analysis. The result connects the communication network to predictive behavior beyond the training data, rather than assessing network structure solely through its effect on optimization.
summary.tldr: Topology-aware stability bounds connect decentralized SGD's generalization to network connectivity and explain benefits of early consensus control.

title: Topology-aware Generalization of Decentralized SGD

abstract: Curriculum learning (CL)- training using samples that are generated and presented in a meaningful order - was introduced in the machine learning context around a decade ago. While CL has been extensively used and analysed empirically, there has been very little mathematical justification for its advantages. We introduce a CL model for learning the class of k-parities on d bits of a binary string with a neural network trained by stochastic gradient descent (SGD). We show that a wise choice of training examples, involving two or more product distributions, allows to reduce significantly the computational cost of learning this class of functions, compared to learning under the uniform distribution. We conduct experiments to support our analysis. Furthermore, we show that for another class of functions - namely the ‘Hamming mixtures’ - CL strategies involving a bounded number of product distributions are not beneficial.

paragraphs: Curriculum learning changes which training examples a model encounters and the order in which it sees them. This paper gives a mathematical account of when that choice can make learning computationally easier. It studies neural networks trained by stochastic gradient descent to learn k-parities: functions determined by the parity of a selected set of k bits within a binary input of length d.

The authors construct curricula using two or more product distributions to generate training examples. With a suitable choice of these distributions, they show a substantial reduction in the computational cost of learning parities compared with training under the uniform distribution. Experiments support this analysis, connecting the mathematical result to observed learning behavior.

The paper also establishes a boundary for the approach. For a different function class called Hamming mixtures, curricula using a bounded number of product distributions do not help. Together, these results explain a concrete benefit of carefully chosen training data while showing that the benefit depends on the functions being learned.
summary.tldr: A mathematical model shows how carefully chosen curricula reduce the cost of learning parities, while identifying another function class where similar curricula do not help.

title: A Mathematical Model for Curriculum Learning for Parities

abstract: Consider the problem of exploration in sparse-reward or reward-free environments, such as in Montezuma’s Revenge. In the curiosity-driven paradigm, the agent is rewarded for how much each realized outcome differs from their predicted outcome. But using predictive error as intrinsic motivation is fragile in stochastic environments , as the agent may become trapped by high-entropy areas of the state-action space, such as a "noisy TV". In this work, we study a natural solution derived from structural causal models of the world: Our key idea is to learn representations of the future that capture precisely the unpredictable aspects of each outcome—which we use as additional input for predictions, such that intrinsic rewards only reflect the predictable aspects of world dynamics. First, we propose incorporating such hindsight representations into models to disentangle "noise" from "novelty", yielding Curiosity in Hindsight : a simple and scalable generalization of curiosity that is robust to stochasticity. Second, we instantiate this framework for the recently introduced BYOL-Explore algorithm as our prime example, resulting in the noise-robust BYOL-Hindsight. Third, we illustrate its behavior under a variety of different stochasticities in a grid world, and find improvements over BYOL-Explore in hard-exploration Atari games with sticky actions. Notably, we show state-of-the-art results in exploring Montezuma’s Revenge with sticky actions, while preserving performance in the non-sticky setting.

paragraphs: Curiosity-based exploration rewards an agent when outcomes differ from its predictions. This can help when external rewards are scarce, but randomness creates a trap: an unpredictable distraction can keep producing prediction error without offering useful discoveries. The paper addresses this distinction between learning something new and repeatedly encountering irreducible noise.

Curiosity in Hindsight learns representations of future outcomes intended to capture their unpredictable components. Those representations become additional inputs to the prediction model, so the curiosity reward reflects the predictable part of the environment’s dynamics. Drawing on structural causal models, the framework uses hindsight information to separate stochastic variation from novelty that the agent can learn about.

The authors apply the framework to BYOL-Explore, producing BYOL-Hindsight. They examine different kinds of randomness in a grid world and report improvements on difficult exploration games in Atari with sticky actions. In Montezuma’s Revenge with sticky actions, they report state-of-the-art exploration results while retaining performance without sticky actions. The findings support making curiosity selective about which prediction errors deserve attention.
summary.tldr: Curiosity in Hindsight separates unpredictable noise from learnable novelty, improving exploration in the reported stochastic environments.

title: Curiosity in Hindsight: Intrinsic Exploration in Stochastic Environments

abstract: Riemannian submanifold optimization with momentum is computationally challenging because, to ensure that the iterates remain on the submanifold, we often need to solve difficult differential equations. Here, we simplify such difficulties for a class of structured symmetric positive-definite matrices with the affine-invariant metric. We do so by proposing a generalized version of the Riemannian normal coordinates that dynamically orthonormalizes the metric and locally converts the problem into an unconstrained problem in the Euclidean space. We use our approach to simplify existing approaches for structured covariances and develop matrix-inverse-free $2^\text{nd}$-order optimizers for deep learning in low precision settings.

paragraphs: Optimization with momentum becomes computationally difficult when solutions must remain on a curved, constrained space. Maintaining that constraint can require solving difficult differential equations. This paper addresses the problem for a class of structured symmetric positive-definite matrices equipped with the affine-invariant metric, rather than for arbitrary constrained spaces.

The authors propose generalized Riemannian normal coordinates that dynamically make the metric orthonormal. In those coordinates, the problem locally takes the form of an unconstrained Euclidean optimization problem. The important qualification is local: the coordinate construction simplifies the nearby optimization geometry while addressing the original structured-matrix setting. This offers a way to reduce the geometric complications involved in momentum-based updates.

The approach is used to simplify existing methods for structured covariance matrices. It also supports the development of second-order deep-learning optimizers that avoid matrix inverses in low-precision settings. The contribution connects a geometric coordinate construction with practical optimizer design, targeting calculations that otherwise make structured positive-definite optimization difficult.
summary.tldr: Adaptive local coordinates simplify structured positive-definite optimization and enable inverse-free second-order optimizers for low-precision deep learning.

title: Simplifying Momentum-based Positive-definite Submanifold Optimization with Applications to Deep Learning

abstract: Deep neural networks perform well on classification tasks where data streams are i.i.d. and labeled data is abundant. Challenges emerge with non-stationary training data streams such as continual learning. One powerful approach that has addressed this challenge involves pre-training of large encoders on volumes of readily available data, followed by task-specific tuning. Given a new task, however, updating the weights of these encoders is challenging as a large number of weights needs to be fine-tuned, and as a result, they forget information about the previous tasks. In the present work, we propose a model architecture to address this issue, building upon a discrete bottleneck containing pairs of separate and learnable key-value codes. Our paradigm will be to encode; process the representation via a discrete bottleneck; and decode. Here, the input is fed to the pre-trained encoder, the output of the encoder is used to select the nearest keys, and the corresponding values are fed to the decoder to solve the current task. The model can only fetch and re-use a sparse number of these key-value pairs during inference, enabling localized and context-dependent model updates . We theoretically investigate the ability of the discrete key-value bottleneck to minimize the effect of learning under distribution shifts and show that it reduces the complexity of the hypothesis class. We empirically verify the proposed method under challenging class-incremental learning scenarios and show that the proposed model — without any task boundaries — reduces catastrophic forgetting across a wide variety of pre-trained models, outperforming relevant baselines on this task.

paragraphs: A pretrained encoder can provide useful representations for new tasks, but adapting a large network can overwrite knowledge from earlier tasks. This paper introduces a discrete key-value bottleneck to make adaptation more localized when training data changes over time, particularly in continual learning.

The architecture first encodes an input, then uses that representation to select nearby keys from a collection of learnable key-value pairs. The corresponding values are passed to a decoder that solves the task. Only a sparse selection of pairs is accessed for any input. This creates a way to make updates depend on the current context rather than involving every stored pair.

In class-incremental experiments, the method reduces catastrophic forgetting across a variety of pretrained models and outperforms relevant baselines. These results are obtained without supplying task boundaries, supporting the architecture’s usefulness when the learner is not explicitly told where one task ends and another begins.
summary.tldr: A sparse, discrete key-value layer enables localized adaptation and reduces forgetting in evaluated continual-learning settings without task boundaries.

title: Discrete Key-Value Bottleneck

abstract: We study the problem of learning functional distributions in the presence of noise. A functional is a map from the space of features to distributions over a set of labels, and is often assumed to belong to a known class of hypotheses $\mathcal{F}$. Features are generated by a general random process and labels are sampled independently from feature-dependent distributions. In privacy sensitive applications, labels are passed through a noisy kernel. We consider online learning , where at each time step, a predictor attempts to predict the actual (label) distribution given only the features and noisy labels in prior steps. The performance of the predictor is measured by the expected KL-risk that compares the predicted distributions to the underlying truth. We show that the minimax expected KL-risk is of order $\tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{T\log|\mathcal{F}|})$ for finite hypothesis class $\mathcal{F}$ and any non-trivial noise level. We then extend this result to general infinite classes via the concept of stochastic sequential covering and provide matching lower and upper bounds for a wide range of natural classes.

paragraphs: The learning target in this paper is a function that assigns a probability distribution over labels to each feature input. Labels are sampled independently from these feature-dependent distributions, then passed through a noisy mechanism in privacy-sensitive applications. The learner therefore tries to recover the underlying label probabilities using observations whose labels have been altered.

The setting is online: at each step, predictions use the available features and noisy labels from earlier steps. Performance is measured by expected KL-risk, which compares predicted distributions with the true ones. For a finite hypothesis class F and any non-trivial noise level, the authors establish a minimax rate of order square root of T times log of the size of F, up to logarithmic factors.

The paper then extends the analysis to infinite hypothesis classes using stochastic sequential covering. Matching upper and lower bounds are obtained for a broad range of natural classes. These paired bounds describe both achievable learning performance and unavoidable difficulty, connecting noisy-label distribution prediction to the complexity of the class of possible functions.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes matching learning-risk bounds for online prediction of label distributions from privacy-noised labels.

title: Learning Functional Distributions with Private Labels

abstract: In this work, we study the issue of reward hacking on the response length, a challenge emerging in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) on LLMs. A well-formatted, verbose but less helpful response from the LLMs can often deceive LLMs or even human evaluators and achieve high scores. The same issue also holds for some reward models in RL. To address the challenges in both training and evaluation, we establish a more reliable evaluation protocol for comparing different training configurations, which inspects the trade-off between LLM evaluation score and response length obtained by varying training hyperparameters. Based on this evaluation, we conduct large-scale studies, where the results shed insights into the efficacy of hyperparameters and tricks used in RL on mitigating length bias. We further propose to improve the reward model by jointly training two linear heads to predict the preference, one trained to correlate with length and the other trained to decorrelate with length and therefore focusing more on the actual content. We then discard the length head in RL to ignore the spurious length reward. Experiments demonstrate that our approach eliminates the reward correlation with length, and improves the obtained policy by a significant margin.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from human feedback can reward longer answers even when their extra text is not helpful. A polished, verbose response may receive high scores from people, language-model evaluators, or reward models. ODIN studies this length-related reward hacking as a problem affecting both training and evaluation.

The authors first introduce an evaluation protocol that examines the trade-off between evaluation score and response length as training hyperparameters vary. Large-scale studies then investigate how training choices affect length bias. To modify the reward itself, they jointly train two linear preference-prediction heads: one encouraged to correlate with response length, and another encouraged to be decorrelated from it and focus more on content.

During reinforcement learning, the length-associated head is discarded. This removes the explicitly separated source of length reward from the training signal. Experiments report elimination of the reward’s correlation with length and a significant improvement in the resulting policy. The contribution combines a way to assess length-sensitive evaluation with a reward-model design intended to reduce that specific incentive.
summary.tldr: ODIN separates length-related reward from content-related preference to reduce verbosity-driven reward hacking in RLHF.

title: ODIN: Disentangled Reward Mitigates Hacking in RLHF

abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has been widely used for model compression and deployment acceleration. Nonetheless, the statistical insight of the remarkable performance of KD remains elusive, and methods for evaluating the uncertainty of the distilled model/student model are lacking. To address these issues, we establish a close connection between KD and a Bayesian model. In particular, we develop an innovative method named Bayesian Knowledge Distillation (BKD) to provide a transparent interpretation of the working mechanism of KD, and a suite of Bayesian inference tools for the uncertainty quantification of the student model. In BKD, the regularization imposed by the teacher model in KD is formulated as a teacher-informed prior for the student model’s parameters. Consequently, we establish the equivalence between minimizing the KD loss and estimating the posterior mode in BKD. Efficient Bayesian inference algorithms are developed based on the stochastic gradient Langevin Monte Carlo and examined with extensive experiments on uncertainty ranking and credible intervals construction for predicted class probabilities.

To address these issues, we establish a close connection between KD and a Bayesian model. In particular, we develop an innovative method named Bayesian Knowledge Distillation (BKD) to provide a transparent interpretation of the working mechanism of KD, and a suite of Bayesian inference tools for the uncertainty quantification of the student model. In BKD, the regularization imposed by the teacher model in KD is formulated as a teacher-informed prior for the student model’s parameters. Consequently, we establish the equivalence between minimizing the KD loss and estimating the posterior mode in BKD. Efficient Bayesian inference algorithms are developed based on the stochastic gradient Langevin Monte Carlo and examined with extensive experiments on uncertainty ranking and credible intervals construction for predicted class probabilities.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a student model using guidance from a teacher, supporting model compression and faster deployment. This paper addresses two questions about that process: how to interpret the teacher’s contribution statistically, and how to quantify uncertainty in the resulting student. It develops Bayesian Knowledge Distillation as a common framework for both.

The key move is to express the teacher’s regularizing influence as a prior over the student’s parameters. Under this formulation, minimizing the distillation objective is equivalent to finding the mode of the student’s posterior distribution. This connects a familiar training procedure to a Bayesian interpretation: the teacher shapes the parameter beliefs used in learning.

The authors then develop efficient inference algorithms based on stochastic gradient Langevin Monte Carlo. These provide tools for examining uncertainty beyond a single fitted parameter setting. Experiments investigate ranking predictions by uncertainty and constructing credible intervals for predicted class probabilities. The contribution therefore combines an explanation of the distillation objective with methods for expressing uncertainty in the distilled model’s outputs.
summary.tldr: Bayesian Knowledge Distillation interprets teacher guidance as a prior and adds Bayesian tools for quantifying student uncertainty.

title: Bayesian Knowledge Distillation: A Bayesian Perspective of Distillation with Uncertainty Quantification

abstract: Recent years have witnessed a paradigm shift in deep learning from task-centric model design to task-agnostic representation learning and task-specific fine-tuning. Pretrained model representations are commonly evaluated extensively across various real-world tasks and used as a foundation for different downstream tasks. This paper proposes a solution for assessing the quality of representations in a task-agnostic way. To circumvent the need for real-world data in evaluation, we explore the use of synthetic binary classification tasks with Gaussian mixtures to probe pretrained models and compare the robustness-accuracy performance on pretrained representations with an idealized reference. Our approach offers a holistic evaluation, revealing intrinsic model capabilities and reducing the dependency on real-life data for model evaluation. Evaluated with various pretrained image models, the experimental results confirm that our task-agnostic evaluation correlates with actual linear probing performance on downstream tasks and can also guide parameter choice in robust linear probing to achieve a better robustness-accuracy trade-off.

title: What Would Gauss Say About Representations? Probing Pretrained Image Models using Synthetic Gaussian Benchmarks

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved impressive performance on various natural language generation tasks. Nonetheless, they suffer from generating negative and harmful contents that are biased against certain demographic groups (e.g., female), raising severe fairness concerns. As remedies, prior works intervened the generation by removing attitude or demographic information, inevitably degrading the generation quality and resulting in notable fairness-fluency trade-offs. However, it is still under-explored to what extent the fluency has to be affected in order to achieve a desired level of fairness. In this work, we conduct the first formal study from an information-theoretic perspective. We show that previous approaches are excessive for debiasing and propose LIDAO, a general framework to debias a (L)LM at a better fluency provably. We further robustify LIDAO in adversarial scenarios, where a carefully-crafted prompt may stimulate LLMs exhibiting instruction-following abilities to generate texts with fairness issue appears only when the prompt is also taken into account. Experiments on three LMs ranging from 0.7B to 7B parameters demonstrate the superiority of our method.

title: LIDAO: Towards Limited Interventions for Debiasing (Large) Language Models

abstract: Recent advancements in automatic 3D avatar generation guided by text have made significant progress. However, existing methods have limitations such as oversaturation and low-quality output. To address these challenges, we propose X-Oscar, a progressive framework for generating high-quality animatable avatars from text prompts. It follows a sequential "Geometry→Texture→Animation" paradigm, simplifying optimization through step-by-step generation. To tackle oversaturation, we introduce Adaptive Variational Parameter (AVP), representing avatars as an adaptive distribution during training. Additionally, we present Avatar-aware Score Distillation Sampling (ASDS), a novel technique that incorporates avatar-aware noise into rendered images for improved generation quality during optimization. Extensive evaluations confirm the superiority of X-Oscar over existing text-to-3D and text-to-avatar approaches. Our anonymous project page: https://anonymous1440.github.io/.

paragraphs: Text-guided avatar generation aims to turn a verbal description into a usable three-dimensional character, but existing methods can produce oversaturated textures and low-quality outputs. X-Oscar addresses those problems through a staged generation process. It also targets avatars that can be animated, rather than only static 3D assets.

The framework proceeds from geometry to texture and then animation, simplifying optimization by separating successive stages. Adaptive Variational Parameter represents the avatar as an adaptive distribution during training to address oversaturation. Avatar-aware Score Distillation Sampling adds avatar-aware noise to rendered images to improve the optimization signal and generation quality.

Extensive evaluations show advantages over existing text-to-3D and text-to-avatar approaches. The contribution combines a progressive pipeline with two training modifications tailored to avatar generation. The abstract does not specify evaluation scores, motion-quality measures, or computational cost, so its reported superiority should be interpreted within the paper’s evaluated methods and settings.
summary.tldr: X-Oscar progressively generates geometry, texture, and animation while using avatar-specific optimization to improve text-guided 3D characters.

title: X-Oscar: A Progressive Framework for High-quality Text-guided 3D Animatable Avatar Generation

abstract: We study the Continuous-Discrete Kalman Filter (CD-KF) for State-Space Models (SSMs) where continuous-time dynamics are observed via multiple sensors with discrete, irregularly timed measurements. Our focus extends to scenarios in which the measurement process is coupled with the states of an auxiliary SSM. For instance, higher measurement rates may increase energy consumption or heat generation, while a sensor’s accuracy can depend on its own spatial trajectory or that of the measured target. Each sensor thus carries distinct costs and constraints associated with its measurement rate and additional constraints and costs on the auxiliary state. We model measurement occurrences as independent Poisson processes with sensor-specific rates and derive an upper bound on the mean posterior covariance matrix of the CD-KF along the mean auxiliary state. The bound is continuously differentiable with respect to the measurement rates, which enables efficient gradient-based optimization. Exploiting this bound, we propose a finite-horizon optimal control framework to optimize measurement rates and auxiliary-state dynamics jointly. We further introduce a deterministic method for scheduling measurement times from the optimized rates. Empirical results in state-space filtering and dynamic temporal Gaussian process regression demonstrate that our approach achieves improved trade-offs between resource usage and estimation accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper studies systems that evolve continuously but are measured by sensors at irregular discrete times. Choosing when to measure involves more than estimation accuracy: frequent measurements can consume energy or generate heat, and accuracy can depend on sensor or target motion. The authors model these interacting effects through an auxiliary state-space system.

Measurement arrivals are assumed to follow independent Poisson processes with a separate rate for each sensor. Under this formulation, the authors derive an upper bound on the Kalman filter's mean posterior covariance along the mean auxiliary state. The bound varies smoothly with measurement rates, enabling gradient-based optimization of a quantity that reflects estimation uncertainty.

A finite-horizon optimal control framework jointly chooses measurement rates and auxiliary-state dynamics while accounting for costs and constraints. A further deterministic procedure converts the optimized rates into actual measurement times. Experiments in state-space filtering and dynamic temporal Gaussian process regression show improved trade-offs between resource use and estimation accuracy. The approach therefore links a tractable uncertainty bound to both sensing decisions and the physical processes that influence their cost.
summary.tldr: A differentiable uncertainty bound enables joint optimization of sensor measurement rates and auxiliary dynamics, improving evaluated resource-accuracy trade-offs.

title: Optimal Sensor Scheduling and Selection for Continuous-Discrete Kalman Filtering with Auxiliary Dynamics

abstract: Catastrophic forgetting – the tendency of neural networks to forget previously learned data when learning new information – remains a central challenge in continual learning. In this work, we adopt a behavioral approach, observing a connection between learning speed and forgetting: examples learned more quickly are less prone to forgetting. Focusing on replay-based continual learning, we show that the composition of the replay buffer – specifically, whether it contains quickly or slowly learned examples – has a significant effect on forgetting. Motivated by this insight, we introduce Speed-Based Sampling (SBS), a simple yet general strategy that selects replay examples based on their learning speed. SBS integrates easily into existing buffer-based methods and improves performance across a wide range of competitive continual learning benchmarks, advancing state-of-the-art results. Our findings underscore the value of accounting for the forgetting dynamics when designing continual learning algorithms.

paragraphs: Continual-learning systems can lose previously acquired knowledge as they learn new information. This paper examines forgetting at the level of individual examples, asking whether their behavior during initial learning offers a useful clue. The authors observe that examples learned more quickly tend to be less susceptible to later forgetting.

They investigate this relationship in replay-based continual learning, where a buffer retains past examples for reuse. The composition of that buffer matters: including quickly learned versus slowly learned examples significantly affects forgetting. Learning speed therefore provides information relevant to choosing what should be replayed, beyond simply knowing that an example belongs to an earlier learning stage.

The proposed Speed-Based Sampling strategy selects replay examples using their learning speed and can be incorporated into existing buffer-based methods. Across a broad set of competitive continual-learning benchmarks, the authors report performance improvements that advance state-of-the-art results. The findings support designing replay around observed forgetting dynamics, using how an example was learned to inform its later role in maintaining knowledge.
summary.tldr: Learning speed helps predict forgetting susceptibility, and using it to select replay examples improves continual-learning performance in the reported benchmarks.

title: Predicting the Susceptibility of Examples to Catastrophic Forgetting

abstract: Diffusion models have emerged as powerful tools for generative modeling, demonstrating exceptional capability in capturing target data distributions from large datasets. However, fine-tuning these massive models for specific downstream tasks, constraints, and human preferences remains a critical challenge. While recent advances have leveraged reinforcement learning algorithms to tackle this problem, much of the progress has been empirical, with limited theoretical understanding. To bridge this gap, we propose a stochastic control framework for fine-tuning diffusion models. Building on denoising diffusion probabilistic models as the pre-trained reference dynamics, our approach integrates linear dynamics control with Kullback–Leibler regularization. We establish the well-posedness and regularity of the stochastic control problem and develop a policy iteration algorithm (PI-FT) for numerical solution. We show that PI-FT achieves global convergence at a linear rate. Unlike existing work that assumes regularities throughout training, we prove that the control and value sequences generated by the algorithm preserve the desired regularity. Finally, we extend our framework to parametric settings for efficient implementation and demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the proposed PI-FT algorithm through numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning diffusion models for particular tasks, constraints, or human preferences has progressed faster empirically than theoretically. This paper develops a stochastic-control framework to provide a firmer mathematical account. It takes a pretrained denoising diffusion probabilistic model as the reference dynamics and combines linear dynamics control with Kullback–Leibler regularization.

The authors establish well-posedness and regularity for the resulting control problem, addressing whether the formulation behaves mathematically as required. They then introduce PI-FT, a policy-iteration algorithm for solving it numerically. The work thus connects a theoretically analyzed fine-tuning formulation with an implementable algorithm.
summary.tldr: A stochastic-control formulation yields PI-FT, a diffusion fine-tuning algorithm with proven regularity preservation and global linear convergence in its framework.

title: Stochastic Control for Fine-tuning Diffusion Models: Optimality, Regularity, and Convergence

abstract: Selecting a sample generation scheme from multiple prompt-based generative models, including large language models (LLMs) and prompt-guided image and video generation models, is typically addressed by choosing the model that maximizes an averaged evaluation score. However, this score-based selection overlooks the possibility that different models achieve the best generation performance for different types of text prompts. An online identification of the best generation model for various input prompts can reduce the costs associated with querying sub-optimal models. In this work, we explore the possibility of varying rankings of text-based generative models for different text prompts and propose an online learning framework to predict the best data generation model for a given input prompt. The proposed PAK-UCB algorithm addresses a contextual bandit (CB) setting with shared context variables across the arms, utilizing the generated data to update kernel-based functions that predict the score of each model available for unseen text prompts. Additionally, we leverage random Fourier features (RFF) to accelerate the online learning process of PAK-UCB. Our numerical experiments on real and simulated text-to-image and image-to-text generative models show that RFF-UCB performs successfully in identifying the best generation model across different sample types. The code is available at: github.com/yannxiaoyanhu/dgm-online-select.

paragraphs: Choosing a generative model by its average evaluation score assumes that one overall ranking is useful across prompts. This paper investigates a more specific choice: which model is best for the prompt currently being processed. If rankings vary with prompt type, adapting the selection can reduce queries spent on less suitable models.

PAK-UCB formulates this as a contextual bandit problem, with candidate models as actions and prompt information shared across those actions. Feedback from generated data updates kernel-based functions that predict each model's score on unseen prompts. Selection and learning proceed online, allowing the system to improve its prompt-dependent choices as it receives results.

The contribution concerns learning a conditional ranking: it makes the input prompt part of the selection decision instead of relying exclusively on a model's average performance.
summary.tldr: PAK-UCB learns prompt-dependent model selection online, with random Fourier features accelerating its score predictions.

title: PAK-UCB Contextual Bandit: An Online Learning Approach to Prompt-Aware Selection of Generative Models and LLMs

abstract: Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) has demonstrated strong generalization capabilities across diverse distributions and tasks, largely due to extensive pre-training datasets. Fine-tuning MLLM has become a common practice to improve performance on specific downstream tasks. However, during fine-tuning, MLLM often faces the risk of forgetting knowledge acquired during pre-training, which can result in a decline in generalization abilities. To balance the trade-off between generalization and specialization, we propose measuring the parameter importance for both pre-trained and fine-tuning distributions, based on frozen pre-trained weight magnitude and accumulated fine-tuning gradient values. We further apply an importance-aware weight allocation strategy, selectively updating relatively important parameters for downstream tasks. We conduct empirical evaluations on both image captioning and visual question-answering tasks using various MLLM architectures. The comprehensive experimental analysis demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed solution, highlighting the efficiency of the crucial modules in enhancing downstream specialization performance while mitigating generalization degradation in MLLM Fine-Tuning.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models gain broad capabilities from pretraining, but tuning them for a specific task can erode that knowledge. This paper addresses the resulting tension between specialization and generalization by deciding which parameters should be updated according to their importance for both the original and downstream distributions.

The method estimates pretraining importance from the magnitudes of frozen pretrained weights. It estimates downstream importance using accumulated gradients during fine-tuning. An importance-aware allocation strategy then selectively updates parameters that are relatively important for the downstream task. Combining the two signals makes the update decision sensitive to both existing knowledge and the demands of new training data.

Evaluations cover image captioning and visual question answering with several multimodal architectures. The reported results show improved downstream specialization while reducing the degradation of generalization, and the experimental analysis supports the effectiveness of the key modules. The approach makes parameter selection an explicit part of managing the trade-off, rather than assuming every parameter should adapt in the same way.
summary.tldr: Importance-aware parameter updates help multimodal models specialize while reducing the loss of general capabilities during fine-tuning.

title: Learn from Downstream and Be Yourself in Multimodal Large Language Models Fine-Tuning

abstract: Trilevel learning (TLL) with zeroth order constraints is a fundamental problem in machine learning, arising in scenarios where gradient information is inaccessible due to data privacy or model opacity, such as in federated learning, healthcare, and financial systems. These problems are notoriously difficult to solve due to their inherent complexity and the lack of first order information. Moreover, in many practical scenarios, data may be distributed across various nodes, necessitating strategies to address trilevel learning problems without centralizing data on servers to uphold data privacy. To this end, an effective distributed trilevel zeroth order learning framework DTZO is proposed in this work to address the trilevel learning problems with level-wise zeroth order constraints in a distributed manner. The proposed DTZO is versatile and can be adapted to a wide range of (grey-box) trilevel learning problems with partial zeroth order constraints. In DTZO, the cascaded polynomial approximation can be constructed without relying on gradients or sub-gradients, leveraging a novel cut, i.e., zeroth order cut. Furthermore, we theoretically carry out the non-asymptotic convergence rate analysis for the proposed DTZO in achieving the $\epsilon$-stationary point. Extensive experiments have been conducted to demonstrate and validate the superior performance of the proposed DTZO.

paragraphs: Trilevel learning involves three interdependent levels of optimization, making it difficult even when gradients are available. DTZO addresses the harder setting in which gradient information is inaccessible at some or all levels and data are spread across multiple nodes. The motivation includes settings where privacy concerns or opaque models prevent conventional gradient-based optimization.

The framework solves these problems in a distributed manner without bringing all data onto a central server. Its central construction is a cascaded polynomial approximation built using a new zeroth-order cut. This allows the approximation to be formed without gradients or subgradients. The framework also accommodates grey-box problems, where only part of the optimization has zeroth-order constraints.

The authors provide a non-asymptotic convergence-rate analysis for reaching an epsilon-stationary point, an approximate stationarity target rather than a claim of global optimality. They also report extensive experiments supporting DTZO’s performance. Together, the theoretical and empirical contributions address whether distributed trilevel optimization can make quantifiable progress when access to derivative information is restricted.
summary.tldr: DTZO tackles distributed trilevel optimization with restricted gradient access and provides a finite-time analysis for approximate stationarity.

title: DTZO: Distributed Trilevel Zeroth Order Learning with Provable Non-Asymptotic Convergence

abstract: Chatbot Arena is an open platform for evaluating LLMs by pairwise battles, in which users vote for their preferred response from two randomly sampled anonymous models. While Chatbot Arena is widely regarded as a reliable LLM ranking leaderboard, we show that crowdsourced voting can be rigged to improve (or decrease) the ranking of a target model $m_{t}$. We first introduce a straightforward target-only rigging strategy that focuses on new battles involving $m_{t}$, identifying it via watermarking or a binary classifier, and exclusively voting for $m_{t}$ wins. However, this strategy is practically inefficient because there are over $190$ models on Chatbot Arena and on average only about 1% of new battles will involve $m_{t}$. To overcome this, we propose an omnipresent rigging strategy, exploiting the Elo rating mechanism of Chatbot Arena that any new vote on a battle can influence the ranking of the target model $m_{t}$, even if $m_{t}$ is not directly involved in the battle. We conduct experiments on around 1.7 million historical votes from the Chatbot Arena Notebook, showing that omnipresent rigging strategy can improve model rankings by rigging only hundreds of new votes. While we have evaluated several defense mechanisms, our findings highlight the importance of continued efforts to prevent vote rigging. Code is publicly available to reproduce all experiments.

paragraphs: Chatbot Arena ranks language models using user preferences between anonymous responses. This paper examines whether coordinated voting can manipulate a target model's ranking. Its central concern is that a crowdsourced leaderboard can reflect deliberate changes to voting behavior as well as genuine differences in response quality.

The authors compare manipulation focused on battles involving the target with an approach that exploits interactions across the rating system. Target-only manipulation is inefficient because the target appears in only about 1% of new battles among more than 190 models. The findings reveal a vulnerability in the aggregation process, extending beyond votes on a target's own responses.
summary.tldr: Historical-vote experiments show that manipulating hundreds of votes can shift a target model's Chatbot Arena ranking.

title: Improving Your Model Ranking on Chatbot Arena by Vote Rigging

abstract: Recently, robust reinforcement learning (RL) methods designed to handle adversarial input observations have received significant attention, motivated by RL’s inherent vulnerabilities. While existing approaches have demonstrated reasonable success, addressing worst-case scenarios over long time horizons requires both minimizing the agent’s cumulative rewards for adversaries and training agents to counteract them through alternating learning. However, this process introduces mutual dependencies between the agent and the adversary, making interactions with the environment inefficient and hindering the development of off-policy methods. In this work, we propose a novel off-policy method that eliminates the need for additional environmental interactions by reformulating adversarial learning as a soft-constrained optimization problem. Our approach is theoretically supported by the symmetric property of policy evaluation between the agent and the adversary. The implementation is available at https://github.com/nakanakakosuke/VALT_SAC.

Alternating their training creates mutual dependencies, making environmental interaction inefficient and complicating the development of off-policy methods.

The proposed approach reformulates adversarial learning as a soft-constrained optimization problem. This change eliminates the need for additional environmental interactions in the proposed off-policy method. It addresses the training relationship between the agent and adversary, which is the source of the interaction overhead identified by the authors.

The theoretical foundation is a symmetry in policy evaluation between the agent and adversary. This supplies support for the reformulation and connects the robustness objective to an off-policy learning procedure. The contribution is a method for handling adversarial observations without the additional interaction requirement of the alternating process described in the paper. Its significance lies in making that long-horizon adversarial training setup more compatible with efficient use of environmental experience.
summary.tldr: The method reformulates adversarial observation training to support off-policy learning without additional environmental interactions.

title: Off-Policy Actor-Critic for Adversarial Observation Robustness: Virtual Alternative Training via Symmetric Policy Evaluation

abstract: Approximate second-order optimization methods often exhibit poorer generalization compared to first-order approaches. In this work, we look into this issue through the lens of the loss landscape and find that existing second-order methods tend to converge to sharper minima compared to SGD. In response, we propose Sassha, a novel second-order method designed to enhance generalization by explicitly reducing sharpness of the solution, while stabilizing the computation of approximate Hessians along the optimization trajectory. In fact, this sharpness minimization scheme is crafted also to accommodate lazy Hessian updates, so as to secure efficiency besides flatness. To validate its effectiveness, we conduct a wide range of standard deep learning experiments where Sassha demonstrates its outstanding generalization performance that is comparable to, and mostly better than, other methods. We provide a comprehensive set of analyses including convergence, robustness, stability, efficiency, and cost.

This paper investigates that gap through the shape of the loss landscape. The authors find that existing second-order methods tend to converge to sharper minima than stochastic gradient descent, motivating an optimizer that explicitly addresses sharpness.

summary.tldr: Sassha combines sharpness reduction with stable, less frequent Hessian updates to improve the generalization of second-order optimization.

title: Sassha: Sharpness-aware Adaptive Second-order Optimization with Stable Hessian Approximation

abstract: The contextual multi-armed bandit (MAB) is a widely used framework for problems requiring sequential decision-making under uncertainty, such as recommendation systems. In applications involving a large number of users, the performance of contextual MAB can be significantly improved by facilitating collaboration among multiple users. This has been achieved by the clustering of bandits (CB) methods, which adaptively group the users into different clusters and achieve collaboration by allowing the users in the same cluster to share data. However, classical CB algorithms typically rely on numerical reward feedback, which may not be practical in certain real-world applications. For instance, in recommendation systems, it is more realistic and reliable to solicit preference feedback between pairs of recommended items rather than absolute rewards. To address this limitation, we introduce the first "clustering of dueling bandit algorithms" to enable collaborative decision-making based on preference feedback. We propose two novel algorithms: (1) Clustering of Linear Dueling Bandits (COLDB) which models the user reward functions as linear functions of the context vectors, and (2) Clustering of Neural Dueling Bandits (CONDB) which uses a neural network to model complex, non-linear user reward functions. Both algorithms are supported by rigorous theoretical analyses, demonstrating that user collaboration leads to improved regret bounds. Extensive empirical evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets further validate the effectiveness of our methods, establishing their potential in real-world applications involving multiple users with preference-based feedback.

Both combine learning from pairwise feedback with adaptive grouping of users.

Theoretical analyses show that collaboration improves regret bounds, which measure accumulated decision loss relative to better choices. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets further support the effectiveness of the methods. The contribution is a way to share information across users while working with the kind of comparative feedback that recommendation applications may more realistically collect.
summary.tldr: COLDB and CONDB cluster users to share information while learning sequential decisions from pairwise preferences, with improved regret bounds.

title: Online Clustering of Dueling Bandits

abstract: The success of large generative models has driven a paradigm shift, leveraging massive multi-source data to enhance model capabilities. However, the interaction among these sources remains theoretically underexplored. This paper provides a first attempt to fill this gap by rigorously analyzing multi-source training in conditional generative modeling, where each condition represents a distinct data source. Specifically, we establish a general distribution estimation error bound in average total variation distance for conditional maximum likelihood estimation based on the bracketing number. Our result shows that when source distributions share certain similarities and the model is expressive enough, multi-source training guarantees a sharper bound than single-source training. We further instantiate the general theory on conditional Gaussian estimation and deep generative models including autoregressive and flexible energy-based models, by characterizing their bracketing numbers. The results highlight that the number of sources and similarity among source distributions improve the advantage of multi-source training. Simulations and real-world experiments validate our theory.
