paragraphs: This paper asks when training a generative model on several data sources offers a theoretical advantage over training on each source separately. It studies conditional generation, treating each condition as identifying a distinct source. The central question is how relationships among source distributions affect the accuracy of the distributions a model learns.

The authors derive an error bound for conditional maximum likelihood estimation, measured by average total variation distance. The bound uses bracketing numbers to characterize the complexity of the candidate distributions. Their key result is conditional: when the sources share suitable similarities and the model is expressive enough, joint training has a sharper error bound than separate training.

The analysis is developed for conditional Gaussian estimation, autoregressive models, and flexible energy-based models. Within the theory, the number of sources and their similarity strengthen the advantage of learning jointly. Simulations and real-world experiments support these conclusions. The contribution gives mathematical substance to data sharing across sources while explicitly tying its benefits to shared structure and sufficient modeling capacity.
summary.tldr: The paper derives conditions under which related data sources give conditional generative models sharper estimation guarantees through joint training.

title: A Theory for Conditional Generative Modeling on Multiple Data Sources

abstract: Unsupervised pretraining has been transformative in many supervised domains. However, applying such ideas to reinforcement learning (RL) presents a unique challenge in that fine-tuning does not involve mimicking task-specific data, but rather exploring and locating the solution through iterative self-improvement. In this work, we study how unlabeled offline trajectory data can be leveraged to learn efficient exploration strategies. While prior data can be used to pretrain a set of low-level skills, or as additional off-policy data for online RL, it has been unclear how to combine these ideas effectively for online exploration. Our method SUPE (Skills from Unlabeled Prior data for Exploration) demonstrates that a careful combination of these ideas compounds their benefits. Our method first extracts low-level skills using a variational autoencoder (VAE), and then pseudo-labels unlabeled trajectories with optimistic rewards and high-level action labels, transforming prior data into high-level, task-relevant examples that encourage novelty-seeking behavior. Finally, SUPE uses these transformed examples as additional off-policy data for online RL to learn a high-level policy that composes pretrained low-level skills to explore efficiently. In our experiments, SUPE consistently outperforms prior strategies across a suite of 42 long-horizon, sparse-reward tasks.

paragraphs: Pretraining for reinforcement learning must prepare an agent to discover solutions through interaction, rather than simply imitate labeled examples. This paper investigates how unlabeled recordings of prior behavior can improve that exploration. It combines two uses of prior data: extracting reusable low-level skills and supplying additional experience to an online learning algorithm.

SUPE first learns low-level skills with a variational autoencoder. It then assigns optimistic reward estimates and high-level action labels to the unlabeled trajectories. These pseudo-labels transform existing recordings into examples that can train decisions over skills and encourage novelty-seeking behavior. The prior data therefore contribute both the building blocks of behavior and guidance for using them.

During online reinforcement learning, a high-level policy learns to compose the pretrained skills, using the transformed trajectories as additional off-policy data. Across 42 long-horizon tasks with sparse rewards, SUPE consistently outperforms earlier strategies in the reported experiments. The findings support the authors’ claim that carefully combining skill pretraining with reuse of prior experience can compound their exploration benefits.
summary.tldr: SUPE turns unlabeled trajectories into reusable skills and exploration-oriented training examples, improving results across 42 sparse-reward tasks.

title: Leveraging Skills from Unlabeled Prior Data for Efficient Online Exploration

abstract: Recent Large Language Models (LLMs) have reported high accuracy on reasoning benchmarks. However, it is still unclear whether the observed results arise from true “reasoning” or from statistical recall of the training set. Inspired by the ladder of causation (Pearl, 2009) and its three levels (associations, interventions and counterfactuals), this paper introduces RE-IMAGINE: a framework to characterize a hierarchy of reasoning ability in LLMs, alongside an automated pipeline to generate problem variations at different levels of the hierarchy. By altering problems in an intermediate symbolic representation, RE-IMAGINE generates arbitrarily many problems that are not solvable using memorization alone. Moreover, the framework is general and can work across reasoning domains, including math, code, and logic. We demonstrate our framework on four widely-used benchmarks to evaluate several families of LLMs, and observe reductions in performance when the models are queried with problem variations. These assessments indicate a degree of reliance on statistical recall for past performance, and open the door to further research targeting skills across the reasoning hierarchy.

paragraphs: RE-IMAGINE addresses a problem in evaluating language-model reasoning: strong benchmark scores may partly reflect recall of training material. The framework organizes reasoning ability into a hierarchy inspired by associations, interventions, and counterfactuals. It pairs that hierarchy with an automated method for generating related problems at different levels.

The contribution is a scalable way to probe how reasoning performance holds up when familiar problems undergo structured changes.
summary.tldr: RE-IMAGINE generates symbolic problem variations that reveal a degree of reliance on statistical recall in reasoning-benchmark performance.

title: RE-IMAGINE: Symbolic Benchmark Synthesis for Reasoning Evaluation

abstract: We propose Plausible Token Amplification (PTA) to improve the accuracy of Differentially Private In-Context Learning (DP-ICL) using DP synthetic demonstrations. While Tang et al. empirically improved the accuracy of DP-ICL by limiting vocabulary space during DP synthetic demonstration generation, its theoretical basis remains unexplored. By interpreting ICL as implicit Bayesian inference on a concept underlying demonstrations, we not only provide theoretical evidence supporting Tang et al.’s empirical method but also introduce PTA, a refined method for modifying next-token probability distribution. Through the modification, PTA highlights tokens that distinctly represent the ground-truth concept underlying the original demonstrations. As a result, generated DP synthetic demonstrations guide the Large Language Model to successfully infer the ground-truth concept, which improves the accuracy of DP-ICL. Experimental evaluations on both synthetic and real-world text-classification datasets validated the effectiveness of PTA.

paragraphs: Differentially private in-context learning can use synthetic demonstrations to guide a language model. The paper asks how those generated examples can better preserve the concept conveyed by the original demonstrations. Earlier work found that restricting the generation vocabulary improved accuracy, but the theoretical reason for that improvement remained unexplained.

The authors interpret in-context learning as implicit Bayesian inference about a concept underlying the examples. This perspective provides theoretical support for the earlier vocabulary restriction method and motivates Plausible Token Amplification, or PTA. PTA modifies next-token probabilities to emphasize tokens that distinctively represent the ground-truth concept in the original demonstrations.

The intended effect is to make private synthetic examples more informative about the task the language model should infer. The method therefore connects token-level generation choices with the usefulness of the resulting demonstrations. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world text-classification datasets validate PTA's effectiveness, supporting its use to improve accuracy in the studied differentially private in-context learning setting.
summary.tldr: PTA adjusts token probabilities so private synthetic demonstrations better communicate the underlying task concept and improve in-context learning accuracy.

title: Plausible Token Amplification for Improving Accuracy of Differentially Private In-Context Learning Based on Implicit Bayesian Inference

abstract: Consider the communication-constrained problem of nonparametric function estimation, in which each distributed terminal holds multiple i.i.d. samples. Under certain regularity assumptions, we characterize the minimax optimal rates for all regimes, and identify phase transitions of the optimal rates as the samples per terminal vary from sparse to dense. This fully solves the problem left open by previous works, whose scopes are limited to regimes with either dense samples or a single sample per terminal. To achieve the optimal rates, we design a layered estimation protocol by exploiting protocols for the parametric density estimation problem. We show the optimality of the protocol using information-theoretic methods and strong data processing inequalities, and incorporating the classic balls and bins model. The optimal rates are immediate for various special cases such as density estimation, Gaussian, binary, Poisson and heteroskedastic regression models.

paragraphs: This paper studies function estimation when data are spread across terminals that can communicate only a limited amount. Each terminal holds multiple independent, identically distributed samples. Under specified regularity assumptions, the authors characterize the best possible worst-case estimation rates across the full range from few samples per terminal to many.

The analysis identifies phase transitions: the form of the optimal rate changes as the number of samples at each terminal increases. This connects regimes that earlier work had treated only at the extremes, with either one sample or dense local samples. It clarifies how local data availability interacts with communication limits in determining achievable statistical accuracy.

To reach these rates, the authors construct a layered estimation protocol using components from parametric density estimation. They prove optimality through information-theoretic arguments, strong data processing inequalities, and the balls-and-bins model. The results also yield rates for density estimation and Gaussian, binary, Poisson, and heteroskedastic regression. The contribution is therefore both a matching protocol and a characterization of the limits it attains.
summary.tldr: Under regularity assumptions, the paper establishes optimal communication-constrained estimation rates across sparse and dense local sample regimes.

title: Distributed Nonparametric Estimation: from Sparse to Dense Samples per Terminal

abstract: Performative prediction captures the phenomenon where deploying a predictive model shifts the underlying data distribution. While simple retraining dynamics are known to converge linearly when the performative effects are weak ($\rho < 1$), the complexity in the regime $\rho > 1$ was hitherto open. In this paper, we establish a sharp phase transition: computing an $\epsilon$-performatively stable point is PPAD-complete—and thus polynomial-time equivalent to Nash equilibria in general-sum games—even when $\rho = 1 + O(\epsilon)$. This intractability persists even in the ostensibly simple setting with a quadratic loss function and linear distribution shifts. One of our key technical contributions is to extend this PPAD-hardness result to general convex domains, which is of broader interest in the complexity of variational inequalities. Finally, we address the special case of strategic classification, showing that computing a strategic local optimum is PLS-hard.

paragraphs: In performative prediction, deploying a model changes the data distribution on which it will subsequently operate. Simple retraining is known to converge linearly when these feedback effects are weak. This paper studies the computational difficulty once the feedback-strength parameter crosses above one, where the general complexity had remained unresolved.

The authors prove that finding an approximately performatively stable point is PPAD-complete, placing it in the same polynomial-time complexity class as computing Nash equilibria in general-sum games. The hardness appears even when feedback exceeds the threshold by only an amount proportional to the approximation tolerance. It also persists with quadratic losses and linear distribution shifts.

For strategic classification, the authors additionally show that finding a strategic local optimum is PLS-hard. These are worst-case computational barriers: even simple-looking ingredients can produce difficult feedback problems, sharply separating the weak-feedback convergence regime from the regime just beyond its threshold.
summary.tldr: Computing approximate performative stability becomes PPAD-complete just beyond the weak-feedback regime, even with quadratic losses and linear shifts.

title: On the Computational Complexity of Performative Prediction

abstract: State-space models (SSMs) offer efficient sequence modeling but lag behind Transformers on benchmarks that require in-context retrieval. Prior work links this gap to a small set of attention heads, termed Gather-and-Aggregate (G&A), which SSMs struggle to reproduce. We propose retrieval-aware distillation, which converts a pretrained Transformer into a hybrid student by preserving only these retrieval-critical heads and distilling the rest into recurrent heads. We identify the essential heads via ablation on a synthetic retrieval task, producing a hybrid with sparse, non-uniform attention placement. We show that preserving just 2% of attention heads recovers over 95% of teacher performance on retrieval-heavy tasks (10 heads in a 1B model), requiring far fewer heads than hybrids that retain at least 25%. We further find that large recurrent states often compensate for missing retrieval: once retrieval is handled by these heads, the SSM backbone can be simplified with limited loss, even with an 8$\times$ reduction in state dimension. By reducing both the attention cache and the SSM state, the resulting hybrid is 5–6$\times$ more memory-efficient than comparable hybrids, closing the Transformer–SSM gap at a fraction of the memory cost.

summary.tldr: Preserving a small set of retrieval-critical attention heads enables distilled Transformer–SSM hybrids with strong retrieval performance and lower memory use.

title: Retrieval-Aware Distillation for Transformer-SSM Hybrids

abstract: Generative Graph Language Models (GLMs) must reconcile topology with causal language modeling. Linearization obscures multi-hop connectivity, while encoder-based methods bottleneck token-level reasoning during generation. Viewing context modeling as a form of message passing, we introduce Weaver, an encoder-free framework that extends the attention mechanism of decoder-only LLMs to enable graph reasoning. Weaver maps graph distances into rotary positional embeddings so that structurally connected nodes become proximate in attention space, propagating information over graph topology as if it were sequential context. To achieve this, we combine: 1) a masking mechanism for causal tokens with graph structures; 2) a unified geometric encoding that couples sequential position and graph distance in joint rotary embeddings (Graph-over-Tokens RoPE); and 3) a design principle to prioritize local information to resolve positional ambiguity under graph symmetries. On zero-shot benchmarks, Weaver achieves state-of-the-art performance among generative GLMs, with gains of up to 30% over prior generative methods on heterophilic graphs, while matching specialized discriminative models on citation networks—all within a unified decoder-only framework.

Flattening a graph into a sequence can hide multi-hop relationships, while separate graph encoders can restrict token-level reasoning during generation. Weaver integrates graph structure directly into the attention mechanism of a decoder-only language model.

These findings support encoding topology within decoder attention as a way to combine graph reasoning and language generation in one framework without a separate encoder.
summary.tldr: Weaver embeds graph distances into decoder attention to support graph reasoning directly within a generative language model.

title: Weaving Graph over Tokens: Contextualizing Structured Sequences for LLMs

abstract: Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) have achieved remarkable progress across various capabilities; however, complex video reasoning in the scientific domain remains a significant and challenging frontier. Current video benchmarks predominantly target general scenarios where perception/recognition is heavily relied on, while with relatively simple reasoning tasks, leading to saturation and thus failing to effectively evaluate advanced multimodal cognitive skills. To address this critical gap, we introduce SciVideoBench, a rigorous benchmark specifically designed to assess advanced video reasoning in scientific contexts. SciVideoBench consists of 1,000 carefully crafted multiple-choice questions derived from cutting-edge scientific experimental videos spanning over 25 specialized academic subjects and verified by a semi- automatic system. Each question demands sophisticated domain-specific knowledge, precise spatiotemporal perception, and intricate logical reasoning, effectively challenging models’ higher-order cognitive abilities. Our evaluation highlights significant performance deficits in state-of-the-art proprietary and open-source LMMs, including Gemini 2.5 Pro and Qwen2.5-VL, indicating substantial room for advancement in video reasoning capabilities. Detailed analyses of critical factors such as reasoning complexity and visual grounding provide valuable insights and clear direction for future developments in LMMs, driving the evolution of truly capable multimodal AI co-scientists. We hope SciVideoBench could fit the interests of the community and help to push the boundary of cutting-edge AI for border science.

Our evaluation highlights significant performance deficits in state-of-the-art proprietary and open-source LMMs, including Gemini 2.5 Pro and Qwen2.5-VL, indicating substantial room for advancement in video reasoning capabilities. Detailed analyses of critical factors such as reasoning complexity and visual grounding provide valuable insights and clear direction for future developments in LMMs, driving the evolution of truly capable multimodal AI co-scientists. We hope SciVideoBench could fit the interests of the community and help to push the boundary of cutting-edge AI for border science.

paragraphs: SciVideoBench evaluates whether multimodal models can reason about scientific experimental videos. The paper argues that general video benchmarks rely heavily on recognition and relatively simple reasoning, allowing performance to saturate without adequately testing more demanding abilities. Scientific experiments provide a setting where understanding what appears on screen must connect to specialized knowledge.

The benchmark contains 1,000 multiple-choice questions drawn from experimental videos across more than 25 academic subjects and checked with a semi-automatic verification system. Its questions require domain knowledge, precise perception of spatial and temporal relationships, and complex logical reasoning. This combination makes the task depend on both scientific understanding and evidence in the video.

Evaluations of proprietary and open-source models, including Gemini 2.5 Pro and Qwen2.5-VL, reveal substantial performance deficits. Analyses examine factors such as reasoning complexity and visual grounding to help explain the difficulty. The benchmark supplies a more demanding test of scientific video reasoning and identifies capabilities that still need improvement in the evaluated models.
summary.tldr: SciVideoBench uses scientific experiment videos to expose gaps in multimodal models' domain knowledge, visual grounding, and complex reasoning.

title: SciVideoBench: Benchmarking Scientific Video Reasoning in Large Multimodal Models

abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown remarkable promise in robotics manipulation, yet their high computational cost hinders real-time deployment. Existing token pruning methods suffer from a fundamental trade-off: aggressive compression using pruning inevitably discards critical geometric details like contact points, leading to severe performance degradation. This forces a compromise, limiting the achievable compression rate and thus the potential speedup. We argue that breaking this trade-off requires rethinking compression as a geometry-aware, continuous token resampling in the vision encoder. To this end, we propose the Differentiable Grid Sampler (GridS), a plug-and-play module that performs task-aware, continuous resampling of visual tokens in VLA. By adaptively predicting a minimal set of salient coordinates and extracting features via differentiable interpolation, GridS preserves essential spatial information while achieving drastic compression (with fewer than 10% original visual tokens). Experiments on both LIBERO benchmark and a real robotic platform demonstrate that validating the lowest feasible visual token count reported to date, GridS achieves a 76% reduction in FLOPs with no degradation in the success rate. The code is available at https://github.com/Fediory/Grid-Sampler.

paragraphs: Vision-language-action models can support robotic manipulation, but processing many visual tokens makes real-time use expensive. Simply discarding tokens can remove small geometric details, including contact points that matter for an action. This paper approaches compression as continuous resampling of visual information inside the vision encoder.

The Differentiable Grid Sampler, or GridS, predicts a small set of task-relevant coordinates and extracts their features through differentiable interpolation. This lets the module gather information at selected spatial locations instead of relying only on keeping or deleting existing tokens. Its purpose is to preserve essential geometry while reducing the visual representation to fewer than 10% of the original tokens.

Experiments on LIBERO and a real robotic platform report a 76% reduction in floating-point operations without a reduction in task success rate. These findings support geometry-aware resampling as a way to compress the visual input aggressively while retaining useful action information. The reported efficiency measure is computational work, and the unchanged success rate is an empirical result from the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: GridS continuously resamples task-relevant visual features, using fewer than 10% of visual tokens with a reported 76% FLOP reduction and unchanged success rate.

title: See What Matters: Differentiable Grid Sample Pruning for Generalizable Vision-Language-Action Model

abstract: Transformer-based multimodal large language models often exhibit in-context learning (ICL) capabilities. Motivated by this phenomenon, we ask: how do transformers learn to associate information across modalities from in-context examples? We investigate this through controlled experiments on small transformers trained on synthetic classification tasks, enabling precise manipulation of data statistics and model architecture. We begin by revisiting core principles of unimodal ICL in modern transformers. While several prior findings replicate, we find that Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) can delay the onset of ICL circuits. Extending to the multimodal setting reveals a fundamental learning asymmetry: when pretrained on high-diversity data from a primary modality, surprisingly low data complexity in the secondary modality suffices for multimodal ICL to emerge. Mechanistic analysis shows that both settings rely on an induction-style mechanism that copies labels from matching in-context exemplars; multimodal training refines and extends these circuits across modalities. Our findings provide a mechanistic foundation for understanding multimodal ICL in modern transformers and introduce a controlled testbed for future investigation. Code is available at: https://github.com/YiranHuangIrene/multimodal-icl

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a model use examples in its input to perform a task. This paper investigates how transformers acquire that ability across modalities using small models trained on synthetic classification problems. The controlled setting lets the authors manipulate both data statistics and architecture while examining the internal mechanisms that emerge.

The study first revisits learning within a single modality. Several earlier findings replicate, but rotary position embeddings can delay the emergence of in-context learning circuits. Moving to multiple modalities reveals an asymmetry: after pretraining on highly diverse data from a primary modality, relatively low complexity in a secondary modality is sufficient for multimodal in-context learning to appear in the studied setting.

Mechanistic analysis identifies an induction-style process that copies labels from matching examples in the context. Multimodal training refines and extends this mechanism across modalities. These results connect observed learning behavior to specific circuit dynamics and provide a controlled experimental setting for further study. Their scope is the small synthetic-task transformers examined, rather than a direct demonstration across all multimodal language models.
summary.tldr: Controlled transformer experiments reveal asymmetric data requirements for multimodal in-context learning and trace it to circuits that copy labels from matching examples.

title: Dissecting Multimodal In-Context Learning: Modality Asymmetries and Circuit Dynamics in modern Transformers

abstract: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in long-horizon, complex environments to solve challenging problems, but this expansion exposes them to long-horizon attacks that exploit multi-turn user–agent–environment interactions to achieve objectives infeasible in single-turn settings. To measure agent vulnerabilities to such risks, we present AgentLAB, the first benchmark dedicated to evaluating LLM agent susceptibility to adaptive, long-horizon attacks. Currently, AgentLAB supports five novel attack types including intent hijacking, tool chaining, task injection, objective drifting, and memory poisoning, spanning 28 realistic agentic environments, and 644 security test cases. Leveraging AgentLAB, we evaluate representative LLM agents and find that they remain highly susceptible to long-horizon attacks; moreover, defenses designed for single-turn interactions fail to reliably mitigate long-horizon threats. We anticipate that AgentLAB will serve as a valuable benchmark for tracking progress on securing LLM agents in practical settings. The code for AgentLAB is available at: https://tanqiujiang.github.io/AgentLAB_main.

paragraphs: AgentLAB examines security failures that develop across extended interactions between a user, an agent, and its environment. These attacks can pursue objectives that are infeasible within a single exchange. The paper therefore treats the full interaction sequence as the unit of evaluation, reflecting how agents operate while solving complex tasks.

The benchmark covers five attack types: intent hijacking, tool chaining, task injection, objective drifting, and memory poisoning. It contains 644 security test cases across 28 realistic agent environments. This breadth lets researchers evaluate several ways an adversary can exploit an agent over time, including changes to its objectives and stored information.

Evaluations of representative agents find substantial susceptibility to these adaptive attacks. Defenses developed for single-turn interactions also fail to reliably mitigate the longer attacks. The findings show why performance on isolated safety checks provides an incomplete assessment of agent security. AgentLAB supplies a common evaluation framework for measuring whether future defenses remain effective throughout an extended task.
summary.tldr: AgentLAB tests attacks that unfold across extended agent interactions and finds that evaluated agents and single-turn defenses remain vulnerable.

title: AgentLAB: Benchmarking LLM Agents against Long-Horizon Attacks

abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in high-level visual understanding. However, extending these models to fine-grained dense prediction tasks, such as semantic segmentation and depth estimation, typically necessitates the incorporation of complex, task-specific decoders and other customizations. This architectural fragmentation increases model complexity and deviates from the generalist design of MLLMs, ultimately limiting their practicality. In this work, we challenge this paradigm by accommodating standard MLLMs to perform dense predictions without requiring additional task-specific decoders. The proposed model is called DenseMLLM, grounded in the standard architecture with a novel vision token supervision strategy for multiple labels and tasks. Despite its minimalist design, our model achieves highly competitive performance across a wide range of dense prediction and vision-language benchmarks, demonstrating that a standard, general-purpose MLLM can effectively support dense perception without architectural specialization. This project is available at github.com/Eli-YiLi/DenseMLLM.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models are strong at high-level visual understanding, but dense prediction asks for detailed information throughout an image. Semantic segmentation and depth estimation are examples. Existing approaches often add specialized decoders for these tasks, increasing architectural complexity and moving the model away from a shared, general-purpose design.

DenseMLLM investigates whether a standard multimodal language model can support these predictions without additional task-specific decoders. Its main change is a vision-token supervision strategy that accommodates multiple labels and tasks. The method therefore places the adaptation in how visual tokens are trained, while grounding the model in the standard architecture.

The authors report highly competitive results across a broad range of dense prediction and vision-language benchmarks. These findings demonstrate that the proposed training approach can support detailed perception alongside broader multimodal capabilities. The significance is architectural simplicity: the reported performance comes from adapting a general-purpose model’s supervision, reducing the need to introduce a separate specialized decoding structure for dense tasks.
summary.tldr: DenseMLLM uses vision-token supervision to enable competitive dense prediction in a standard multimodal language model without task-specific decoders.

title: DenseMLLM: Standard Multimodal LLMs for Dense Prediction

abstract: Cross-modal 2D–3D gait recognition is impeded by inherent domain discrepancies between 2D silhouette and 3D point cloud distributions. While prior methods align only final embeddings, we propose DiffCrossGait, which enforces trajectory-level alignment by driving both modalities with shared noise in a unified latent diffusion process. By driving both modalities with shared Gaussian noise within a latent space, we enable continuous alignment throughout the generative evolution. We introduce a Tri-Phase Alignment Strategy that exploits varying noise intensities to enforce identity anchoring, dynamics consistency, and cross-modal structural recoverability, thereby constraining both modalities to share denoising dynamics and bottleneck structure, which promotes modality-invariant gait features. Crucially, our framework decouples generative alignment from the discriminative backbone; the diffusion mechanism serves exclusively as a training objective, ensuring high inference efficiency by eliminating the computational overhead of iterative denoising. Extensive experiments on the SUSTech1K and FreeGait benchmarks demonstrate that DiffCrossGait achieves state-of-the-art performance.

Crucially, our framework decouples generative alignment from the discriminative backbone; the diffusion mechanism serves exclusively as a training objective, ensuring high inference efficiency by eliminating the computational overhead of iterative denoising. paragraphs: DiffCrossGait tackles gait recognition across two different representations: two-dimensional silhouettes and three-dimensional point clouds. Their distributions differ, making it difficult to learn identity features that work across both. The paper extends alignment beyond the final feature vectors by also constraining how the two modalities evolve during a latent diffusion process.

Both modalities receive shared Gaussian noise in a common latent space. A three-phase strategy uses different noise intensities to anchor identity, encourage consistent dynamics, and support recovery of structure across modalities. This creates alignment throughout denoising, encouraging the representations to share both their evolution and their compressed internal structure. The intended result is gait information that depends less on the sensing modality.

The diffusion component is used only as a training objective and is separated from the recognition backbone. Recognition therefore does not require repeated denoising at inference time. The authors report state-of-the-art performance on SUSTech1K and FreeGait. These findings support using richer generative alignment during training while retaining an efficient recognition procedure when the model is deployed.
summary.tldr: DiffCrossGait aligns silhouette and point-cloud gait features throughout diffusion training without adding iterative denoising at inference.

title: DiffCrossGait: Trajectory-Level Alignment for 2D-3D Cross-Modal Gait Recognition via Latent Diffusion

abstract: Biophysically detailed neural networks represent a promising frontier for brain-inspired AI, offering intrinsic spatio-temporal dynamics to enhance the expressivity and computational density of deep learning systems. However, general-purpose deep learning frameworks suffer from a fundamental mismatch between their dense parallel optimizations and the irregular, tree-structured complexity of biological mechanisms. In this work, we propose HelioX, a GPU-native framework designed to unify high-performance simulation with scalable training. Unlike approaches that adapt biology to existing deep learning tools, HelioX adopts a “GPU-to-Biophysics” paradigm. We tailor the underlying GPU parallelism to biological structures by implementing custom-fused CUDA kernels for both the Dendritic Hierarchical Scheduling (DHS) algorithm and its gradient propagation. This design eliminates the runtime overhead of generic automatic differentiation and enables multi-stream concurrency for spike generation and equation assembly. Experimental results demonstrate that HelioX outperforms standard simulators (NEURON) by orders of magnitude and surpasses prior GPU-based solvers in both speed and scalability. We successfully train deep biophysical MLPs and whole-brain-scale biophysical circuits (e.g., the BAAIWorm C. elegans model) on a single consumer-grade GPU. HelioX establishes a new standard for computational efficiency, enabling the training of biophysically detailed models at scales previously unattainable.

paragraphs: Biophysically detailed neural models have irregular, tree-shaped computational structures that fit poorly with the dense operations favored by general deep-learning frameworks. HelioX tackles this mismatch by designing GPU execution around biological structure, with the aim of making both simulation and training efficient.

summary.tldr: HelioX uses biology-aware GPU kernels to accelerate detailed neural simulation and enable large biophysical models to train on a single consumer GPU.

title: HelioX: A GPU-Native Framework for Simulation and Training of Biophysically Detailed Networks

abstract: Medical workflows routinely combine reading images with producing visual and textual outputs, making both image understanding and generation central to medical AI. Most existing systems, however, address these abilities in isolated models, losing the shared knowledge that a unified architecture could exploit. To bridge this gap, we present UniMedVL, the first unified medical model that seamlessly integrates multimodal understanding and generation capabilities within a single model without switching weights. We achieve this via a tailored progressive training pipeline where understanding and generation mutually reinforce each other. To effectively train UniMedVL, we curate UniMedVL-5M, the first large-scale medical dataset comprising over 5.6M instances across 8 medical imaging modalities, tailored for multimodal input-output tasks in unified medical understanding and generation. Experimental results demonstrate that UniMedVL achieves competitive performance on five medical understanding benchmarks. Crucially, UniMedVL natively supports diverse interleaved generation tasks, e.g., virtual staining, super-resolution, cross-modal synthesis, essential for complex medical workflows. Our code and dataset are publicly available.

paragraphs: Medical workflows can require both interpreting images and producing new visual or textual outputs. When separate models handle these abilities, they cannot fully share the knowledge a unified architecture could use. UniMedVL combines multimodal understanding and generation in one model that performs these roles without switching weights.

The model uses a progressive training pipeline designed for understanding and generation to reinforce each other. title: UniMedVL: Unifying Medical Multimodal Understanding and Generation through Observation-Knowledge-Analysis

abstract: Automatic differentiation (AD) frameworks such as JAX and PyTorch have enabled gradient-based optimization for a wide range of scientific fields. Yet, many ”hard” primitives in these libraries such as thresholding, Boolean logic, discrete indexing, and sorting operations yield zero or undefined gradients that are not useful for optimization. While numerous ”soft” relaxations have been proposed that provide informative gradients, the respective implementations are fragmented across projects, making them difficult to combine and compare. This work introduces SoftJAX and SoftTorch, open-source, feature-complete libraries for soft differentiable programming. These libraries provide a variety of soft functions as drop-in replacements for their hard JAX and PyTorch counterparts. This includes (i) elementwise operators such as clip or abs, (ii) utility methods for manipulating Booleans and indices via fuzzy logic, (iii) axiswise operators such as sort or rank – based on optimal transport or permutahedron projections, and (iv) offer full support for straight-through gradient estimation. Overall, SoftJAX and SoftTorch make the toolbox of soft relaxations easily accessible to differentiable programming, as demonstrated through benchmarking and a practical case study. Code is available at github.com/a-paulus/softjax and github.com/a-paulus/softtorch.

paragraphs: Automatic differentiation makes gradient-based optimization convenient, but some operations provide little useful direction for learning. Thresholds, Boolean decisions, discrete indexing, and sorting can yield zero or undefined gradients. Smooth alternatives exist, yet their implementations are scattered across projects and can be difficult to combine or compare.

SoftJAX and SoftTorch collect these alternatives into libraries designed as replacements for corresponding JAX and PyTorch operations. They cover elementwise functions such as clipping and absolute value, fuzzy-logic utilities for Booleans and indices, and axiswise operations such as sorting and ranking. The latter include approaches based on optimal transport and permutahedron projections.

The libraries also fully support straight-through gradient estimation, expanding the available tools for optimization involving hard operations. Benchmarking and a practical case study demonstrate their use. The contribution is an integrated implementation toolkit: developers can access multiple relaxation techniques through familiar operations instead of assembling disconnected implementations. This makes soft differentiable programming easier to incorporate into workflows that otherwise contain uninformative gradients.
summary.tldr: SoftJAX and SoftTorch provide integrated soft replacements for hard operations that otherwise obstruct gradient-based optimization.

title: SoftJAX & SoftTorch: Empowering Automatic Differentiation Libraries with Informative Gradients

abstract: This paper studies the use of kernel density estimation (KDE) for linear algebraic tasks involving the kernel matrix of a collection of $n$ data points in $\mathbb{R}^d$. In particular, we improve upon the best existing algorithms for computing the following up to $(1+\varepsilon)$ relative error for a Gaussian kernel matrix and other kernels: matrix-vector products, matrix-matrix products, the spectral norm, and sum of all entries. The runtimes of our algorithms depend linearly on the dimension $d$, sub-quadratically in the number of points $n$, and polynomially on the target error $\varepsilon$. Importantly, the dependence on $n$ in each case is far lower when accessing the kernel matrix through KDE queries as opposed to reading individual entries. Our improvements over existing best algorithms (particularly those of [Backurs et al. ICML ‘21]) for these tasks reduce the polynomial dependence on $\varepsilon$, and additionally decrease the dependence on $n$ in the case of computing the sum of all entries of the kernel matrix. For example, we reduce the power of $1/\epsilon$ from $\approx 7.7$ to $\approx 3.2$ for a $1-\varepsilon$ relative error estimation of the spectral norm of a Gaussian kernel matrix. We complement our upper bounds with several lower bounds for related problems, which provide (conditional) quadratic time hardness results and additionally hint at the limits of KDE based approaches for the problems we study.

paragraphs: A kernel matrix records similarities between pairs of data points, so working through its entries can become expensive as the dataset grows. This paper develops approximate linear algebra algorithms that access such matrices through kernel density estimation queries. These queries provide a different route to information than reading individual matrix entries.

The algorithms improve matrix-vector products, matrix-matrix products, spectral-norm estimation, and estimation of the sum of all entries for Gaussian and other kernels. Their runtimes are linear in the input dimension and subquadratic in the number of points, with polynomial dependence on the requested accuracy. The improvements particularly reduce how quickly computational cost grows as tighter error tolerances are requested.

For Gaussian spectral-norm estimation, the reported exponent on inverse error decreases from about 7.7 to about 3.2. The entry-sum algorithm also improves dependence on dataset size. Alongside these upper bounds, the paper establishes lower bounds for related problems, including conditional quadratic-time hardness results. Those results help identify where density-estimation access may have limits despite its substantial algorithmic benefits.
summary.tldr: Kernel density estimation enables faster approximate kernel-matrix operations, especially by reducing their computational dependence on accuracy.

title: Even Faster Kernel Matrix Linear Algebra via Density Estimation

abstract: Electrostatic generative models such as PFGM++ have recently emerged as a powerful framework, achieving competitive performance in image synthesis. PFGM++ operates in an extended data space with auxiliary dimensionality $D$, recovering the diffusion model framework as $D\to\infty$, while yielding superior empirical results for finite $D$. Like diffusion models, PFGM++ relies on expensive ODE simulations to generate samples, making it computationally costly. To address this, we propose Inverse Poisson Flow Matching (IPFM), a principled distillation framework that accelerates electrostatic generative models across all values of $D$. Our IPFM reformulates distillation as an inverse problem: learning a generator whose induced electrostatic field matches that of the teacher. We derive a tractable training objective for this problem and show that, as $D\to\infty$, our IPFM closely recovers Score Identity Distillation (SiD), a recent method for distilling diffusion models. Empirically, our IPFM produces distilled generators that achieve near-teacher or even superior sample quality using only a few function evaluations. Moreover, we find that one-step generator distillation converges faster at finite $D$ than in the $D\to\infty$ diffusion limit, aligning with prior evidence that finite-$D$ PFGM++ models offer more favorable optimization and sampling behavior.
originalAbstract: Electrostatic generative models such as PFGM++ have recently emerged as a powerful framework, achieving competitive performance in image synthesis. PFGM++ operates in an extended data space with auxiliary dimensionality $D$, recovering the diffusion model framework as $D\to\infty$, while yielding superior empirical results for finite $D$. Like diffusion models, PFGM++ relies on expensive ODE simulations to generate samples, making it computationally costly. To address this, we propose Inverse Poisson Flow Matching (IPFM), a principled distillation framework that accelerates electrostatic generative models across all values of $D$. Our IPFM reformulates distillation as an inverse problem: learning a generator whose induced electrostatic field matches that of the teacher. We derive a tractable training objective for this problem and show that, as $D\to\infty$, our IPFM closely recovers Score Identity Distillation (SiD), a recent method for distilling diffusion models. Empirically, our IPFM produces distilled generators that achieve near-teacher or even superior sample quality using only a few function evaluations. Moreover, we find that one-step generator distillation converges faster at finite $D$ than in the $D\to\infty$ diffusion limit, aligning with prior evidence that finite-$D$ PFGM++ models offer more favorable optimization and sampling behavior.

paragraphs: Electrostatic generative models such as PFGM++ can produce competitive images but require costly differential-equation simulations during sampling. Their formulation adds an auxiliary dimension parameter, D, with diffusion recovered as D tends to infinity. This paper introduces Inverse Poisson Flow Matching to distill these models into generators requiring only a few function evaluations.

The method frames distillation as an inverse problem: learn a generator whose induced electrostatic field matches the teacher's field. The authors derive a tractable training objective that applies across values of D. In the infinite-dimensional limit, the formulation closely recovers Score Identity Distillation, connecting the proposed approach to an existing diffusion-distillation method.

Experiments show that the distilled generators can approach or exceed their teachers' sample quality with few evaluations. For one-step generation, training converges faster at finite D than in the diffusion limit. This finding aligns with the paper's motivation that finite-dimensional electrostatic models can have favorable optimization behavior, and shows that their advantages can extend to the process of learning accelerated generators.
summary.tldr: Inverse Poisson Flow Matching distills electrostatic generators into fast samplers that achieve near-teacher or better image quality.

title: Overclocking Electrostatic Generative Models

abstract: Domain transfer (DT) maps source to target distributions and supports tasks such as unsupervised image-to-image translation, single-cell analysis, and cross-platform medical imaging. However, DT is fundamentally ill-posed: push-forward mappings are generally non-identifiable, as measure-preserving automorphisms (MPAs) preserve marginals while altering cross-domain correspondences, leading to content-misaligned translation. Recent work shows that MPAs can be eliminated by jointly transferring multiple corresponding source/target conditional distributions, but supervision signals labeling such conditionals are not always available in practice. We develop an alternative route to DT identifiability. Under a structural sparsity condition on the Jacobian support pattern, we show that distribution matching together with a single paired anchor sample suffices to identify the ground-truth transfer—requiring substantially less supervision than prior approaches. To enable practical high-dimensional learning, we further propose an efficient Jacobian sparsity regularizer based on randomized masked finite differences, yielding a scalable surrogate without explicit Jacobian evaluation. Empirical results on synthetic and real-world DT tasks validate the theory.

paragraphs: Matching a source distribution to a target distribution does not generally determine which individual examples should correspond. Several transformations can preserve the same overall distribution while changing the content associations between domains. This paper studies how to remove that ambiguity with less paired supervision than approaches that align multiple corresponding conditional distributions.

The main result is conditional on a structural sparsity pattern in the transfer map's Jacobian, which describes how output coordinates depend on input coordinates. Under that condition, distribution matching plus a single paired anchor sample is sufficient to identify the ground-truth transfer. The anchor supplies a correspondence constraint, while the structural condition restricts the transformations that could otherwise fit the distributions.

To make this idea practical in high dimensions, the authors introduce a sparsity regularizer using randomized masked finite differences. It avoids explicitly evaluating the Jacobian and provides a scalable surrogate for the desired structure. Synthetic and real-world experiments support the theory. The result establishes when one alignment can suffice, rather than asserting that a single pair resolves arbitrary domain-transfer problems.
summary.tldr: Under a structural Jacobian sparsity condition, distribution matching and one paired example suffice to identify the ground-truth domain transfer.

title: Domain Transfer Becomes Identifiable via a Single Alignment

abstract: We study query time bounds for the fundamental problem of estimating the kernel mean $\frac1{|X|}\sum_{x\in X}\mathbf{\mathrm{k}}(x,y)$ of a query $y$ in a finite dataset $X\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ up to a prescribed additive error $\varepsilon$. The best known bounds for the Gaussian kernel are $O(d/\varepsilon^2)$, $\widetilde O(d+1/\varepsilon^4)$, and $\widetilde O(d+\Delta^2/\varepsilon^2)$, where $\Delta$ is the diameter of a region containing the points. We prove the new bound $\tilde O(d+\varepsilon\Delta^2+1/\varepsilon^3)$, which improves over the previous ones in regimes with small error $\varepsilon$ and intermediate diameter $\Delta$. At the center of our proof is a new fast spherical embedding theorem in the sense introduced by Bartal, Recht and Schulman (2011), which limits the embedded data diameter while preserving local Euclidean distances and avoiding “distance collapse” at larger scales. This fast embedding theorem may be of independent interest.

The best known bounds for the Gaussian kernel are $O(d/\varepsilon^2)$, $\widetilde O(d+1/\varepsilon^4)$, and $\widetilde O(d+\Delta^2/\varepsilon^2)$, where $\Delta$ is the diameter of a region containing the points. We prove the new bound $\tilde O(d+\varepsilon\Delta^2+1/\varepsilon^3)$, which improves over the previous ones in regimes with small error $\varepsilon$ and intermediate diameter $\Delta$. paragraphs: A kernel mean measures the average kernel similarity between a query and points in a dataset. This paper studies how quickly that average can be estimated within a specified additive error. For the Gaussian kernel, the computational bounds depend on the data dimension, the required accuracy, and the diameter of a region containing the points.

The authors prove a query-time bound of approximately d + εΔ² + 1/ε³, suppressing logarithmic factors, where d is dimension, ε is allowed error, and Δ is diameter. This improves previous bounds in regimes combining small error with intermediate diameter. The improvement is therefore sensitive to the relationship between accuracy and geometry, rather than being an unconditional replacement for every previous bound.

The proof introduces a fast spherical embedding that limits the embedded dataset’s diameter while preserving nearby Euclidean distances and preventing far-apart points from collapsing together. Those properties let the analysis reshape the geometry without destroying essential distance information. Beyond the kernel-mean result, the authors suggest that the embedding theorem may have independent value.
summary.tldr: A fast spherical embedding yields a better Gaussian kernel-mean query bound for small-error, intermediate-diameter regimes.

title: New Bounds for Kernel Sums via Fast Spherical Embeddings

abstract: Agentic multimodal models have garnered significant attention for their ability to leverage external tools to tackle complex tasks. However, it is observed that such agents often meet premature interaction collapse, caused by two primary reasons: 1) the terminal reward often appending on the last token prevents the advantage from distinguishing trajectories with exploratory behavior; 2) excessively redundant context hinders the agent from absorbing useful feedback. To address these issues, we propose the Deepening Reasoning MMSearchAgent, the framework leverages the structural proximity to derive advantage signals from the whole rollout trajectories in an entire batch, such that trajectories of different lengths are further encouraged to be generated, even when containing the same correct answer. Additionally, differentiated gaussian rewards are employed to dynamically calibrate interaction tolerance, thereby ensuring information reliability and reducing redundancy. To support multi-turn interaction training, we have constructed a multi-step deep-reasoning dataset including 3602 high-quality QA pairs with at least 3 reasoning steps. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming the MMSearch-R1 by 8.4% on FVQA-test.

paragraphs: Multimodal search agents can stop interacting before they have explored enough to solve a task well. The authors identify two contributing problems: rewards concentrated at the end fail to distinguish useful exploratory behavior, and redundant context makes feedback harder to absorb. DR-MMSearchAgent changes training signals to address both issues.

The framework uses structural proximity among complete trajectories within a training batch to derive advantage signals. This encourages trajectories of different lengths, including cases where they reach the same correct answer. Differentiated Gaussian rewards dynamically adjust tolerance for interaction, with the stated goals of maintaining information reliability and reducing redundant material.

The authors also construct a training dataset containing 3,602 question-answer pairs, each requiring at least three reasoning steps. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance, including an 8.4% improvement over MMSearch-R1 on FVQA-test. The results support rewarding the structure of exploration alongside answer correctness, while managing the amount of information accumulated during multi-turn search.
summary.tldr: DR-MMSearchAgent changes trajectory-level rewards to encourage useful exploration and reduce redundancy, improving reported multimodal search performance.

title: DR-MMSearchAgent: Deepening Reasoning in Multimodal Search Agents

abstract: When the color distribution of input images changes at inference, the performance of conventional neural network architectures drops considerably. A few researchers have begun to incorporate prior knowledge of color geometry in neural network design. These color equivariant architectures have modeled hue variation with 2D rotations, and saturation and luminance transformations as 1D translations. While this approach improves neural network robustness to color variations in a number of contexts, we find that approximating saturation and luminance (interval valued quantities) as 1D translations introduces appreciable artifacts. In this paper, we introduce a color equivariant architecture that is truly equivariant. Instead of approximating the interval with the real line, we lift values on the interval to values on the circle (a double-cover) and build equivariant representations there. Our approach resolves the approximation artifacts of previous methods, improves interpretability and generalizability, and achieves better predictive performance than conventional and equivariant baselines on tasks such as fine-grained classification and medical imaging tasks. Going beyond the context of color, we show that our proposed lifting can also extend to geometric transformations such as scale.

paragraphs: A model can struggle when an image's colors differ from those seen during training. Color-equivariant architectures address this by making their internal representations transform predictably when colors change. This paper identifies a geometric problem in earlier designs: saturation and luminance occupy bounded intervals, but those designs treat changes in them as translations along an unbounded line.

The proposed architecture instead lifts each interval onto a circle using a double-cover construction. This gives the network a space in which it can build equivariant representations without the interval-to-line approximation. The central contribution is therefore a change in how color transformations are represented, resolving the artifacts attributed to the earlier geometry.

The authors report improved interpretability, generalization, and predictive performance compared with conventional and color-equivariant baselines on fine-grained classification and medical imaging tasks. They also show that the lifting construction can extend to geometric transformations such as scale. These findings connect the practical gains to a representation that respects the structure of the transformed quantities.
summary.tldr: A circle-based representation of bounded color quantities removes approximation artifacts and improves color-equivariant image models.

title: A Hypertoroidal Covering for Perfect Color Equivariance

abstract: Unified audio–visual generation is rapidly gaining industrial and creative relevance, enabling applications in virtual production and interactive media. However, when moving from general audio–video synthesis to music–dance co-generation, the task becomes substantially harder: musical rhythm, phrasing, and accents must drive choreographic motion at fine temporal resolution, and such rhythmic coupling is not captured by unimodal metrics or generic audiovisual consistency scores used in current evaluation practice. We introduce TMD-Bench, a benchmark for text-driven music–dance co-generation that assesses systems across unimodal generation quality, instruction adherence, and cross-modal rhythmic alignment. The benchmark integrates computable physical metrics with perceptual multimodal judgments, and is supported by a curated rhythm-aligned music–dance dataset and a fine-grained Music Captioner for structured music semantics. TMD-Bench further reveals that (i) modern commercial audio–visual models (e.g., Veo 3, Sora 2) produce high-quality music and video, while rhythmic coupling remains less consistently optimized and leaves room for improvement, and (ii) our unified baseline RhyJAM trained on rhythm-aligned data achieves competitive beat-level synchronization while maintaining competitive unimodal fidelity. This presents prospects for building next-generation music–dance models that explicitly optimize rhythmic and kinetic coherence. The code is available at https://github.com/MM-Speech/TMD-Bench.

paragraphs: Generating attractive music and convincing dance video does not ensure that the movement follows the music. Rhythm, phrasing, and accents need to connect with choreography at precise moments. TMD-Bench addresses this evaluation gap, which separate audio or video quality scores and generic audiovisual consistency measures do not adequately capture.

The benchmark evaluates text-driven music–dance generation along three dimensions: quality within each medium, adherence to instructions, and rhythmic alignment across music and motion. It combines computable physical measures with perceptual multimodal judgments. A curated dataset of rhythm-aligned music and dance supports the benchmark, alongside a Music Captioner that produces structured descriptions of musical meaning.

The evaluation finds that commercial audiovisual models such as Veo 3 and Sora 2 produce high-quality outputs while optimizing rhythmic coupling less consistently. The authors' unified baseline, RhyJAM, trained on rhythm-aligned data, achieves competitive beat synchronization and competitive quality in each medium. These findings highlight rhythmic coordination as a distinct target for both evaluation and model development.
summary.tldr: TMD-Bench evaluates whether jointly generated music and dance follow instructions, look and sound good, and synchronize rhythmically.

title: TMD-Bench: A Multi-Level Evaluation Paradigm for Music–Dance Co-Generation

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently generate output that contradicts explicit input evidence, limiting their reliability in real-world applications. We identify cognitive inertia in LLMs—a tendency to overly rely on co-occurrence associations learned during pretraining and to resist adaptation when conflicting input evidence appears—as a critical factor behind such hallucinations. We further empirically show that adherence to input evidence declines as co-occurrence associations are strengthened—driven by either higher data frequency or intensified training. Inspired by human counter-inertial thinking, we propose an adaptive counter-inertial reasoning framework that probes input-related cognitive inertia in the LLM and generates adaptive counter-inertial reminders, which are then injected into the prompt to promote evidence-based reasoning. Experiments on co-occurrence induction datasets show that LLMInertia reduces hallucination rates by up to 35% and improves accuracy by up to 35.68%. Extensive evaluations on four context-rich summarization and QA datasets, across three LLM backbones of varying scales, further validate its effectiveness and robustness. Our work provides new insight into the causes of input-unfaithful hallucinations in LLMs, contributing to the development of more reliable AI.

paragraphs: Language models sometimes contradict explicit evidence in their input. This paper identifies cognitive inertia as an important contributor: associations learned during pretraining can remain influential even when the current evidence conflicts with them. Empirically, the authors find that evidence adherence decreases as co-occurrence associations strengthen through higher data frequency or more intensive training.

LLMInertia addresses this behavior through adaptive prompting. The framework probes the model's inertia related to the current input, then generates reminders intended to counter the detected tendency. These reminders are inserted into the prompt to encourage reasoning grounded in the supplied evidence. The intervention therefore responds to the particular input rather than using only a fixed reminder.

On co-occurrence induction datasets, the method reduces hallucination rates by up to 35% and improves accuracy by up to 35.68%. Evaluations on four context-rich summarization and question-answering datasets, using three model backbones of varying sizes, further support its effectiveness and robustness. The findings connect a measurable source of evidence resistance with a prompt-based way to reduce it.
summary.tldr: LLMInertia probes learned associations that conflict with input evidence and adds adaptive reminders to improve evidence-faithful reasoning.

title: LLMInertia: Adaptive Counter-Inertial Reasoning to Improve Evidence Faithfulness in Large Language Models

abstract: We argue that many Anthropomorphic Misalignment Research (AMR) studies need stronger evidence to ensure that they can provide a robust foundation for critical safety decisions, such as model deployment and regulation. By evaluating failure modes across different misalignment concepts, such as deception, emergent misalignment, and sycophancy, we show how conceptual ambiguity, non-robust datasets, experimental design, and insufficient causal interventions can lead to overinterpretation of model behaviors. This position paper aims to offer guidance on evidentiary considerations that can help improve methodological rigor in AMR. To achieve this, we provide a clear call to action through a proposed framework of evidence levels and a diagnostic checklist. These shared standards will enable more productive scientific discourse and ensure that claims about AI risks rest on solid empirical foundations.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that many studies of anthropomorphic misalignment need stronger evidence before they can reliably inform deployment or regulation. It examines research involving concepts such as deception, emergent misalignment, and sycophancy. The concern is that observations of model behavior can be interpreted more strongly than the underlying evidence supports.

The authors evaluate several routes to that overinterpretation: unclear concepts, datasets that do not support robust conclusions, weaknesses in experimental design, and insufficient interventions to establish causes. These issues matter because recording a behavior and explaining why it occurred are different evidentiary achievements. Ambiguity in either the target concept or the experiment can blur that distinction.

The proposed response is a framework of evidence levels accompanied by a diagnostic checklist. These shared tools are intended to help researchers assess the support for their claims and communicate disagreements more productively. The contribution is methodological guidance for strengthening empirical foundations, with particular importance when interpretations of model behavior influence consequential safety decisions.
summary.tldr: Studies of deception and related AI behaviors need clearer concepts and stronger evidence to support consequential safety decisions.

abstract: Feature selection is the task of choosing a small set out of a given set offeatures that capture the relevant properties of the data. In the context ofsupervised classification problems the relevance is determined by the givenlabels on the training data. A good choice of features is a key for buildingcompact and accurate classifiers. In this paper we introduce a margin based feature selection criterion andapply it to measure the quality of sets of features. Using margins we devisenovel selection algorithms for multi-class classification problems and providetheoretical generalization bound. We also study the well known Reliefalgorithm and show that it resembles a gradient ascent over our margincriterion. We apply our new algorithm to various datasets and show that ournew Simba algorithm, which directly optimizes the margin, outperforms Relief.

paragraphs: Feature selection seeks a small collection of inputs that preserves information relevant to the training labels. The paper introduces a margin-based criterion for judging entire sets of features. This connects the selection problem to how well the chosen representation separates classes, with the aim of supporting compact and accurate classifiers.

Using this criterion, the authors develop feature-selection algorithms for multiclass problems and provide a theoretical generalization bound. They also examine Relief, an established selection algorithm, through the same framework. Their analysis shows that Relief resembles gradient ascent on the proposed margin criterion, giving an existing method an interpretation in terms of this objective.

The new Simba algorithm optimizes the margin directly. Experiments on various datasets show that it outperforms Relief in the reported evaluation. The paper therefore contributes both a way to assess feature sets and an algorithm guided by that assessment. The relationship to Relief helps explain the connection between the new objective and an existing approach, while the experiments support the benefit of direct optimization.
summary.tldr: A margin-based feature-set criterion leads to Simba, connects Relief to gradient ascent, and improves on Relief in the reported experiments.

title: Margin based feature selection - theory and algorithms

abstract: We present in this paper a novel approach for training deterministic auto-encoders. We show that by adding a well chosen penalty term to the classical reconstruction cost function, we can achieve results that equal or surpass those attained by other regularized auto-encoders as well as denoising auto-encoders on a range of datasets. This penalty term corresponds to the Frobenius norm of the Jacobian matrix of the encoder activations with respect to the input. We show that this penalty term results in a localized space contraction which in turn yields robust features on the activation layer. Furthermore, we show how this penalty term is related to both regularized auto-encoders and denoising auto-encoders and how it can be seen as a link between deterministic and non-deterministic auto-encoders. We find empirically that this penalty helps to carve a representation that better captures the local directions of variation dictated by the data, corresponding to a lower-dimensional non-linear manifold, while being more invariant to the vast majority of directions orthogonal to the manifold. Finally, we show that by using the learned features to initialize an MLP, we achieve state of the art classification error on a range of datasets, surpassing other methods of pre-training.

paragraphs: An auto-encoder learns features while trying to reconstruct its input. This paper adds a penalty that directly discourages the encoder's activations from changing too strongly when the input changes locally. The penalty uses the Frobenius norm of the encoder's Jacobian, a matrix describing the sensitivity of its activations to input changes.

The authors show that this penalty contracts the local representation space and produces robust features. Empirically, the representation better captures directions of variation associated with the data's lower-dimensional nonlinear manifold, while becoming more invariant to most directions orthogonal to it. This distinguishes preserving meaningful local variation from simply suppressing every possible change.

Across a range of datasets, the method matches or exceeds other regularized and denoising auto-encoders. The paper also explains connections between these approaches, positioning the penalty as a link between deterministic and nondeterministic auto-encoders. Using the learned features to initialize a multilayer perceptron yields state-of-the-art classification errors on the evaluated datasets and surpasses other pretraining methods.
summary.tldr: A sensitivity penalty helps auto-encoders learn locally robust features that improve classification when used for pretraining.
